Surah al-Qasas (The Narratives)

It is Meccan in its entirety according to what has been related from al-Hasan, ʿAtaʾ, Tawus and ʿIkrimah. Muqatil said: among it is Medinan material, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾. Al-Tabarani related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that these verses and the end of Surat al-Hadid were revealed concerning the companions of al-Najashi (the Negus) who came and witnessed the Battle of Uhud.

In another narration from him, may Allah be pleased with him, the aforementioned verse was revealed at al-Juhfah during the Prophet's departure for the Hijrah, ﷺ. It has also been said that it was revealed between Makkah and al-Juhfah. Al-Madaʾini said in the book al-ʿAdad: Muhammad narrated to me, ʿAbd Allah narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said:

ʿAli ibn al-Husayn narrated to me from Ahmad ibn Musa from Yahya ibn Sallam, who said: It reached me that "when the Prophet ﷺ migrated, Jibril, peace be upon him, descended upon him at al-Juhfah while he was heading from Makkah to Madinah, and said: Do you long, O Muhammad, for your land in which you were born? He said: Yes. He said: Indeed He who imposed the Qur'an upon you will surely return you to a place of return," the verse. It has 88 verses by consensus. The reason for its connection with what precedes it is that it includes an explanation of some of what was stated in summary concerning the affair of Musa, peace be upon him.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: When He, glory be to Him, related in al-Shuʿara' the saying of Pharaoh to Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life?﴾ ﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾, up to the saying of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you, then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me among the messengers﴾. Then He, glory be to Him, related in Ta-Sin (Surat al-Naml) the saying of Musa, peace be upon him, to his family: ﴿Indeed I have perceived a fire﴾, up to its end, which is in sequence after the flight. Both matters were in the manner of allusion and summary. So He, majestic and exalted, expanded in this surah what He had abbreviated in the two surahs, and detailed, exalted is His affair, what He had summarized in them, in accordance with their order. He, mighty and majestic, began with explaining Pharaoh's upbringing of him, prefacing it with the cause of that, namely Pharaoh's haughtiness and the slaughter of the sons of the Children of Israel, which necessitated placing Musa, peace be upon him, in the river at his birth out of fear of his being slaughtered. He expanded the story of his upbringing and what occurred in it until his adulthood, to the cause for which he killed the Qibti, to the killing of the Qibti, which is the deed he did, to the accusation against him because of that which necessitated his flight to Madyan, to what happened to him with Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, and his marriage to his daughter, until he set out with his family and perceived a fire from the side of the Mount, and said to his family: "Wait, indeed I have perceived a fire," up to what happened to him there of intimate discourse with his Lord, majestic is His majesty, and His sending him as a messenger, and what followed from that, up to the end of the story. Thus this surah was an explanation of what had been summarized in the two surahs together, in order. By this the wisdom of placing Ta-Sin before this surah and its being placed after al-Shuʿara' in the mushaf is known, and likewise in revelation, for it has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Jabir ibn Zayd that al-Shuʿara' was revealed, then Ta-Sin, then al-Qasas. Also, He, glory be to Him, mentioned in the previous surah the rebuke of the disbelievers by questioning on the Day of Resurrection what was mentioned, and He, majestic is His affair, mentioned in this one from that what is more expansive and more than what preceded. Also, He, mighty and majestic, mentioned here about the matter of the night and the day more than what He mentioned of it there. It may also be said regarding the connection: He, exalted, detailed in that surah the conditions of some of the destroyed peoples of Salih and the people of Lut, and summarized here in His saying, exalted: ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed﴾ and the verses. Also, He generally expanded there on the condition of the one who brings a good deed and the condition of the one who brings an evil deed, and He, glory be to Him, abbreviated here where He, exalted, said: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and whoever comes with an evil deed, those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except for what they used to do﴾. So He, mighty and majestic, did not mention the security of the first from terror, nor the second's being thrown on their faces into the Fire, among other things that appear to the reflecting person.

﴿Ta-Sin-Mim﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾. What pertains to it has already been discussed in similar places. ﴿We recite to you﴾, i.e., We read through the intermediary of Jibril, peace be upon him, so the attribution is metaphorical, as in "the governor built the city." Recitation (tilawah) in their speech, according to what al-Raghib said, is specific to following the revealed books of Allah, exalted, sometimes by reading and sometimes by impression of what it contains of command, prohibition, encouragement and warning, or what is imagined to contain that; and it is more specific than reading (qira'ah). It is permissible that recitation here be a metonymy (majaz mursal) for revelation (tanzil), with the relation that revelation is necessary to it or is its cause in general, and that it be a metaphor for it because of the resemblance between them, as each of them is a means of conveying. So the meaning is: We send down to you ﴿some of the news of Musa and Pharaoh﴾, i.e., of their wondrous account. The prepositional phrase is related to a deleted element that is a qualifier of the deleted object of "We recite," i.e., We recite something that is from their news.

The apparent reading is that "min" is partitive. Some allowed that it is explicative and that it is extra (silah) according to the view of al-Akhfash, so that "naba'" is genitive in form and accusative in position as the object of "We recite." The speech of some implies that "min" is the object, as if it were said: "We recite some of the news." There is discussion on this, and in any case it is not permissible for the news to be recited, since it is a type of utterance. His saying, exalted: ﴿with truth﴾ is related to a deleted element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "We recite," i.e., We recite while bound up with truth; or its object, i.e., We recite something of their news bound up with truth; or it is a qualifier of the verbal noun of "We recite," i.e., We recite a recitation bound up with truth. His saying, exalted: ﴿for a people who believe﴾ is related to "We recite," and the "la" is causal. The specification of the believers by mention, despite the generality of the call and the exposition, is because they are the ones who benefit from it. The discussion of the inclusion of "yu'minun" for believers in the present and future has already been mentioned in the previous surah.

The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*, a new sentence that follows on from what precedes it) that functions as an explanation of the general matter that was promised. It opens with the emphatic particle *inna* to give emphasis to the reality of what follows. The meaning is: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh﴾ acted arrogantly and transgressed in the land of Egypt, and went beyond the usual limits in wrongdoing and aggression. ﴿And he made its people into factions (*shiya*)﴾, that is, into groups that back him in everything he wills of evil and corruption; or, some of them back one another in obeying him; or, into categories for his service, each category being employed in a task of building, tilling, digging and other laborious works, and whoever did not work, he imposed the poll-tax (*jizya*) on him, so that he serves him by paying it; or, into different groups that he had set against one another with enmity and hatred, so that their word would not be united. ﴿He oppresses a group of them﴾, that is, he makes them weak and subjugated. The intended "group" here is the Children of Israel, and he counted them among its people for the sake of predominance (*taghlib*), or because they had been among them for a long time. The clause may be either a grammatical resumptive clause or an explanatory one, answering the question "what did he do after that?"; or it may be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the subject or the object of *ja'ala*; or it may be a qualifying clause (*sifa*) for *shiya*. The use of the present tense is to narrate a past situation vividly. The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He slaughters their sons and spares their women﴾ is either a substitution (*badal*) for the clause before it, a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*), or an explanation, or a circumstantial clause relating to the subject of *yastad'if*, or a qualifying clause for *ta'ifa*, or a circumstantial clause from it, since it is specified by the description. That practice on his part was because a soothsayer (*kahin*) had told him: "A boy will be born among the Children of Israel who will bring about the end of your kingdom at his hand."

Al-Suddi said: He saw in his dream that a fire came from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) until it engulfed the houses of Egypt, burning the Copts but leaving the Children of Israel alone. So he asked the scholars of his people, and they said: "A man will emerge from this land, and the ruin of Egypt will be at his hand." So he began doing what he did. It is not hidden that this is a matter of great folly, for if the soothsayer or the dream was true, then what is the benefit of killing, and if not, then what is its justification?

In the verse there is evidence that the killing of children in order to preserve sovereignty was a Pharaonic law (*shari'a fir'awniyya*).

Abu Haywa and Ibn Muhaysin read *yudhabbih* (﴿yadhbahu﴾) with a fatha on the *ya'* and a sukun on the *dhal*. ﴿Indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾, that is, among those firmly established in corruption (*al-rasikhin fi al-ifsad*). For this reason he dared to commit such a great crime as killing those who had no offence, from among the offspring of the prophets, peace be upon them, due to a corrupt imagination.

[Page 44]

﴿And We wished to bestow favour﴾, that is, We would show kindness (*yatafaddal*) ﴿upon those who were abased in the land﴾, in the manner mentioned, by saving them from His affliction. The imperfect form in "nuridu" (We wish) is for narrating a past state, whereas "namunnu" (We bestow favour) is future relative to the wishing, so there is no need to interpret it otherwise. It is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) with the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself﴾ and so on, because the two share the same position within the explanation (*tafsir*) of "the news" (*naba'*). This is the apparent meaning.

It has also been permitted that the clause be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring back to the object of "yastad'if" (abases), with an implied subject, meaning: Pharaoh abases them, while We wish to bestow favour upon them. The subject was supposed in order to allow beginning with the conjunction "wa" (and). It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause referring to the agent (the subject), again with an implied subject. The absence of a returning pronoun to it, or of something standing in its place, does no harm, since a nominal circumstantial clause needs only the "wa" to link it. This was judged weak, because there is no doubt that it is objectionable when the subject is omitted. The view that it is validly a circumstantial clause without qualification was criticised on the ground that the basic principle for a circumstantial clause is simultaneity, whereas the bestowing of favour comes long after the abasement. This was answered by saying that the circumstance is not the bestowing of favour but the wish for it, and that wish is simultaneous. Its connection is only with the occurrence of the favour in the future, so simultaneity of the wish does not entail simultaneity of the favour. Moreover, since God's bestowing favour upon them by deliverance was in the nobility of being certain to occur, it was permissible to treat it as though it had already occurred, simultaneous with the abasement. If the clause is made a prospective circumstance (*hal muqaddara*), the dispute is removed.

Some have permitted coordinating this with "natlu" (We recite) and "nastad'if" (We abase). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is not correct. The reason for this in *al-Kashf* is as follows. As for the first, it would entail that it lies outside what is reported, and that is its greatest and most important part. As for the second, it is either a circumstance relating to the pronoun in "ja'ala" (made), or to its object, or a qualifier of "shi'a" (sects), or a resumptive statement. On the first two, the impossibility is obvious, and on the third it is even more obvious, since it has no bearing on the answer to the question that the Exalted's words "made its people into sects" suggest. Coordination requires sharing, but there is a possibility of coordinating it with "yastad'if" if it is taken as a qualifier, meaning: He made its people into sects, abasing a group of them, and We wish to bestow favour upon them, that is, upon that group of the sects. The apparent noun is put in place of the pronoun referring back to the group, and the returning pronoun to the sects is omitted because it is known, as if it were said: He abases them, and We wish to make them strong, as al-Zamakhshari argued in the case where he made it a circumstance of the object of "yastad'if". The sum is: sects described as abasing a group, and the wish to bestow favour upon that group by removing its weakness.

"If you say" that this is refuted by the fact that knowledge of the second attribute was not present, unlike the first. We reply: likewise, knowledge of abasement restricted to the state of wishing was not present. The truth is that both views are weak for this reason, and we raised it against al-Zamakhshari only because he permitted the circumstantial reading. End of quotation.

It was objected to him that coordination with it, on the supposition that it is a circumstance, is also permissible for the same reason, so there is no basis for restricting it to the qualifying reading. Also, the absence of knowledge of the second attribute, after granting that knowledge of the attribute is required without exception, is not accepted, for the cause of knowledge of the first, namely revelation or the report of the People of the Book, may be a cause of knowledge of the second too. Also, the permissibility of the circumstantial reading of "nuridu" and so on may be restricted by the possibility of its being a resumption, with the circumstantial reading applying to "yastad'if" rather than the qualifier, so it is not jointly obligatory. In reply: the possibility of the circumstantial reading from the object was not mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, so the author of *al-Kashf* did not turn to the point that coordination with it is permissible. And the requirement of knowledge of the attribute is something he explicitly stated in several places in the *Kashshaf*, and the discussion is with him. Also, knowledge of the attribute of abasement, since it is explained as slaughtering and sparing of the women, is known by observation, and the cause of knowledge is not what was mentioned of revelation or the report of the People of the Book. There is room for examination in this.

The fairest view is that the words of the Exalted "Indeed, Pharaoh" and so on do not clearly appear to be an explanation of the news of Moses, peace be upon him, and Pharaoh together, on any of the possibilities. Its appearance is clearer on the possibility of coordination with "Indeed, Pharaoh", bringing it into the scope of the explanation. Otherwise, the apparent meaning of "Indeed, Pharaoh" and so on, without this coordinated element, is that it explains only the news of Pharaoh. So consider this carefully.

﴿And We would make them leaders﴾, followed and taken as examples in religion and in worldly affairs, according to what is in *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*). Mujahid said: summoners to good. Qatada said: rulers, as in the Exalted's words: ﴿and made you kings﴾. Al-Dahhak said: prophets. Whichever it is, there is in it the attribution of a part to the whole. ﴿And We would make them the inheritors﴾ of everything that was included within the domain of the kingship of Pharaoh and his people, in the most complete manner, as the definite article indicates. That is, that no one would contend with them over it.

﴿And We wished to establish for them in the land﴾, that is, in the land of Egypt. The root meaning of *tamkin* (establishment, empowerment) is to make a thing a place in which it becomes firmly settled. It was then borrowed for giving authority and granting free rein, and this usage spread until it became a literal linguistic usage. So the meaning is: We will give them power over the land of Egypt, where they will act and their command will be executed there as they wish. The apparent sense of some scholars' words is that by "the land" is meant what includes Egypt and Syria, although the known reference is the land of Egypt alone. It seems that this is because Syria was the dwelling place of the Children of Israel. Al-A'mash read *wa-li-numakkina* with the *lam* of purpose (*lam al-kay*), meaning: "and We desired that for the purpose of establishing them," or "and We did that for the purpose of establishing them."

﴿And We would show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts﴾. The attribution of the hosts (*junud*) to their two pronouns is either by way of prevalence (*taghlib*), or because Haman had his own specific soldiers, although he was a minister, or because the army of the sultan is the army of the minister. *Nuri* (We show) is from the seeing of the eye (*ru'yah basariyyah*), as is most appropriate for eloquence. It is also permissible that it be from the seeing of the heart (*ru'yah qalbiyyah*), which means knowledge (*ma'rifah*). On both readings, the verb governs two objects by virtue of the *hamzah* (of causation). So "Pharaoh and what is conjoined to him" is its first object. The words of the Exalted, ﴿from them﴾, meaning from those oppressed people, are connected to it. The words of the Exalted, ﴿what they used to fear﴾, meaning what they were guarding against, is its second object, namely the loss of their kingdom and their destruction at the hand of a boy born among them. The seeing, on the assumption that it is of the eye, is in reality of the preliminaries of that and its signs, but it is attributed to them as an intensification. Its like is widespread among them, to the extent that one says "he saw his death with his own eye" and "he witnessed his destruction." On this is the verse of one of the later poets:

"Separation made me weep until I saw my own washing with my eye."

It has been said: the meaning is the seeing of the time of that. This is not correct. The matter, on the assumption that it means knowledge, is clear, because they had indeed known the loss of their kingdom and their destruction, through what they witnessed of the rise of those oppressed people over them and the emergence of the vanguard of that from the paths of their humiliation. Some commentators interpreted the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) as the emergence of Moses, peace be upon him. This goes against the apparent sense, which is supported by reports. It seems that this was from them because of the obscurity of the connection between the seeing of Pharaoh and those with him and the loss of their kingdom and their destruction at his hand. You have known its aspect.

Abdullah, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *wa-yara*, with the *ya'* as the imperfect of *ra'a*, and "Pharaoh" in the nominative as the subject, and likewise what is conjoined to it.
