Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 7:

﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses﴾. It has been said: she was Mahyana daughter of Yasahr son of Lawi (Levi). It has also been said: Yukhabidh; it has been said: Yarkha; it has been said: Yarakht; and other things have been said. The apparent meaning is that the revelation (al-Iyha') to her was by sending an angel. The report of Abu Hayyan that there is consensus (ijma') on her not being a prophetess does not conflict with this, since angels, peace be upon them, may be sent to non-prophets and speak to them. This is the view of Qutrub and a group, and Muqatil among them said: the angel sent to her was Jibril, peace be upon him. From Ibn Abbas and Qatada it is reported that it was inspiration (ilham), and the saying of God Most High does not contradict this: ﴿Indeed, We will return him to you and make him of the messengers﴾. Yes, it is more fitting with the first view. Some people said: it was a true dream (ru'ya manam) in which the matter was related to her, and God Most High placed certainty in her heart. It is related from al-Jubba'i that she saw a dream about this, and she related it to someone among the scholars of the Children of Israel whom she trusted, and he interpreted it for her. It has been said: it was by the information of a prophet in her time to her. The apparent meaning is that this revelation was after the birth, and there are reports that support this; so there is an omitted clause in the speech, and it is as if the estimation, and God Most High knows best, is: "His mother gave birth to Moses at the time of the slaughter (al-dhabh), and she did not know what to do regarding his matter. And We revealed to her ﴿that you should suckle him﴾." It has been said: it was before the birth. "That" (an) is either explanatory (tafsiriyya) or verbal (masdariyya), and the meaning is: suckle him as long as you are able to conceal him. Umar ibn Abd al-Wahid and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz read "an irdi'ihi" with a kasra on the nun after dropping the hamza, contrary to analogy (ghayr qiyas), because the analogical form in it would be transferring its vowel, which is the fatha, to the nun, as in the recitation of Warsh.

﴿So when you fear for him﴾ from the spies of Pharaoh and his agents who kill the sons, or from the neighbours and the like, that they might inform on him, ﴿then cast him into the sea (al-yamm)﴾, that is, into the river. What is meant by it is the Nile, and something like it is called a sea (bahr), although the term is predominantly used for salt water. ﴿And do not fear﴾ for him any loss or hardship from not being suckled during the age of suckling, ﴿and do not grieve﴾ over your separation from him. ﴿Indeed, We will return him to you﴾ soon, in such a way that you are secure concerning him; the context points to nearness. It has been said that the use of the active participle (ism al-fa'il) is because it is literally for the present, and this is taken into account in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and make him of the messengers﴾. The difference between the two nearnesses does no harm. The clause is a reason for the prohibition against fear and grief. The choice of the nominal sentence and its opening with the particle of emphasis (harf al-tahqiq) is for the concern with confirming its content, meaning: We will certainly carry out his return and make him, without doubt, one of the messengers. Al-Asma'i tested the eloquence of an Arab woman who recited poetry, and she said: "Is after the saying of God Most High: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses﴾ (the verse) eloquence? It has combined two commands, two prohibitions, two reports, and two good tidings."

The fa' in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up﴾, is explicative (faṣīḥa), and the implied sense is: "so she did what she was commanded regarding his nursing and his being cast into the river, when she feared for him." What was omitted has been omitted, relying on the indication of the situation and to signal the perfection of swiftness in carrying out the command.

Page 46

It is narrated that when the labour pains seized her, she summoned a midwife from among those appointed over the pregnant women of the Children of Israel, and she attended to her. When Moses, peace be upon him, fell to the ground, a light between his eyes overwhelmed her, every joint of her body trembled, and his love entered her heart to the extent that it prevented her from carrying out her task. She said to his mother: "Keep him safe." When she left, Pharaoh's spies came, so she wrapped him in a cloth and put him into a kindled oven, not knowing what she was doing, because her reason had been bewildered. They searched and found nothing, so they left, and she did not know his whereabouts. Then she heard his crying from the oven, went to him, and God, exalted is He, had made the fire cool and safe for him, so she took him. When Pharaoh insisted in seeking the boys and the spies strove to examine them, God, exalted is He, revealed to her what He revealed, and she nursed him for three months, or four, or eight, according to the differing reports. When she feared for him, she set about a papyrus reed and fashioned from it an ark, that is, a chest, and she coated it with bitumen from the inside. 

It is also related from al-Suddi that she summoned a carpenter, who made an ark for her. She placed the key on the inside, put Moses, peace be upon him, into it, and cast him into the Nile among some rocks near Pharaoh's house. Then the maidservants of Asiya, Pharaoh's wife, came out to bathe, found him, took him in to her, and thought there was wealth in it. When they opened it, Asiya saw him, mercy for him fell upon her, and she loved him. Pharaoh wanted to kill him, but she kept speaking to him until he left him to her.

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others that Pharaoh had at that time a daughter, who was his only child, and she was among the dearest people to him. She had a severe leprosy that had defeated the physicians. It had been told to him that she would not be cured except by something from the sea: a creature resembling a human, taken on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month, when the sun rises; its saliva would be taken and smeared on her leprosy, and she would be healed. When that day came, Pharaoh went out to a gathering of his on the bank of the Nile, with his wife Asiya with him, and his daughter came with her maidservants until she sat on the bank of the Nile. Suddenly there was an ark tossed by the waves, which became caught on a tree. Pharaoh said: "Bring it to me." They rushed in boats and brought it before him. They tried to open it but could not, and they aimed to break it but failed. Asiya looked, and there was revealed to her a light within it that no one else saw. She worked on it and opened it, and there was a small infant in it, with a light between his eyes, sucking his thumb for milk. God, exalted is He, placed love for him, peace be upon him, in her heart and in the hearts of the people. The daughter of Pharaoh went to his saliva and smeared her leprosy with it, and she was healed at once.

It has been said: when she looked at his face, she was healed. The deluded among Pharaoh's people said: "We think this is the one we are wary of, who was cast into the sea out of fear of you, so kill him." He intended to kill him, but Asiya asked him to be given to her, and he left him, as will come, God willing, exalted is He. The reports concerning this story are numerous, and we have already presented some of them.

Al-Ali (the family) of Pharaoh are his followers. As for the saying that al-Ali is used only for what has dignity, it is based on what is predominant, or that dignity in it is more general than real and apparent dignity. The meaning of their picking him up is their taking him as one takes a found thing (luqṭa), that is, taking him with care and protecting him from being lost. ﴿That he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾: here there is a mocking metaphor (isti'āra tahakkumiyya), since the reason for their picking him up was not that he would become an enemy and a grief to them; rather, something else prompted them, such as adoption and the benefit he would bring them when he grew up.

Regarding the explanation of this, there are several views. The first: his being an enemy and a grief is likened to the final cause (al-'illa al-ghā'iyya), such as adoption and benefit, through an implicit comparison in the mind, without explicitly naming anything other than the compared item, and this is indicated by mentioning what is peculiar to the compared-to item, namely the particle of causation (lām al-ta'līl). Thus there is an original implicit metaphor in the genitive noun, while the lām remains in its literal sense. The second: one first likens the ordering of what is not a final cause to the ordering of a final cause, so that the comparison is considered between the two general orderings in order to extend to their particulars. Consequently, by implication, the ordering of his being an enemy and a grief, namely the specific ordering upon the picking up, is likened to the ordering of adoption and the like, which is a final cause, namely the specific ordering upon it too. Then the particle lām, which is established to indicate the ordering of the final cause, is used for the compared item, which is the ordering of the final cause, so the metaphor is first in the causation and the accidental quality, and by implication in the lām. The ruling of the lām thus becomes like the ruling of the lion, in that it is used for what resembles the cause, just as the lion is used for what resembles the lion; however, the metaphor here is a subsequent implicit metaphor. The third is what the words of al-Khatib al-Dimashqi in al-Talkhis and al-Idah imply: that the comparison is first assumed between his being an enemy and a grief and the final cause, then that comparison extends to the comparison of its ordering with the ordering of the final cause, so the lām established for the ordering of the final cause is borrowed for the ordering of his being an enemy and a grief, without any metaphor in the genitive noun. This comparison is like the comparison of spring to the capable and choosing agent, then the attribution of growth to it, and this is what the Kashshaf implies. Al-Allama 'Abd al-Hakim chose this and said: "It is the truth in my view, because since the meaning of the lām requires the mention of the genitive noun, the appropriate thing is that the metaphor and comparison in it should follow the comparison of the genitive noun, not follow the comparison of a universal meaning with a universal meaning, the meaning of the particle being one of its particulars, as al-Sakkaki maintained and al-Allama al-Taftazani followed." End. So reflect.

It has been questioned whether the basis of explaining the picking up by a cause is sound, since picking up means finding without intention, whereas causation requires genuine intention. This is a misconception, because finding without intention does not contradict intending to take what has been found for a purpose. You know that the meaning here is: "so the family of Pharaoh took him as one takes a found thing, that is, took him with care, that he might become for them..." etc., and the causation here belongs only to the taking, and there is no difficulty in it.

Some have said: the lām may be connected to an implied element, that is, "We decreed the picking up that he might become..." etc. On this reading, it would not be permissible in speech except according to those who say that God's acts are not subject to causation, which is a different matter from what we are discussing. It is not hidden that the words of God, glorified is He, are too exalted to admit such a possibility, and in making him, peace be upon him, the very embodiment of grief there is no small hyperbole. 

Ibn Wththab, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Sa'dan read ḥuzanan (grief) with a damma on the ḥā' and a sukūn on the zāy; the reading of the majority is with two fatḥas, the dialect of Quraysh. ﴿Indeed Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts were sinners﴾, in all that they do and all that they leave undone, or it is of their nature to err. Therefore it is no wonder that they killed thousands for his sake and then took him up to raise him so that he would grow and do to them what they feared. It is narrated that in the search for him, peace be upon him, they slaughtered ninety thousand infants.

Here ﴿khāṭi'īn﴾ means erring in judgment. It may also be from khati'a meaning "to sin," for in al-Asas it is said: khati'a khata'an when one deliberately commits a sin. The meaning is: they were sinners, so God, exalted is He, punished them by making their enemy-to-be arise at their own hands. The clause, on the first reading, is a parenthetical insertion between the coordinated elements, to emphasise their error implied by His words ﴿that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾, for as you have heard, that is a mocking metaphor. On the second reading, it is a parenthetical insertion to emphasise their sin implied from the overall statement. It has been said that on this reading it must be a parenthetical insertion explaining the cause of what they were afflicted with; on this reading it may also be a explanatory resumptive clause if by what they were afflicted with is meant his being an enemy and a grief, and this does not conflict with it being parenthetical in their view. It was read khāṭīn without hamza; its underlying form may have been with hamza and it was dropped, which is the apparent case. It has been said it is from khaṭā yakhṭū, meaning "turning the right into its opposite," and so it is then a metaphor.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 9]

﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said﴾: She was Asiya bint Muzahim ibn Ubayd ibn al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, the one who was Pharaoh of Egypt in the time of Yusuf al-Siddiq (peace be upon him). On this view, she was not of the Children of Israel. It has also been said that she was of them, from the tribe of Musa (peace be upon him). Al-Suhayli (d. 581 AH), a noted scholar of the Prophet's biography and Arabic grammar, reported that she was his paternal aunt (peace be upon him), but this is a strange view. The well-known view is the first. The clause is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the clause "so the family of Pharaoh picked him up." That is, the wife of Pharaoh said to him (Musa) when she took him out of the chest.

﴿A coolness of the eye for me and for you﴾: That is, he is a coolness of the eye that belongs to me and to you. "Coolness" (qurrah) is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), and the adverbial phrase (zarf) is in the position of a descriptive modifier (sifah) of it. As al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan) notes, it is far-fetched to make it a subject whose predicate is the clause of the Exalted's words: ﴿Do not kill him﴾. She said this either because God had placed love for him in her heart, or because she was shown (in unveiling, kashf) a light between his eyes, or because she witnessed the healing of Pharaoh's daughter from leprosy (baras) by his saliva, or merely by looking at his face. To magnify the greatness of the coolness, she departed from "for us" (lana) to "for me and for you" (li wa-laka). It seems that, knowing the great love Pharaoh had for her, and that her welfare was more important to him than his own welfare, she placed herself before him, so that this would be more effective in urging him to spare the child's life. It cannot be said that the more apparent way of encouraging him to this would be the reverse. Something that may be taken as support for her welfare being more important to him than his own is what al-Nasa'i (d. 303 AH) transmitted from Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with them both): when she said this to him, he said: "For you, not for me. Had he said, 'For me as it is for you,' God would have guided him as He guided her." This is a hypothetical matter (amr fardi), so it does not contradict what has been reported, that he (may the curse of God be upon him) was sealed as a disbeliever.

The address in ﴿Do not kill him﴾ is said to be to Pharaoh. The attribution of the verb to him is figurative (majazi), because he was the one giving the command, and the plural is for glorification (ta'zim). The claim that this usage (the plural for a single person) is not found in the speech of the trustworthy Arabs except in the first-person pronoun, as in "we did" (fa'alna), is something al-Radi (Radi al-Din al-Astarabadi, d. 686 AH) alone asserted, and those who followed him in it. It has no basis in transmission or in reasoned understanding (riwayah wa-dirayah). Abu Ali al-Farisi (d. 377 AH) said in Fiqh al-Lughah (The Jurisprudence of the Language), among the customs (sunan) of the Arabs: addressing one person with the plural form, so that one says to a great man, "Look into my matter." Likewise in Sirr al-Adab and in Ibn Jinni's Khasa'is. It is an eloquent figure of speech (majaz baligh), and in the Noble Qur'an there is an instance of it, where insisting on interpreting it otherwise is folly. It has also been said that the address is to Pharaoh and his assistants who were present. This is preferred on the basis of what is reported: when he was brought out, the misguided people of his nation said, "This is the boy we were afraid of, so permit us to kill him." It has also been said that the address is to him and to those who fear being killed by him, though they were not present, by way of prevalence (taghlib). Some have chosen that it is addressed to those commanded to kill the boys. This is because, after she had addressed Pharaoh and informed him of what would move him to compassion regarding Musa (peace be upon him), she felt secure from a sudden fresh decision by him to kill the child. So she turned to the address of those commanded earlier, forbidding them from killing him, giving as her reason the words of the Exalted quoted from her:

﴿Perhaps he will benefit us, or we may take him as a son.﴾ This is more fitting to the variation in style, since she first separated in her words "for me and for you," and used the singular pronoun for addressing Pharaoh. Then she addressed a plural, and used the plural pronoun in ﴿Do not kill him﴾. Then she left off the separation in ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾ and so on, and did not express it in the pattern of "a coolness of the eye for me and for you," by saying, for example, "Perhaps he will benefit me and benefit you." So reflect on this. Her hope that he would benefit them was because of the signs of blessing and indications of nobility she saw in him:

In the cradle his grandfather's happiness speaks through
the trace of nobility, shining with clear proof.

Adopting him as a son is because he is suitable for the adoption of kings, given the splendor in him. The coordination of this with what precedes it is coordination of the particular with the general (atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm), or a distinction is considered between them, and this is more appropriate with "or" (aw). ﴿While they perceive not﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the family of Pharaoh." The estimated meaning is: "so the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he would become for them an enemy and a grief, and the wife said to him such and such, while they perceive not that they were in great error in what they did." Qatadah said: "They do not perceive that he is the one who will ruin their kingdom at his hand." Mujahid said: "They do not perceive that he is an enemy to them." Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "I do what I want, not what they want." The first estimate is the most comprehensive. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause of both the speaker and the one addressed together. The meaning of the plural here is two, on the supposition that the address in ﴿Do not kill him﴾ is to Pharaoh alone, and that it is a circumstantial clause of the speaker alone. That is, Pharaoh's wife said this to him, and those who pointed to killing him did not perceive her speech to him or her appeal to his heart concerning him, lest they incite him to kill him. On all three suppositions, it is from the speech of God, the Exalted. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause of one of the two pronouns in "we adopt him," on the basis that the pronoun refers to the people, not to the one in the circumstance, since the waw suffices for the connection. That is: "we adopt him as a son, while the people do not know that he is of other than us, though we have adopted him." On this, it is from the speech of Asiya (may God be pleased with her).

[Page 49]

﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became empty﴾: meaning, it became void of everything except the remembrance of Moses, peace be upon him. Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related this from several chains from Ibn Abbas. The same was also reported from Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Mujahid, and similarly from Ikrimah. A group said: "empty of patience." Ibn Zayd said: "empty of the promise of God Most High and His revelation to her, so she forgot it because of the grief." Abu Ubaydah said: "empty of worry, since she did not fear he would drown, and she heard that Pharaoh had shown affection toward him and adopted him, just as one says, 'So-and-so is free of mind (fariq al-bal).'" Some said: "empty of reason, because of the fear and bewilderment that overwhelmed her when she heard of his falling into the hand of his enemy, Pharaoh," like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and their hearts are air﴾, meaning hollow, with no intellect in them. Both of these views have been objected to on the grounds that the discourse does not fit what follows them, but this is open to consideration. Ahmad ibn Musa related from Abu Amr: "fuwad" with a waw. He also read "Musa" with a hamzah in place of the waw. Fadalah ibn Ubayd, al-Hasan, Yazid ibn Qutayb, and Abu Zur'ah ibn Amr ibn Jarir read "fazi'an" with a zay and an unpointed ayn, from al-fazaʿ, which is fear and anxiety. Ibn Abbas read "qari'an" with a qaf, a kasrah on the ra' or its sukun, from qara'a ra'suhu, when his hair receded, as if she were emptied of everything except the remembrance of Moses, peace be upon him. It was also said: "qar'an" with a sukun, as a verbal noun, meaning she was struck with a blow from al-qari'ah, which is a great grief. Some of the Companions read "fizgh" with a kasrah on the fa', a sakin zay, and a ghayn with a dot, meaning going away in vain. The intended sense is perishing from the intensity of grief, as if she were a slain person for whom there is neither retaliation nor blood-money. From this is the saying of Tulayhah al-Asadi about his brother Habbal:

"If their souls were struck before me, they will not go away in vain with the killing of Habbal."

Khalil ibn Ahmad read "furugh" with a dammah on the fa' and the ra'. ﴿if she had almost disclosed it﴾: meaning, she almost... etc., on the basis that "in" is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy "inna," and the lam is the distinguishing lam (al-lam al-fariqah). Or: "she had almost only disclosed it," on the basis that "in" is a negation particle and the lam has the meaning of "illa" (except). This is the view of the Kufan grammarians. Ibdaʾ (disclosure) is the manifestation of a thing, and its transitivity with the preposition "bi" is because it has been given the implicit meaning (tadmin, the incorporation of one verb's sense into another) of tasrih (explicit declaration). It was also said: the object is omitted and the "bi" is causal, meaning she would disclose the true state of affairs because of it, that is, because of what befell her from separation from him. It was also said: the "bi" is redundant (silah), meaning she would disclose him. Both views, as you see, are weak. The apparent reading is that the pronoun governed by the preposition refers to Moses, peace be upon him, and the meaning is that she almost declared him, peace be upon him, saying "Oh, my son!" from the intensity of grief and passion. This was related by the group from Ibn Abbas, and it was also reported from Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Muqatil that she almost cried out "Oh, my son!" upon seeing the waves dashing against him out of compassion for him from drowning. It was also said: the meaning is that she almost revealed his affair from the intensity of joy at his deliverance and Pharaoh's adopting him. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the revelation, meaning she almost disclosed the revelation, which is the revelation concerning him, peace be upon him, mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses: Suckle him﴾, up to the end of the verse. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the narrations do not support it. ﴿Had We not bound up her heart﴾: meaning, by what We sent down to her of tranquility. The intended meaning is: had We not made her heart firm and given her patience. Thus "binding upon the heart" is a metaphor for that. The answer to "law la" (had it not been) is omitted, indicated by ﴿if she had almost disclosed it﴾, meaning: had We not bound up her heart, she would have disclosed it. It was also said: "she would have almost disclosed it." His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so that she might be among the believers﴾ is the reason for the binding upon the heart. Faith here means assent, meaning: We gave her patience and made her heart firm so that she would be steadfast in affirming Our promise that We would return him to her and make him one of the messengers.

[Page 50]

And whoever takes the "emptiness" to mean grief and sorrow, and the "disclosure" to mean joy at Pharaoh's adoption of him, peace be upon him, which is a blameworthy joy, takes faith to mean trust, as in the saying they related from Abu Zayd: "I did not feel secure (ma amantu) that I would find a companion," meaning "I did not trust," and its literal sense is "I became one who has security," meaning one who has calm and tranquility. He said: the meaning is: had We not bound up her heart and calmed her anxiety, which arose from corrupt delight, so that she might be among those who trust in the promise of God Most High, those who rejoice in what truly merits rejoicing.

ومعنى ﴿وقالَتْ لأُخْتِهِ﴾ (And she said to his sister): مريم، وقيل: كلثمة، وقيل: كلثوم. والتعبير عنها بأخوته دون أن يقال لبنتها للتصريح بمدار المحبة الموجبة للامتثال بالأمر ﴿قُصِّيهِ﴾ (Follow him) أي اتبعي أثره وتتبعي خبره. والظاهر أن هذا القول وقع منها بعد أن أصبح فؤادها فارغا، فإن كانت لم تعرف مكانه إذ ذاك فظاهر، وإن كانت قد عرفته فتتبع الخبر ليعرف هل قتلوه أم لا وليُنكشف ما هو عليه من الحال. ﴿فَبَصُرَتْ بِهِ﴾ (and she saw him) أي أبصرته، والفاء فصيحة أي فقصت أثره فبصرت. وقرأ قتادة "فَبَصَرَتْ" بفتح الصاد وعيسى بكسرها. ﴿عَنْ جُنُبٍ﴾ (from a distance) أي عن بُعد. وقيل: أي عن شوق إليه، حكاه أبو عمرو بن العلاء وقال: هي لغة جذام يقولون "جَنُبْتُ إليك" أي اشتقت. وقال الكرماني: "جُنُبٌ" صفة لموصوف محذوف أي عن مكان جُنُب أي بعيد، وكأنه من الأضداد فإنه يكون بمعنى القريب أيضا كالجار الجنب. وقيل: أي عن جانب، لأنها كانت تمشي على الشط. وقيل: النظر عن جنب أن تنظر إلى الشيء كأنك لا تريده.

وقرأ قتادة والحسن وزيد بن علي رضي الله تعالى عنه، والأعرج "عن جَنْبٍ" بفتح الجيم وسكون النون، وعن قتادة أنه قرأ بفتحهما أيضا، وعن الحسن أنه قُرئ بضم الجيم وإسكان النون، وقرأ النعمان بن سالم "عن جانبٍ"، والكل على ما قيل: بمعنى واحد، وفي البحر: الجنب والجانب والجنابة والجناب بمعنى. ﴿وهم لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (while they did not perceive) أنها تقصه وتتعرف حاله أو أنها

And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses (﴿وحَرَّمْنا عَلَيْهِ المَراضِعَ﴾), that is, We prevented him from them. Thus the "forbidding" (al-tahrim) is a figurative usage (majaz) for "preventing" (al-man'), since whoever is forbidden something is thereby prevented from it. It is not valid to take it as legal prohibition (al-tahrim al-shar'i, prohibition in the sense of religious law), because the infant is not among those subject to legal obligation (ahl al-taklif), and there is no evidence that this was specific to him (wa-la dalil 'ala al-khususiyyah).

Al-marāḍi' is the plural of murḍi' (with a damma on the mim and a kasra on the ḍad), meaning the woman who nurses. The ta' is omitted either because the term is specific to women, or because it carries the sense of a person who nurses (bi-ma'na shakhs murḍi'), or it is the plural of marda' (with a fatha on the mim), a mimi verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī) meaning "nursing," pluralized because its occurrences are multiple. Or it is a noun of place, meaning the place of nursing, which is the breast.

"Min qabl" means: from before her cutting his track (qaṣṣihā), or from before her seeing him (ibṣāriha), or from before his being brought to those who have him. Or it means "from before that," that is, from the beginning of his affair. The apparent preference of Abu Hayyan is for this last sense.

﴿فَقالَتْ هَلْ أدُلُّكُمْ﴾ ("then she said, 'Shall I direct you'"), that is, do you wish that I direct you ﴿عَلى أهْلِ بَيْتٍ يَكْفُلُونَهُ لَكُمْ﴾ ("to a household who will take charge of him for you"), that is, who will undertake him and attend to his upbringing on your behalf. The fa' is fasihah (an eloquent fa' indicating an omitted clause), meaning: so she entered upon them and said.

Her saying "a household" rather than "a woman" indicates that the intended person is a woman of noble standing, one fit to serve kings. ﴿وهم لَهُ ناصِحُونَ﴾ ("and they are sincere to him"), meaning they will not fall short in serving and raising him.

It is narrated that when Haman heard this from her, he said: "She surely knows him and his family, so seize her until she tells us of his condition." She said: "I only meant, 'and they are sincere to the king (lil-malik).'" Thereby she was saved from the harm for which lying is permissible for one in her situation. She acted well, and this is nothing novel, for she was from the household of prophethood, so this befits her.

That the pronoun may carry two meanings is not something peculiar to the Arabic language; it occurs in all languages. The Pharaohs were among the remnants of the Amalekites, who spoke Arabic, so perhaps she spoke in their language. This style of speech is called al-kalam al-muwajjah (speech with a double-directed meaning).

[p. 51]

﴿So We returned him to his mother﴾. The *fa'* here is *fasihah* (the "eloquent" *fa'*, which signals an omitted clause). The meaning is: they accepted that from her, and she guided them to his mother, and they spoke to her about nursing him, so she agreed, and "So We returned him" to her. Or one may supply something similar to that. It is narrated that when his sister said what she said, Pharaoh ordered her to bring someone who would nurse him. So she brought his mother, while Musa, peace be upon him, was in Pharaoh's hand, crying, and Pharaoh was trying to soothe him. So he handed him to her. When he smelled her scent, he felt at ease, took her breast into his mouth. Pharaoh said, "Who are you to him? He has refused every breast except yours." She said, "I am a woman of good scent and good milk. No child is brought to me without taking to me." So he placed him in her care, and she went back with him to her house that same day. He also ordered that her maintenance be paid to her. Her receiving this is not the same as taking a wage for nursing him. Even if it were granted, we do not accept that it was forbidden in what she believed. The maintenance, according to what is in the sea, was a dinar each day. ﴿That her eye may be cooled﴾ by his arrival back to her. ﴿And that she may not grieve﴾ over his separation. ﴿And that she may know that the promise of Allah﴾, that is, all that He, glorified be He, promised of his return to her and of making him one of the messengers, ﴿is true﴾, with no failure in it, through witnessing part of it and reasoning from part of it to the rest. Otherwise, her knowledge of the truth of this was already present beforehand through revelation.

Abu Hayyan used the verse as evidence against the view of those who held that the *iyha'* (inspiration) was *ilham* (intuitive inspiration) or a dream, because it is far-fetched to describe that as a promise. There is room for scrutiny in this. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, that is, they do not recognize Allah the Exalted's promise or its truth, or they do not affirm what He, the Majestic and Exalted, promised them, because they allow for His promise to fail, whereas He, glorified be He, does not break the appointment. It was also said: they do not know that the primary purpose of returning him to her was her knowledge of this, and that what else there was, such as the cooling of her eye and the removal of her grief, is secondary. In response: what the speech indicates is that each of the cooling of the eye and the knowledge is a purpose or an independent purpose; but that the other than knowledge is subordinate to it, especially with the other being mentioned first, is not indicated. As for the attribution of that to the particle of cause being omitted from the first, its condition is not hidden. In His saying, exalted be He, "But most people..." etc., it was said: it is an allusion to what had passed from his mother when she heard that he had fallen into Pharaoh's hand, out of fear and bewilderment. You know that what came over her was among the requirements of human nature, and it coexists with knowledge that what she feared would not happen. Negating knowledge in such a case can only be done through some kind of interpretation, as is not hidden. Then, the *istidrak* (corrective addition) is on what he chose, of what occurred after knowledge. It is also permitted that it be from knowledge itself, and that is when the meaning is: they do not know that the primary purpose of returning him to her is her knowledge of the truth of Allah's promise, the exalted. So reflect.

﴿Wa-lamma balagha ashuddahu﴾ [And when he reached his maturity]: that is, the point beyond which his growth does not increase. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wa-istawa﴾ [and attained full strength], means he was perfected and completed. It is an emphasis and an explanation of what precedes it. So it has been said. There is disagreement about the time of reaching al-ashudd (full maturity, the peak of physical strength) and of al-istiwa' (balance and completeness). Ibn Abi al-Dunya transmitted, through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "Al-ashudd is between eighteen and thirty years, and al-istiwa' is between thirty and forty. When he exceeds forty, he begins to decline." 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted, from Mujahid, that he said: "Al-ashudd is thirty-three years, and al-istiwa' is forty years." This is also a report from Ibn 'Abbas, and something similar is related from Qatada. Al-Zajjaj said once: "Reaching al-ashudd is from about seventeen years to forty," and another time: "It is between thirty and forty." Some scholars preferred the latter here, and they justified it by its agreement with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿hatta idha balagha ashuddahu wa-balagha arba'ina sanatan﴾ [until, when he reached his maturity and reached forty years], because it implies that it ends at forty, which is the age of standing still, so its beginning should be the beginning of that period. This is not free from objection. The truth is that reaching al-ashudd, in its basic sense, is arriving at the limit of strength, and that is the time when growth ends and reaches its end. This varies with regions, eras and conditions, and for this reason there are different explanations of it in the books of lexicography and tafsir. Perhaps the better view, according to what has been said, is that reaching al-ashudd is an expression for reaching the measure at which the body and its physical powers become strong and its significant growth ends. Al-istiwa' is the balance and completeness of his intellect. It is not appropriate to fix a specific time for this in the case of Musa, peace be upon him, except by a report on which one can rely, because of what you have heard, that this varies with regions, eras and conditions. Yes, it is well known that this generally happens at the age of forty, and the poet's verse on this is:

When a man reaches forty and has not
Modesty or concealment beyond what he desires,

then leave him, and do not grudge him what has passed,
even if the causes of life have dragged his years along for him.

In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿hatta idha balagha ashuddahu wa-balagha arba'ina sanatan﴾, there is something that supports this. Some discussion of al-ashudd has already passed in the commentary on Surat Yusuf, so recall it and do not be negligent. Then, the meaning overall, according to what was said last, is: when his body became strong and his intellect became balanced, ﴿ataynahu hukman﴾ [We gave him judgment], that is, prophethood, according to what is related from al-Suddi, or knowledge which is one of the special qualities of prophethood, according to how some scholars interpreted his words. ﴿Wa-'ilman﴾ [and knowledge] of the religion and the law. In al-Kashshaf: "Al-'ilm is the Torah, and al-hukm is the Sunnah, and the wisdom of the prophets, peace be upon them, is their Sunnah." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿wadhkurna ma yutla fi buyutikunna min ayati Allahi wa-al-hikmah﴾ [and remember what is recited in your houses of the signs of God and the wisdom]. It was also said: "We gave him the way and the conduct of the wise scholars and their manner before the mission, so he, peace be upon him, would not do any act that would be considered ignorance," end of quote. It has been preferred that what was said is more in harmony with the structure of the story than what came before, because his appointment as a prophet, peace be upon him, came after the striking of the Copt, and after the migration to Madyan and his return from it; and the giving of the Torah to him came after the drowning of Pharaoh. So it was long after the striking. It is also preferred because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa-kadhalika﴾ [and thus], that is, like what We did to Musa and his mother, peace be upon them both, ﴿najzi al-muhsinin﴾ [We reward the good-doers] for their good deeds, rejects understanding what precedes as prophethood, because prophethood is not a reward for action. Whoever holds the first view takes this as a general explanation of the fulfillment of the promise by making him one of the messengers after returning him to his mother, and what follows is a detailed explanation of it. The conjunction with waw does not require order. That what He did with Musa and his mother, peace be upon them both, was a reward for action is by way of the principle of predominance. It may be said that the essence of prophethood, although it is not a reward for action, has some of its ranks, namely those in which there is greater nearness to God, exalted is He, which, because of greater nearness, is a reward for it. This returns to the view that greater nearness is the reward, and the difference among the prophets, peace be upon them, in nearness to Him is something that should not be doubted. What was mentioned before was preferred because it is more in harmony with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa-li-ta'lama anna wa'da Allahi haqq﴾ [so that you may know that the promise of God is true]. Its implication that prophethood is given to every good-doer is nothing at all. Whoever holds that this giving was before the migration said: "It may be that the meaning is: We gave him leadership among his people, the Children of Israel, by making him distinguished among them, so they return to him in their affairs and comply when he orders them to do something or forbids them from it, and knowledge by which he benefits and which benefits others. This is either by pure inspiration, or by God's granting him success in deriving subtleties and secrets from the sayings of his fathers, the prophets, peace be upon them, from the Children of Israel that were transmitted to him. There is nothing strange in his, peace be upon him, knowing what his prophet fathers were upon and what they practiced of the laws, through inspiration or through hearing reports that yield knowledge. Perhaps this is better than what is related in al-Kashshaf." In the discussion of the end of Surat al-Baqarah there is something whose review will benefit you, so let it be reviewed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 28, verse 15:

﴿And he entered the city﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said, according to what is reported from him in the *Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*): it is Memphis (*Manf*). ﴿At a time of unawareness on the part of its people﴾, meaning at a time when entering it was not customary, or when they did not expect him at that time. According to what is reported from the scholar (*al-Habr*, i.e. Ibn 'Abbas), it was the time of the midday rest (*al-qa'ilah*). In another report from him, it was between the evening prayer (*al-'isha'*) and the late night (*al-'atamah*). That is because Pharaoh had ridden out one day and set off for that city, so Moses, peace be upon him, learned of his departure, hastened, and entered the city at that time.

Ibn Ishaq said: it is Egypt (*Misr*). Moses, peace be upon him, had openly confronted Pharaoh and his people with what they disliked, so he went into hiding and disappeared, and he entered it in disguise.

Ibn Zayd said: Pharaoh had expelled him from it, so he stayed away for years, and [Pharaoh] forgot him. He came and entered it while its people were unaware, because they had forgotten him and their acquaintance with him had grown distant.

It was also said: he entered on a day of festival while they were occupied with their revelry. It was said: he left Pharaoh's palace and entered Egypt at the time of the midday rest or between the two evening prayers. It was said: the city is 'Ayn Shams (Heliopolis). It was said: it is a village two farsakhs (about six miles) from Egypt called Habin.

It was also said: it is Alexandria, but the more well-known view is that it is Egypt. Perhaps this is the more evident and the more immediately understood, that *'ala hin* (at a time of) is connected to *dakhala* (he entered). On this view, the evident meaning is that *'ala* here carries the sense of *fi* (in), like its use in the verse of the Exalted: ﴿and they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon﴾, according to one opinion.

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) relative to *al-madinah* (the city). It may also be in the position of a *hal* relative to the subject of the verb, meaning "stealthily." End of quotation. Perhaps what led him to depart from the more immediate reading is his need to make *'ala* mean *fi*, and the subtlety of expressing it with *'ala* rather than *fi*, or the sufficiency of the adverbial phrase alone. The matter is clear to anyone with slight reflection.

It was also said: the reason for this is that entering the city at a time of unawareness on the part of its people is not explicit about entering it while its people were unaware, as the *hal* reading relative to *al-madinah* would indicate, nor about entering it stealthily, as the *hal* reading relative to the pronoun would indicate. The time of unawareness is like the time of the midday rest, and the period between the two evening prayers may not be a time of unawareness. There is a point of discussion in this.

﴿min ahliha﴾ (on the part of its people) is in the position of a qualifier (*sifah*) of *ghaflah* (unawareness). The wording of the noble text is more eloquent than "the unawareness of its people" in the construct form, because of what the nunation (*tanwin*) conveys of magnification. Perhaps he departed from that to what he mentioned for this reason, so reflect.

Abu Talib al-Qari' read *'ala hin* with a *fatha* on the *nun* (*'ala hina*). It is explained that he gave it a *fatha* because of its proximity to the *ghayn* (in *ghaflah*), just as the *dal* in *al-hamdu lillah* was given a *kasra* in some readings because of its proximity to the *lam*. Or it is explained that he treated the verbal noun (*masdar*) as if it were a verb, as though it were said: "at a time when its people were unaware," so *hin* is indeclinable, as it is when it is annexed to a clause beginning with a past-tense verb, such as the line of poetry:

"At the time when I reproached grey hair for youth"
And this, as you see, [is weak].

﴿And he found in it two men fighting﴾, meaning they were fighting each other. The clause is a qualifier (*sifah*) of *rajulayn* (two men). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), and this is based on the opinion of Sibawayh, that a *hal* may come from an indefinite noun without any condition. Nu'aym ibn Maysarah read *yaqtatilan* with the assimilation of the *ta'* into the *ta'* and the transfer of its vowel to the *qaf*.

﴿This is of his faction﴾, meaning of those who supported him and followed him in his command and prohibition, or in religion, according to what a group has said, and they are the Children of Israel. In *al-Itqan* it is said: he is the Samiri. ﴿And this is of his enemy﴾, meaning of his opponents in what he wants, or in religion, according to what the group has said, and they are the Copts. Its name, as also in *al-Itqan*, is Qanun. It is a qualifier following another qualifier of *rajulayn*. The demonstrative *hadha* (this) here is used in the manner of narration (*hikayah*) of what occurred at the time of finding them, as if the one who saw them were saying it, not in the report addressed to the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him.

Al-Mubarrad said: the Arabs use *hadha* to refer to an absent person. Jarir said:

"This is my paternal cousin in Damascus, a caliph; had I wished, he would have driven you to me as captives."

This demonstrative stands in place of a pronoun in linking, and the conjunction precedes the qualifying function.

There is disagreement about the cause of the fighting of these two men. It was said: it was a religious matter. It was said: it was a worldly matter. It is related that the Copt had commissioned the Israelite to carry firewood to Pharaoh's kitchen, but he refused, so they fought over that. The Copt, according to what Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, was a baker for Pharaoh.

﴿So the one of his faction called for his help﴾, meaning he sought his aid and support ﴿against the one of his enemy﴾. Because the verb is taken to include the sense of *nasr* (support), it takes *'ala*. This is supported by the Exalted's words after this: ﴿who had sought his help the day before﴾. It is also possible that its construction with *'ala* is because it has been given the sense of *i'anah* (assistance). This is supported by the fact that it was read as *fasta'anahu* with the unpointed *'ayn* and *nun* replacing the *tha'*. This reading was transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh from Sibawayh, and Abu al-Qasim Yusuf ibn 'Ali ibn Jubarah from Ibn Miqsam and al-Za'farani. As for Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement that al-Akhfash mentioned it, this is a scribal error (*tashif*), not a reading, and it has no basis in the transmission. The first element (*sadr*) of the relative clause has been omitted, meaning *alladhi huwa min shi'atihi* (the one who is of his faction) and *alladhi huwa min 'aduwwihi* (the one who is of his enemy). Even if this omission is not accepted, the sense is sound.

﴿So Moses struck him﴾, meaning he struck the Copt with the gathering of his palm, that is, with his hand with its fingers gathered together, according to what many have reported from Mujahid.

Abu Hayyan said: *al-wakz* is striking with the hand with its fingers gathered like the gesture of counting seventy-three. On both views, peace be upon him struck him with the hand. Ibn al-Mundhir and a group reported from Qatadah that he, peace be upon him, struck him with his staff. It seems that he interpreted *al-wakz* as pushing or thrusting, and that is among its meanings, as in the *Qamus*. Perhaps he meant by "his staff" a staff that he had, for his well-known staff was given to him by Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, after this incident, as is well known and recorded in the books of tafsir.

'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) read *fa-lakazahu* with the *lam*. It is reported from him as *fa-nakazahu* with the *nun*. *Al-lakz*, according to the *Qamus*, is the same as *al-wakz*, and also a blow to the chest and the palate. *Al-nakz*, according to the same source, is striking and pushing. It was said: *al-wakz*, *al-nakz*, and *al-lakz* all mean pushing with the tips of the fingers. It was also said: *al-wakz* is on the heart and *al-lakz* is on the beard (jaw).

It is reported that when the quarrel intensified, the Copt said to Moses, peace be upon him: "I have resolved to put this [wood] on your back," meaning the firewood. So Moses's anger intensified, and he had been given strength, so he struck him.

﴿So he dispatched him﴾, meaning Moses killed him. The root sense of *qada 'alayhi* is that he brought his life to an end, that is, made it terminated and finished. In this meaning it takes *'ala*, as in the *Asas*, so there is no need to interpret it as "he brought down a judgment upon him." The verb may take *ila* by being given the sense of *ihya'* (revelation), as in the Exalted's words: ﴿and We decreed to him that matter﴾. The pronoun of the subject in *qada* refers to Moses, which is the evident reading. It was also said that it refers to God the Exalted, meaning that God, glorified is He, decreed death upon him, so *qada* here means *hakama* (decreed). It was also said that it may refer to the verbal noun implied by *wakazahu*, meaning the striking decided his fate, that is, brought his life to an end.

﴿He said: "This is of the work of Satan"﴾, meaning of his embellishment. It was also said: it is of the same kind as his work. The first view is more fitting with the Exalted's words: ﴿Indeed, he is an enemy, a misleader, clearly manifest﴾, meaning manifestly hostile. The word *mubin* (clearly manifest) is a second qualifier of *'aduww* (enemy). It was also said: [it means] manifestly hostile and misleading. This has been explained by saying that it is a qualifier of *'aduww*, with the attribute of misleading kept in view alongside it, or that it is a case of competition (*tanazu'*) between *'aduww* and *mudill* (misleader), each seeking it as its qualifier. Whichever is the case, *mubin* is from *abana*, which is intransitive.

Page 55

﴿He said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself"﴾ by a blow that resulted in killing, ﴿so forgive me﴾ my sin. He, peace be upon him, said what he said because he did an act he had not been permitted to do, and it was not among the practices of his forefathers, the prophets, peace be upon them, in an incident like this one that he witnessed, which led to the killing of a soul whose killing was not prescribed in any of the revealed laws. This does not conflict with the view that the prophets, peace be upon them, are preserved from major sins both after and before prophethood, because the origin of the striking was a minor sin, and the killing that occurred was accidental, as Ka'b (al-Ahbar) and others said. An accidental act, although it is not free from sin, which is why expiation (kaffarah) was prescribed for it, is nevertheless also a minor sin. Indeed, it has been said that it does not conflict even with the view that they are preserved from both major and minor sins absolutely, because it is possible that he, peace be upon him, thought that the blow would repel an oppressor from an oppressed person, so he did it without intending to kill, and the killing occurred as a consequence of it, not deliberately. That accidental acts are not free from sin in the laws of the earlier prophets, peace be upon them, as in the law of our Prophet (ﷺ), is not known. Likewise the prescription of expiation for it is not known. It seems that he, peace be upon him, after what had happened, reflected and it became clear to him that the repelling could have been done without the blow, and that he had not been steady in his judgment because of the anger that overtook him. So he knew that he had done what was less than the best (khilaf al-awla) for someone of his station, and he said what he said in the manner of those brought near (to God), who regard even what is less than the best as grave.

Then this act occurred from him, peace be upon him, before prophethood, as is evident from the words of the Exalted, quoted about him in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you, and my Lord granted me wisdom and made me one of the messengers﴾. This is what al-Naqqash and others said. It is narrated from Ka'b that he, peace be upon him, was at that time twelve years old. As for the one who interpreted "istiwa'" (maturity) as reaching forty years, and made what is mentioned after reaching "ashudd" (full strength) and "istiwa'" and being given judgment and knowledge refer to a meaning that does not necessitate prophethood, he is obliged to say that he, peace be upon him, was then forty years old or a little more.

Some have claimed that by his words ﴿I have wronged myself﴾ he, peace be upon him, meant that he had exposed himself to destruction by killing this disbeliever, since if Pharaoh learned of it he would kill him for it. And by his words ﴿so forgive me﴾ he meant: conceal that from me. They regarded this as the work of Satan, because it involves falling into whispering and anticipating a harm. What is in this is not hidden, and the Exalted's words reject it: ﴿So He forgave him; indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. The linking of "forgave" to what precedes it by "fa" (so) indicates that the meaning is that He forgave him because of his seeking forgiveness. The clause ﴿indeed He﴾ etc. serves as a reason for the causality, meaning: indeed He, the Exalted, is the one who is abundant in forgiving the sins of His servants and in showing them mercy. For this reason his seeking forgiveness was a cause of his being forgiven. The placing of "qala" (he said) between his two statements, peace be upon him, is because of the difference between them, in that the second is a private supplication and invocation, unlike the first.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 17:

As for the placement of *qala* (he said) in His words, ﴿He said: "My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me..."﴾, its rationale is evident. The *ba'* in *bima* is for oath (*qasam*), and *ma* is a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyyah*). The answer to the oath is omitted, meaning: "I swear by Your favor upon me that I will surely refrain from such an act."

It has also been said that the answer is: "I will surely repent." His words, ﴿so I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾, are coordinated (*ataf*) with the answer. Perhaps the intended meaning of God's favor upon him is His protecting him from the evil of Pharaoh, returning him to his mother, distinguishing him above the rest of the Children of Israel, and similar things.

It has also been said that the intended meaning is His forgiveness of him, which is not far-fetched. And [Moses'] knowledge, peace be upon him, that God (Glorified is He) had forgiven him, [would be possible] if this statement was made before prophethood, through inspiration (*ilham*) or a dream. *Zahir* means one who helps. *Al-mujrimin* is the plural of *mujrim*, and what is meant by it is one who leads another into a crime, or one whose assistance leads to a crime, such as the Israelite whom the Copt quarreled with, whose assistance led to what was a crime in the view of Moses, peace be upon him. In this case, there is a metonymy (*majaz*) in the attribution of the *al-mujrimin* [to the helper], through attributing the act to its cause. It is also permissible that what is meant is the disbelievers, and by them he meant those who sought his help and the like, on the basis that he had not yet become a Muslim. It has also been said that by "the criminals" he meant Pharaoh and his people, and the meaning is: "I swear by Your favor upon me that I will repent, so I will never be a helper to the disbelievers by accompanying them and increasing their numbers." Indeed, he, peace be upon him, used to accompany Pharaoh and ride with his riding, like a child with a parent, and he was called "the son of Pharaoh." It is not hidden that what came before is more suitable to the context.

It is also permissible that the *ba'* is the oath of entreaty (*al-qasam al-isti'tafi*), on the basis that it is connected to an omitted supplicatory verb, and the clause ﴿so I will never...﴾ and so on is a consequence of it, and the *fa'* falls in the answer to the supplication or to the implied condition, meaning: "By the right of Your favor upon me, protect me, so I will not be..." or "If You protect me, then I will never be..." The oath of entreaty is that which is used to emphasize a imperative clause, like your saying, "By God Most High, visit me." The non-entreaty oath is that which is used to emphasize a declarative clause, like "By God Most High, I will surely stand." This is the view of Ibn al-Hajib. It has also been said that the oath of entreaty is that in which the sworn-by carries an implication of tenderness and compassion, like "By Your generosity that encompasses all, bestow upon me." This applies to what is here. The non-entreaty oath is that in which the sworn-by is more general than that. According to both views, they are two kinds of the general oath. The apparent meaning of al-Zamakhshari's words is that what is understood by oath is that which emphasizes a declarative statement and from which an oath (*yamin*) is formed, so what is meant by it as entreaty is a counterpart to it. Some have considered the application of the term "oath" to the oath of entreaty to be a metaphorical usage (*tajawwuz*). What makes the intention of entreaty here unlikely is what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, that Moses, peace be upon him, did not make an exception, that is, he did not say "if God wills," so he was tested with it, that is, with being a supporter of the criminals, a second time, and that is what is in His words, ﴿then behold, the one who had sought his help...﴾ and so on, because an exception does not fit with the entreaty, since the negation is conditioned upon God's protection, Mighty and Majestic.

It is also permissible that the *ba'* is causal, connected to an omitted verb to which ﴿so I will never...﴾ and so on is coordinated, and *ma* is a relative pronoun. The meaning is: "Because of the strength You have bestowed upon me, I will thank You; so I will never use it except in supporting Your friends, and I will not leave a Copt overcoming an Israelite." This is a binding of himself to support His friends, Mighty and Majestic, like a vow (*nadhr*). There is no oath in it in any way, contrary to whoever imagined that. It is not hidden that this, although the narration does not rule it out, is not free from a distance from the context (*siyaq*). The *la* (never) in all the aspects mentioned is for negation. In al-Bahr it is said that it is for supplication, and Ibn Hisham related its refutation, on the grounds that the supplicatory verb is not attributed to the speaker but to the addressee or the third person, like "O Lord, punish so-and-so," and it is permissible to say "may God Most High not punish 'Amr." Then he said: "And what refutes it is his saying: 'Then may I not cease to be yours forever, like the eternity of the mountains.'" It is not hidden from you that its being for supplication in the last aspect of the verse is not apparent, and in the first aspect it is not free from obscurity. Perhaps whoever considered it for supplication took *bima an'amta 'alayya* as entreaty, connected the prepositional phrase to something like "protect me," made the *fa'* explanatory, and made "so I will never be..." and so on an explanation of that omitted element, as was said regarding His words, ﴿So We answered him and removed...﴾. So let it be pondered.

The scholars have used this verse as evidence for the prohibition of aiding the oppressors and serving them.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Walid al-Rasafi that he asked 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah about a brother of his who was a scribe. He said to him: "My brother has no share in the affairs of the authority except that he writes for it with a pen what enters and what leaves. If he leaves his pen, he incurs debt and is in need; and if he takes it up, he has sufficiency through it." He asked: "For whom does he write?" He said: "For Khalid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Qasri." He said: "Have you not heard what the righteous servant said: ﴿My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, so I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾? So let your brother not be concerned about anything, and let him throw down his pen, for God Most High will surely bring him provision."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hanzalah Jabir ibn Hanzalah al-Dabbi, the scribe, who said: A man said to 'Amir: "O Abu 'Amr, I am a man who is a scribe. I write what enters and what leaves, and I take a provision by which I and my dependents are sufficed." He said: "Perhaps you write about blood being shed?" He said: "No." He said: "Perhaps you write about wealth being seized?" He said: "No." He said: "Perhaps you write about a house being demolished?" He said: "No." He said: "Have you heard what Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, so I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾?" He said: "You have conveyed to me, O Abu 'Amr. By God, Mighty and Majestic, I will never write for them with a pen, ever." He said: "By God Most High, God, Glorified is He, will never leave you without provision, ever."

The predecessors (*salaf*) used to avoid completely any service to them. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Salamah ibn Nubayt, who said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muslim sent to al-Dahhak, saying: "Go with the grants of the people of Bukhara and give them to them." He said: "Excuse me." He kept asking to be excused until he excused him. Then one of his companions said to him: "What harm is there in your going and giving them, while you do not diminish anything for them?" He said: "I do not like to help the oppressors in any part of their affair."

And if the hadith is authentic: "A caller will call out on the Day of Resurrection: Where are the oppressors, the likes of the oppressors, and the helpers of the oppressors, even whoever has provided them with an inkwell or sharpened a pen for them? They will be gathered in a coffin of iron and cast into Hell." Then let whoever knows that he is among their helpers weep for himself, and let him desist from what he is upon before his grave is dug. Among what breaks the back is what is narrated from one of the great scholars: that a tailor asked him, saying: "I am among those who sew for the oppressors; am I counted among their helpers?" He said: "No. You are among them, and the one who sells you the needle is among their helpers." So there is no power and no strength except through God, the Exalted, the Great. Alas for the one who sold his religion for his worldly life, and bought the pleasure of the oppressors with the anger of his Master.

This is what has been said, and the flood has reached the top of the hill (*zuba*), and the river has run and overflowed onto the villages.

So he woke up in the city, fearful [of the harm that might befall him], watching out (yataraqqab, meaning he kept a lookout) for whether that [harm] would come, or for news of whether they had learned of what he had done. It is related that he [Moses], upon him be peace, had buried the Copt after the man died in the sand. It has also been said: "fearful" of harm from Pharaoh, "watching out" for the victory of his Lord, Mighty and Majestic. It has been said: he was watching out for his people to hand him over. It has been said: he was watching out for the guidance of his people. It has been said: "fearful" of his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, watching out for forgiveness. All of these, as you see, [are weak]. The most apparent reading, according to what has been said, is that "in the city" is connected to *asbaha* (he woke up), the subject of *asbaha* is the pronoun referring to Moses, upon him be peace, "fearful" is its predicate, and the clause "watching out" is a predicate following a predicate, or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in "fearful." Abu al-Baqa' said: "watching out" is a circumstantial clause replacing the first circumstantial clause, or an emphasis of it, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "fearful." End of quotation. There is also the possibility that *asbaha* is a complete verb (*tammah*, meaning "he entered the morning"), and the possibility that it is a defective verb (*naqisah*, a linking verb), in which case the predicate is "in the city." Your own judgment will show which of these is preferable.

﴿Then behold, the one who had sought his help the day before﴾, namely the Israelite whose cause Moses, upon him be peace, had been drawn into when he killed the Copt, ﴿was crying out to him for help﴾, that is, he was calling on him for aid against another Copt, raising his voice. The root meaning of *yastasrikhu* (crying out for help) is shouting; it was then used figuratively for seeking help, because a call for help is almost always accompanied by shouting, and this usage became so common that it became a customary literal meaning (*haqiqah 'urfiyyah*). It has also been said: the meaning of *yastasrikhuhu* is that he asks him to stop his shouting. *Idha* is used for the sudden discovery (*lil-mufajaah*), and what follows it is the subject, while the clause *yastasrikhuhu* is the predicate.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the clause be a circumstantial clause, with *idha* as the predicate. By "the day before" is meant the day before the day of calling for help. In the Shihabi marginal notes it is said: if Moses, upon him be peace, entered the city between the two evening prayers, then "the day before" is a figurative expression for the recent past. It is declined (*mu'rab*), because the definite article *al-* is attached to it, and this is the usual case when *al-* is attached. It has also been built (*buniya*) together with *al-*, as an exception (*nudrah*), as in the verse:

*"I was held back today and the day before it, until the sun, until the sun nearly set."*

﴿He said﴾, that is, Moses, upon him be peace, ﴿to him, Moses﴾, that is, to the Israelite who was crying out to him for help: ﴿"Indeed you are clearly misguided"﴾, going astray, ﴿"plainly so"﴾, obviously in error. [He said this] either because you have caused the killing of a man and are now fighting another, or because your habit is quarrelsome disputation. Some of the eminent scholars chose this second view, saying: the first [explanation] does not fit.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 19:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When he intended﴾, etc., because remembering his causing of what he had mentioned is what restrains him, not what drives him forward. It is answered that the remembering is a certainty, in accordance with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿fearful, watching out﴾. The motive for it, as mentioned, was his compassion for those of his people who had been wronged, and his zeal to support the truth. It has also been said that the pronoun in *lahu* (for him) and the address in *innaka* (you) refer to the Copt. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿who sought his help﴾, but it contradicts the apparent meaning. What makes it more remote is the explicit noun in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When he intended to strike the one who was an enemy to both of them﴾, for the apparent reading of that is that *alladhi* (the one who) is a substitute (*badal*). *Al-batsh* means seizing with force and violent assault. The tanwin (nunation) in *"ʿaduwwun"* (an enemy) is for *tafkhim* (magnification), meaning an enemy of great hostility. Because that is what is intended, he did not put it in the construct form (*lam yudhfhu*). The one who was an enemy to both of them is the Copt, and the Copts were among the greatest of people in enmity toward the Children of Israel. It has also been said that his enmity toward them both was because he was not of their religion. Al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far read *"yabtushu"* with a *damma* on the *ta'* (i.e., *yabṭushu*).

﴿He said: "O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?"﴾ This was said by the Israelite who was seeking his help, according to what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and most of the commentators. It seems that he imagined the intent to strike was against him and not against the Copt, from Musa's calling him *ghawiyyan* (one who is astray). Al-Hasan said: It was said by the Copt who is an enemy to both of them. It seems that from his saying to the Israelite, "Indeed you are clearly astray," he imagined that he (Musa) was the one who had killed the Copt yesterday. There is no remoteness in this, because what was mentioned is either a summary of a statement from which that is understood, or because his saying that to the one who was wronged and sought his support is contrary to the apparent meaning, so there is no remoteness in shifting to that interpretation. What is in the Torah that is in the hands of the Jews today contains something explicit that these two men were from the Children of Israel. As for the two men he saw yesterday, one of them was an Israelite and the other an Egyptian. The enmity is explained on this basis: this one whom he intended to strike was a wrongdoer toward the one who sought his help, so he would be an enemy to him and a disobeyer of God, may He be exalted, and therefore an enemy to Musa, peace be upon him. It is also possible that his enmity toward them both was because he opposed their religion, even though he was an Israelite. The Torah also contains something explicit that the wrongdoer is the one who said this.

You know that this Torah is not to be relied upon in matters that contradict the Qur'an or the authentic Sunnah. In other matters it is like the rest of the reports of the Children of Israel: it is neither to be believed nor to be disbelieved. Yes, it may be used as a supporting indication for some matters. Furthermore, what is in it of the story of Musa, peace be upon him, differs from what God, may He be exalted, related from it here, and in other places, by addition and omission. This is evident to whoever has examined it, and the ruling on that is not hidden. Here the account is free of mention of the coming of the believer from the family of Pharaoh and his advice to Musa, peace be upon him. Likewise it is free of mention of what indicates His saying: ﴿You want only to be a tyrant (jabbaran) in the land﴾, i.e., you want nothing but to be a tyrant in the land, and the *jabbar* is one who does everything he wishes of striking and killing and does not consider the consequences. It has also been said: the one who exalts himself and does not humble himself before the command of God, may He be exalted. Its root, as it is said, is the tall palm tree, and it was borrowed for what has been mentioned, either by way of his exalting himself in a figurative sense or his magnifying himself. ﴿And you do not want to be among the reformers﴾ between people, so that you would prevent disputes by means of what is better.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Sha'bi that he said: Whoever kills two men, meaning without right, is a *jabbar*, then he recited this verse. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from ʿIkrima. When he said this, the matter spread and reached Pharaoh and his chiefs, and they resolved to kill Musa, peace be upon him. Then a believer from the family of Pharaoh, who was a cousin of Pharaoh, came out to inform him of that and to advise him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 20:

As Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And there came a man running from the farthest part of the city﴾, and so on. His name is said to be Sham'an, or Sham'un ibn Ishaq, or Hizqil, and it is said to be something other than these. That this man who came is the believer of the family of Pharaoh is the well-known view, though it is said that he is someone else. "Yas'a" (running) means he hastens on foot, and he hastened because his place was far away and because of his great concern for informing Musa, peace be upon him, and advising him. It is also said that "yas'a" means he intends the Face of Allah, Exalted, as in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿and strove for it with the striving due to it﴾. Although this is a metaphorical usage, it is permissible to take it in this sense because of its fame.

The apparent view is that ﴿from the farthest part﴾ is a complement to (jaa, came), and the clause ﴿running﴾ is a description of ﴿a man﴾. It is also permitted that ﴿from the farthest part﴾ is in the position of a description of "a man", and the clause "running" is a description after a description.

It is also permitted that the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) from "a man". As for when the prepositional phrase is made to be in the position of a description of him, it is clear, because although it is indefinite, it is assimilated to definites, so it may have a circumstantial phrase. As for when it is connected to (jaa, came), the majority of grammarians prohibit this, while Sibawayh permitted it. It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase be connected to "running", and this, as you see, is weak.

﴿He said: O Musa, indeed the chiefs﴾, namely the notables of Pharaoh's state, ﴿are conspiring against you﴾, meaning they are consulting together because of you. The consultation was called "i'tamar" (conspiring) because each of the consulting parties commands the other and is commanded. ﴿to kill you, so leave﴾ the city before they gain power over you. ﴿Indeed I am to you among the sincere advisers﴾. The lam here is for clarification (lil-bayan), as in "suqya laka" (may you have water), so it is connected to an omitted verb, meaning "I mean you" (a'ni). The majority did not permit its being connected to "sincere advisers" because the alif-lam in it is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), and what depends on the relative clause does not precede the relative pronoun, nor does an omitted, preceding element which is explained by the mentioned element, because what does not govern cannot explain a governing element. According to those who permit the preceding of a dependent of the relative clause when the relative pronoun is specifically "al", because it is in the form of a particle, or when the preceding element is an adverbial, for the sake of expansion in it, or who say: the "al" here is a definite article for the sake of expressing permanence, it is permissible for "laka" to be connected to "sincere advisers" or to an omitted element explained by that.

Al-Qurtubi and others took from the verse the permissibility of tale-bearing (namimah) for a religious benefit.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verses 21–22:

﴿So he went out from it﴾, that is, from the city, complying (mumtathilan).

﴿Fearful, watching out (yataraqqabu)﴾ for the pursuit of those who sought him. ﴿He said: "My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿And when he turned his face (tawajjaha)﴾, that is, he turned his face, ﴿toward Madyan﴾, that is, toward what faces its side. "Tilqa'" originally is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf). Madyan is the town of Shu'ayb, named after Madyan ibn Ibrahim, upon him peace. It was not within the authority of Pharaoh, and so he turned toward his town. It was said that he turned toward it because of his knowledge of it, and it was said that it was because of his kinship with it, upon both of them be peace. Between it and Egypt was a distance of eight (days' journey).

﴿He said: "It may be that my Lord will guide me to the right way (sawa' al-sabil)"﴾, that is, the middle of the path that leads to salvation. Moses, upon him peace, said this out of reliance upon Allah the Exalted and confidence in the goodness of His guidance, Mighty and Majestic. He, upon him peace, did not know the roads. There were three paths; he took the middle one, and those who sought him took the other two. They said: "The one who is guided does not take the greatest of the roads, and does not travel except with its (proper) intentions." So he remained eight nights, barefoot, eating nothing but the leaves of trees. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he, upon him peace, did not arrive until the soles of his feet fell off. It is also related that he, upon him peace, began walking without knowing (the way), and Gabriel, upon him peace, guided him to Madyan. From al-Suddi: he, upon him peace, took to the scattered paths (bi-niyat al-tariq), and there came to him an angel on a horse, holding a staff (anzah). When Moses, upon him peace, saw him, he prostrated to him, that is, he submitted out of fear. He said: "Do not prostrate to me, but follow me." So he followed him and went on until he brought him to Madyan.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verses 21–22:

﴿So he went out from it﴾, that is, from the city, complying (mumtathilan).

﴿Fearful, watching out (yataraqqabu)﴾ for the pursuit of those who sought him. ﴿He said: "My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿And when he turned his face (tawajjaha)﴾, that is, he turned his face, ﴿toward Madyan﴾, that is, toward what faces its side. It was not within the authority of Pharaoh, and so he turned toward his town. It was said that he turned toward it because of his knowledge of it, and it was said that it was because of his kinship with it, upon both of them be peace. Between it and Egypt was a distance of eight (days' journey).

﴿He said: "It may be that my Lord will guide me to the right way (sawa' al-sabil)"﴾, that is, the middle of the path that leads to salvation. Moses, upon him peace, said this out of reliance upon Allah the Exalted and confidence in the goodness of His guidance, Mighty and Majestic. He, upon him peace, did not know the roads. There were three paths; he took the middle one, and those who sought him took the other two. They said: "The one who is guided does not take the greatest of the roads, and does not travel except with its (proper) intentions." So he remained eight nights, barefoot, eating nothing but the leaves of trees. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he, upon him peace, did not arrive until the soles of his feet fell off. It is also related that he, upon him peace, began walking without knowing (the way), and Gabriel, upon him peace, guided him to Madyan. So he followed him and went on until he brought him to Madyan.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 23:

﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾: that is, he reached it and came to it. Wurud (arrival) has the meanings of entering and of drinking, and neither of them is intended here.
