The intended meaning of "the water of Madyan" is a well from which they used to water (their flocks), so it is a metaphor by mentioning the locality while meaning the place (majaz min iṭlaq al-hal wa iradat al-mahall). ﴿He found upon it﴾: that is, above its brink and its drawing-place, ﴿a community of people﴾: that is, a large group of differing kinds. The indefinite form (tanwin) indicates the first qualification, and "of people" (min al-nas) indicates the second, since it includes the different kinds, and this is the benefit of mentioning it. It has been said that its benefit is to belittle those groups, and that they were base people who are not known except by their kind, or that they needed to be told that they were of mankind. ﴿Watering﴾: the apparent meaning is that they were watering livestock of various kinds, in the sense that some of them watered camels and some watered sheep, and so on. Specifying their watering with one type needs a transmitted report (tawqif). ﴿And he found, apart from them﴾: that is, in a place lower than their place. It has been said: from near them, or from others, or from the side that faced him when he came to them. Ibn 'Atiyya went to this last view when he said: the meaning is that he found, from the direction he reached before he arrived at the community, ﴿two women﴾. The name of one of them is said to be Layya, and it is said Abra, and it is said Sharfa. The name of the other is said to be Safuriyya, and it is said Safura, and it is said Sufayra. In al-Kashshaf, Sufayra is the name of the younger and Safra is the name of the elder. ﴿Holding back﴾: they were keeping their sheep from the water out of fear of the strong watering men, as Ibn 'Abbas and others said. It has been said: they were keeping their sheep from advancing to the well so that they would not mix with others; this is reported from al-Zajjaj. Qatada said: they were keeping people away from their sheep. Al-Farra' said: they were holding their sheep back from scattering. In all these sayings there is a clear statement that what was being held back was sheep, and the apparent meaning is that this is from a transmitted report. It has been said: they were turning away from their faces the gaze of onlookers, so that they might cover themselves, and this, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿He said: what is your affair?﴾: that is, what is your matter and what is your aim in what you are doing, of holding back and driving away? And why do you not undertake the watering as others do? The root of khatb is the verbal noun of khataba, meaning "to seek", and then it was used in the sense of the object (maf'ul). In his, peace be upon him, addressing the two of them, there is evidence for the permissibility of speaking with a non-related woman concerning what is needed.

Shamir read "ma khitbukuma" with a kasra on the kha'. In al-Bahr he said: that is, "who is your husband?" and "why does he not water?" This is an irregular and rare reading, end of quote. What is in it is not hidden, and the answer does not fit it. Some said: al-khatb in it means the one sought and the object of seeking, as in the mutawatir reading, and its parallel is al-hibb with a kasra on the unpointed ha', meaning the beloved.

﴿They said: we do not water until the shepherds send away (their flocks)﴾: that is, our custom is not to water until the shepherds have turned their livestock away from the water after they have quenched their thirst, because we are unable to compete with them, not that we do not water today up to that limit. Ibn Musarrif read "la nusqi" with a damma on the nun, from the causative (isqa). Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-Hasan, Qatada, and the two Arab readers Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "yasdura" with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the dal, meaning until the shepherds bring their flocks away (from the water). Some kings asked about the difference between the two readings in terms of meaning. He was answered that the reading yasdura with a fatha on the ya' indicates the extreme of their modesty and their concealing themselves from mixing with strangers, while the reading yusdura with a damma on the ya' indicates the shepherds sending away the livestock, and from it is not understood their own departure from the water. It was read with a pure za' and with a letter between the sad and the za'. "Al-ri'a'" was read with a damma on the ra'. The known form of plurals is fi'al with a kasra on the fa', as in the reading of the majority. As for fu'al with a damma, it is contrary to analogy, since it is one of the patterns of verbal nouns and singular nouns, like nubah and sura<u>kh</u>. When it is used in the sense of the plural, as in the irregular reading, it is said to be a collective noun (ism jam') and not a plural; it is said that it is an original plural; it is said that it is a plural but its original form is with a kasra, and the damma in it is a substitute for the kasra, just as it is a substitute for the fatha in words like sukara (drunkards). The words of this type attested in Arabic speech are a limited set, which al-Khafaji mentioned in his commentary on Durrat al-Ghawwas, and the well-known ones of them, according to what he said, are eight. Sadr al-Afadil, not al-Zamakhshari, according to the more correct view, versified them with his saying:

We have heard no words other than eight which are plurals and in the form fi'al:
Rabab, Firar, Tu'am, 'Iram, 'Iraq, Rikhal, Zu'ar,
the plural of zi'r, and bisat, the plural of busut, so it is said.

Abu Hayyan held that al-ri'a' in the reading of the majority is also not analogical. He said: because it is the plural of ra'in, and the analogical plural of an active participle denoting a rational being is fi'la, like qadin and qudat, and anything other than this plural is not analogical. 'Ayyash, from Abu 'Amr, read "al-ra'a'" with a fatha on the ra', and it is a verbal noun placed in the position of an adjective, so the singular and plural forms are the same. It is also allowed that it is from what has had its genitive term (mudaf) omitted, meaning "the people of the shepherding".

﴿And our father is an old man, advanced in years﴾: this is a statement by them of an excuse on their part for his peace be upon him, regarding their taking charge of the watering themselves, as if they said: we are two weak women, veiled, unable to compete with men or to crowd among them, and we have no man to undertake this for us; our father is an old man, of advanced age, whom old age has weakened, so we must delay the watering until the people have satisfied their needs from the water. Some have mentioned that he, peace be upon him, phrased the question in the way that his generosity and mercy toward the weak require, when he asked them about what they sought from their delay and driving away, intending that they be answered by a request for help. However, because of their high rank, they took his words as referring to the cause that is answered, and within it is a request for help, since their showing of incapacity is for nothing but that. It has also been said: there is nothing in the speech that indicates their weakness; rather it contains signs of their modesty and concealment. And if they had wished to show incapacity they would have said, "we are unable to water." The meaning of "and our father is an old man" is that we, with our modesty, have only undertaken this matter because of his old age and weakness, and otherwise it would have been incumbent upon him to take it on. Perhaps the preferable view is that they meant to show their incapacity to compete because of weakness and because of the modesty they were created with. Although the speech does not explicitly indicate their weakness, it does point to it for one who has a heart, and one understands from explaining the meaning of their answer passing just now that the clause "our father is an old man" is coordinated with an implied clause. It is also allowed that it be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: we leave off watering until the shepherds send away, while the situation is that our father is an old man. According to most exegetes, their father was Shu'ayb, peace be upon him.

If it is asked: how was it permissible for a prophet of God to be content for his two daughters to water sheep? The answer: the matter in itself is not forbidden, and religion does not reject it. As for manliness (muruwwa), people differ regarding it, customs vary about it, the conditions of the Arabs in this regard differ from those of non-Arabs, and the way of the people of the desert in it differs from the way of the people of the settled towns, especially when the situation is one of necessity. A group went to the view that he was not Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu 'Ubayda that he said: the companion of Musa, peace be upon him, was Athrun, the nephew of Shu'ayb the prophet, peace be upon him. Abu Hayyan also related this view from him, except that he mentioned Harun instead of Athrun. He also related it from al-Hasan, except that he mentioned Marwan instead. Al-Tabarsi related from Wahb and Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar to what Abu Hayyan related from Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj that he said: it reached me that the father of the two women was the nephew of Shu'ayb, whose name is Ra'awil, and someone whom I trust has told me that his name in the Book is Yathrun, the priest of Madyan, and the priest is a rabbi. Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the one who hired Musa, peace be upon him, was Yathrib, the lord of Madyan. In another narration from him it came that his name is Yathrun, which agrees with what was quoted from the Book regarding the name. In these two narrations his being attributed to Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, is not mentioned, so it is possible that the one named by what is in them is his nephew, and it is possible that he is a foreign man unrelated to him. It has been said that their father is not a relative of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, but is a righteous man. Al-Tabarsi related from some of them that Yathrun is the name of Shu'ayb, and some people of the Book informed me of this too, except that he said: with us it is Yathru without a nun at its end. What I myself saw in the second section of the second book of their Torah I have translated. When Pharaoh heard this news, that is, the news of the killing, he sought to kill Musa, so Musa fled from before him and went to the land of Madyan and sat by a well of water. The chief of Madyan had seven daughters; they came, drew water, and filled the troughs to water their father's flock. When the shepherds came and drove them away, Musa stood up, helped them, and watered their flock. When they came to Ra'awil their father, he said: why have you come so quickly today, etc. At the beginning of the third section of it is what I translated: Musa was tending the flock of Yathru, the zeal of the chief of Madyan, etc. So do not be heedless. In al-Bahr, when discussing the phrase "indeed my father invites you", it is said: it was said that their uncle was the owner of the flock, and he is the one who married her off; she referred to him as "father" since he occupied the father's place. The apparent meaning is that the one who says this means by "father" here the uncle. You know that this and similar things mentioned earlier are not said on the basis of opinion, so the criterion for accepting any of that is a report that can be relied upon, and the reports we have examined on this subject differ, and it has not become clear to us which of them is most probable among them. I think you will rely on the well-known view, held by most exegetes, that their father in reality was Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, until there appears to you what requires departing from it. And the apparent meaning of the Almighty's saying:

[p. 62]

﴿فَسَقى لَهُما﴾ (So he watered [their flock] for them). That is, peace be upon him hastened to water [the flock] for them, out of mercy toward them. The source of his compassion was that the two women were [standing] apart with their animals, while the group of people was occupied with watering. For this reason, Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qahir [al-Jurjani] and the author of al-Kashshaf [al-Zamakhshari] held that the omission of the object in يَسْقُونَ (yasquna, "they water") and تَذُودانِ (tadhudani, "they hold back") was for the purpose of focusing on the act itself and treating the verb as intransitive, meaning: watering proceeds from them [the people], and holding back proceeds from them [the two women]. He said: the fact that what is watered and what is held back are camels or sheep lies outside the intended meaning, and may even give a misleading impression. For if it were said, or if it were assumed, that they water "their camels" and the two hold back "their sheep," one would wrongly suppose that the compassion toward them was not because they were [standing] apart with their animals and the people were occupied with watering, but because their flock was sheep and the people's watered animals were camels. This is based on the principle that the locus of benefit in eloquent speech is the final qualifier. Al-Sakkaki (al-Sakkaki) disagreed with them in this, and held that the omission of the object in يَسْقُونَ and تَذُودانِ was merely for brevity, and that the intended meaning is: they water their livestock, and the two hold back their sheep. The same applies to the other verbs mentioned in this verse. Al-ʿAllama al-Thani [al-Taftazani] adopted this view, saying: this is closer to verification, because the compassion did not arise from the fact that the two held back [their animals] and the people watered [theirs], but from the fact that the two held back their sheep and the people watered their livestock. Indeed, had the two been holding back something other than their own sheep, namely their livestock, and the people were watering something other than their livestock, namely, for example, their sheep, the compassion would not have been valid. Al-Sayyid al-Sanad [al-Jurjani] agreed with him on this, and said in clarifying the two positions: The two Shaykhs (ʿAbd al-Qahir and al-Zamakhshari) considered the object toward which the two verbs were transitive to be camels and sheep, for example, that is, the two kinds of livestock, without any attached possessive. This is indicated by their statement, "the fact that what is watered and what is held back are camels or sheep, etc." Each of the two is opposed to the other in itself, and each of them was made, in the statement or the assumed supposition, to be what is attached to it, outside the object, insofar as it is an object not considered together with it. Thus, for them, the object is nothing but the absolute notion of camels and sheep. So if the object were assumed, it would lead to corruption of the meaning, for if the two were holding back camels belonging to them, by way of supposition, the compassion would remain as it is, because it was due only to their inability to water. Al-Sakkaki considered that the object is the sheep attached to the two women and the livestock attached to the people, and each of these is opposed to the other insofar as it is attached. So if the object is not assumed, the meaning is corrupted. This is the more subtle in analysis and the more correct in meaning. [End of his words.] Mawla ʿAbd al-Hakim al-Sialkuti responded to him, saying: There is an objection to this. If non-specification is intended to be general, that is, [they water] their livestock and other than their livestock, and [they hold back] their sheep and other than their sheep, then corruption follows. But if it is intended merely as watering and holding back, without considering a connection to a specific object, as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَوِي الَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ والَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (Are those who know equal to those who do not know?), then there is no corruption. This is because the fact that the nature of watering and holding back is the source of compassion does not require that, when it is connected to a specific object, it should be so, such that watering other than their livestock or holding back other than their sheep would have to be a locus of compassion. So reflect on this. The source of what al-Sakkaki mentioned is his failure to distinguish between the absolute and the general. [End of his words.] It is not hidden that one should add to the nature of watering and holding back some circumstances, such as the circumstance of the nature of watering being realized by strong, dominant men, and the nature of holding back being realized by two weak, veiled women, in a place where people gather for watering. Otherwise, the apparent meaning is that the mere nature of watering and holding back is not fit to be the source of compassion.

Some eminent scholars said: The omission of the object in يَسْقُونَ and يَذُودانِ is because the purpose is the act itself, not the object, for the act is sufficient to prompt the request of Musa, peace be upon him. Anything beyond the intended purpose is an ungainly excess. As for prompting compassion, this is not its place, for it has its own statement: ﴿نَسْقِي حَتّى يُصْدِرَ الرِّعاءُ وأبُونا شَيْخٌ كَبِيرٌ﴾ (We cannot water until the shepherds have driven away, and our father is a very old man). Whoever does not distinguish between the two prompts said what he said. This is refuted by the claim that the source of the request is compassion for their condition, as they [the scholars] have explicitly stated. So his request, peace be upon him, was a means of reaching their assistance and kindness, for he perceived their weakness and helplessness. Had it not been so, there would have been no reason to speak to a non-related woman. Their statement, "we cannot water, etc.," prompts greater compassion, as it is open to increase and decrease. This was objected to: this would only hold if it were granted that he, peace be upon him, perceived their weakness and helplessness from matters he had witnessed. Otherwise, holding back does not indicate that, for it occurs due to weakness and due to other causes. Al-Khafaji reported the words of a group of eminent scholars on this matter, including what we have mentioned from one of the eminent scholars, and he refuted it and raised objections, then said: As for what was objected to regarding compassion, it is a corrupt fantasy. The core of his statement, may God have mercy on him, is to defend what the two Shaykhs held, and he defended it, and more than one scholar has agreed with their statement.

Some objected to the assumption of the object as a construct (muḍāf), saying: the construct indicates ownership, and no one among the people or the two women owns anything. For the apparent meaning regarding the people is that they were shepherds, and it is most common that shepherds do not own [the flocks]. The apparent meaning is that what was in the hands of the two women belonged to their father. It is not hidden that this objection is on the margin of the thyme plant (i.e., trivial). And God Most High knows best. Furthermore, the apparent meaning is that he, peace be upon him, watered for them from the well at which the people were. This is indicated by what is reported: that he, peace be upon him, pushed the people back from the water until he had watered for them. Also, what Ibn Abi Shaybah reported in al-Musannaf, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, and which he judged to be sound, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, who said: When Musa, peace be upon him, came to the water of Madyan, he found on it a group of people watering. When they finished, they replaced the stone over the well, which only ten men could lift. Then he found two women, and said, "What is your affair?" They told him. So he came to the stone and lifted it by himself, then drew water, and drew only one bucket, until the sheep were satisfied. But this contradicts what the apparent meaning of the verse requires: that when he arrived at the water of Madyan, he found the group watering and found the two women holding back. This is clearly about the simultaneity of his finding them with his finding the people, and of their holding back with the people's watering. It is hardly understood from it that his finding the two was after the people had finished watering, as the report indicates. Therefore, perhaps the report is not sound. The judgment of al-Hakim is subject to a ruling that it is not authoritative. It seems that whoever holds it to be sound denies that the verse requires that finding the people watering and finding the two women holding back occurred at the very beginning of their arrival. For it is said: When the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, came to Madinah, fasting became obligatory, and zakat became obligatory, for example, although the obligation of each was not at the very beginning of his arrival. So it is possible that he, peace be upon him, found a group watering at the very beginning of his arrival, and after they finished watering and set the stone over the well, he found the two women holding back, and addressed them with, "What is your affair?" and what happened happened. And their holding back may be interpreted as preventing their sheep from advancing to the well, since they knew that it had been covered with a stone that they could not lift. One may elaborate on the answer as much as one wishes. Or one may say the verse is to be taken in its apparent sense, and grant that it requires the simultaneity of the two findings and the holding back and watering in time, but deny that the report contains anything contradicting that. For it is possible that the meaning is: when he arrived at the water of Madyan, he found on it a group watering, and he found, beyond them, two women holding back. When they finished, they replaced the stone, and behold, the two women were present with him, before him. He asked them, and they told him, etc. So after finishing the watering, what occurred is not the finding of the two women holding back, but their presence before him. All of this is as you see. And it seems to me that you rely on the report not being sound.

It was said: He, peace be upon him, watered for them from another well. For ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, in a lengthy report, that when he asked the two women and they answered, he said: "Is there water near you?" They said: "No, except for a well covered with a stone that a group cannot lift." He said: "Then go and show it to me." So they went with him, and he pushed the stone with his hand and removed it, then drew for them one bucket, and watered the sheep. Then he replaced the stone in its place.

[Quran] ﴿ثُمَّ تَوَلّى إلى الظِّلِّ﴾ (Then he turned back to the shade): the shade that was there. According to what is reported from Ibn Masʿud, it was the shadow of a tree, said to be a samurah (acacia-type tree). It was also said to be the shadow of a wall that had no roof.

It was also said: he, peace be upon him, placed his back toward what had been facing his face from the sun. This is what is meant by the saying of God Most High: ﴿ثُمَّ تَوَلّى إلى الظِّلِّ﴾. And this, as you see, is [weak]. [Quran] ﴿فَقالَ رَبِّ إنِّي لِما أنْزَلْتَ إلَيَّ﴾ (and he said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need"). That is: for whatever You send down to me from the treasures of Your bounty.

[Quran] ﴿مِن خَيْرٍ﴾ (of good), whether great or small. [Quran] ﴿فَقِيرٌ﴾ (in need), that is, in want. It is the predicate of إنَّ (inna), and to it is connected لِما (li-ma). Because of what we have pointed to, namely its implying the sense of need, it takes the preposition اللام (lam, "to/for"). It was permitted that it implies the sense of seeking, and the lam is for emphasis. It was also said that the lam may be explanatory, so it is connected to a deleted verb "aʿnī" (I mean). And (ما, ma) in all these possibilities is an indefinite relative pronoun (nakirah mawsufah), and the sentence after it is its description, and the resumptive pronoun is deleted, and مِن خَيْرٍ (min khayr) is an explanation of it, and the tanwin in it signifies generality. The statement is an allusion to what he would be given to eat, due to the intensity of hunger he had suffered. The use of the past tense in أنْزَلْتَ (anzalta, "You sent down") instead of the present is for the sake of entreaty, like the opening with "Lord" (rabb). Repetition of the clause is for emphasis. What indicates that the statement is an allusion to this is what Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas ibn Malik, may God be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'When Musa, peace be upon him, watered for the two maidens, then turned to the shade and said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need," he was then in need of a handful of dates.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Musa, peace be upon him, said: 'My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need.' He was the most honored of God's creation, and he was in need of half a date, and his belly was stuck to his back from the intensity of hunger."

In another narration from him: "He, peace be upon him, asked for a piece of bread with which to brace his back against hunger, and he, peace be upon him, had arrived at the water of Madyan." And as Ahmad reported in al-Zuhd and others from the rabbi (scholar), "so that the greenness of the herbs could be seen through his belly from emaciation." Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, and most of the exegetes held that the statement is an allusion to this. ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, used to say: "By God, he asked only for bread to eat." It was also permitted that the lam is for causation, and that ما (ma) is a relative pronoun, and min is for explanation, and the indefiniteness in khayr is for the sake of indicating a type and for magnification. The complement of فَقِيرٍ (faqir) is implied: that is, "indeed I am in need of food, or of worldly things, for the sake of what You have sent down to me of the good of religion, which is salvation from the wrongdoers. For he, peace be upon him, had been with Pharaoh in dominion and wealth. The purpose for him is not an allusion to what he would be given to eat, nor complaint and impatience, but rather to display pride and gratitude for that." The reason for the use of the past tense in this interpretation is clear.

You know that this is contrary to what is transmitted, on which the majority rests. A similar case is what is reported from al-Hasan, that he, peace be upon him, asked for an increase in knowledge and wisdom. This too is not free from distance. There also came from Ibn ʿAbbas that the two women heard what he said, so they returned to their father. He was surprised at the speed of their coming, so he asked them, and they told him. He said to one of them: "Go and call him."

[Page 65]

﴿Then one of the two women came to him﴾. It is said she was the elder of the two, and it is said she was the younger. According to some narrations, they were twins, and one was born half a day before the other.

Ibn Muhaysin read "حِداهُما" (*ḥidāhumā*) with the hamzah dropped for ease, which is irregular, like the saying "ويْلُمِّهِ" (*waylummih*) for "ويْلِ أُمِّهِ" (*wayl ummih*). ﴿Walking﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of "came."

God's words ﴿with modesty﴾ are attached to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause referring to the pronoun in "walking." The meaning is: she came to him walking, being with modesty. So the meaning is that she was modest both while walking and while coming, not only when coming. The indefinite form of "modesty" (*istiḥyāʾ*) is for emphasis. From here it is said that she came "shy and veiled" (*mutakhaffirah*), that is, extremely bashful.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted, through ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī al-Hudhayl, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: she came concealed, with the sleeve of her garment over her face. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted it from Abū al-Hudhayl as a statement of his own (mawqūf). In another narration traced to ʿUmar, which al-Ḥākim authenticated, the wording is: "placing her garment over her face."

﴿She said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*) following from a question that arises from the narration of her coming to him (peace be upon him). It is as if it were asked: "What did she say to him (peace be upon him)?"

It is said: She said: ﴿Indeed my father invites you so that he may reward you for the watering you did for us.﴾ That is, a recompense for your watering. Here "mā" is a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle. It cannot be a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), because what deserves a reward is the action, not the water itself, since the water was permissible to all. She attributed the invitation to her father and gave the reason as recompense, so that her speech would not give rise to suspicion. In this there is clear evidence of perfect intellect, modesty and chastity.

It is related that he (peace be upon him) answered her and went with her. He said to her: "Walk behind me and direct me to the path, for I dislike that the wind should blow against your garments and reveal your body to me." And she did so.

In another narration, he said to her: "Be behind me, for I am a man who does not look at the backs of women, and guide me to the path, to the right or to the left."

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, Ibn Zayd and others that she first walked in front of him, but the wind pressed her garment against her body, and she described it to him. So he said to her: "Walk behind me and direct me to the path," and she did so until they reached the house of Shuʿayb (peace be upon him).

﴿So when he came to him and related the account to him﴾: that is, what had happened to him of the story that was told. "Qaṣaṣ" is a verbal noun used as the name of the thing narrated, like "ʿilal" (for "causes"). ﴿He said: Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾: meaning Pharaoh and his people. He said this because Pharaoh had no authority in his land. It is possible that he said it by inspiration or something similar.

Scholars differ about who prompted him (peace be upon him) to accept the invitation. It is said that what appears from the apparent sense of the noble text is that Moses (peace be upon him) answered the woman who summoned him without hesitation, in order to seek the blessing of seeing the elderly man and to gain support from his opinion, not out of desire for the wage she had mentioned. Do you not see what

Ibn ʿAsākir transmitted from Abū Ḥāzim, who said: When Moses entered upon Shuʿayb (peace be upon them both), he found food prepared. Shuʿayb said to him: "Eat." Moses said: "I seek refuge in Allah, the Exalted." He said: "Why? Are you not hungry?" He said: "Yes, but I fear that this is a return for what I gave to drink to the two of them. We are a family that does not sell any part of the deeds of the Hereafter for the fill of the earth in gold." He said: "No, by Allah. But it is my custom and the custom of my forefathers to host guests and feed the food." So Moses (peace be upon him) sat and ate.

It is also said that what prompted him (peace be upon him) was his need, and it is not objectionable that he (peace be upon him) should accept a wage because of the harm of poverty and destitution.

Aḥmad transmitted from Muṭarrif ibn al-Shikhkhīr, who said: "By Allah, if the Prophet of Allah had anything, he would not have followed her with the draught of milk; but hunger drove him to it."

Some scholars cited, as evidence that his going was out of desire for recompense, what is related from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib: that he (peace be upon him) raised his voice when he said: ﴿My Lord, indeed I am in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾, so that the two of them might hear. For this reason it was said to him: "so that he may reward you," and so on. It is answered that this is not explicit, since it is possible that he did it so that it would be a means of inviting him, not to obtaining the wage. There is no harm, in my view, in his (peace be upon him) having gone out of desire to satisfy his hunger and to gain support from the old man's opinion and knowledge. I do not say that desire to satisfy hunger is desire to obtain a reward for an act of the Hereafter, or that it entails it. The claim that what appears from the apparent sense of the noble text is that he (peace be upon him) answered only for blessing and for support of opinion is not free from obscurity. His acting on the word of a woman is because it falls under the category of reporting, and one acts on the word of a single reporter, whether free or slave, male or female, if they are such. His walking behind a non-related woman is something not objectionable in similar circumstances, together with that caution and scrupulousness.

[Page 66]

﴿She said, one of them﴾: she is the one who invited him to her father, and she is the one who gave him in marriage to Musa, peace be upon them both. ﴿O my father, hire him﴾, i.e., to tend the sheep and take charge of their affairs. The root meaning of *istijar* (hiring, a contract of employment), as al-Raghib said, is seeking something in exchange for a wage, and then it was used figuratively for taking possession of it for a wage, and this is the meaning intended here. Similarly in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾. This is a reason that serves as evidence that he, peace be upon him, is deserving of being hired, as understood from the request to hire him.

Some of them arranged from the verse a syllogism of the first figure, thus: he is strong and trustworthy; and every strong and trustworthy person is fit for hiring; it follows that he is fit for hiring, which is the claim understood from the request. It was objected that this is evident only if *khayr* (best) were a predicate, and it is not so. It was answered that the meaning is as stated, except that it was made a subject (the noun of *inna*) for the sake of drawing attention to the matter of excellence, since it is the foundation of perfection upon which other qualities are built.

In *al-Kashshaf* (Zamakhshari's commentary) it says: If it is asked, how was *khayra man ista'jarta* (the best of whom you hired) made the subject of *inna* while *al-qawiyy al-amin* (the strong, the trustworthy) is the predicate? I say: it is like his saying:

*Indeed the best of people, living and dead, is the captive of Thaqif among them in chains.*

The point is that concern (*ina'ya*) is the reason for the fronting, and it has indeed been fulfilled, to the extent that what is more deserving of being the predicate was made the subject. He meant by this, as it has been said, the greater fitness of *khayr* to be the predicate from the standpoint of grammatical construction. It was argued that *khayr* is attached to *man*, which is indefinite, so it too is indefinite, and to make an indefinite noun the subject of a definite predicate is contrary to what is apparent, although they permitted this with the two comparative and interrogative forms. Also, if *man* were a relative pronoun, then the attachment of the elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*) would be merely verbal and would not confer definiteness, as is one of the two opinions of the grammarians on this point. And according to the view that it confers definiteness, one would say: the definite with *al-* is more definite than the relative pronoun and what is attached to it. It was objected that the definiteness of *al-qawiyy al-amin* is generic, and what has generic definiteness may take the place of the indefinite. It was answered that when the relative pronoun is intended generically, it is likewise, and here this intention is valid so that the plurality required by *khayr* may come about. Since the thing attached to something inferior to it is the one that is more fitting to be the noun, *al-qawiyy al-amin* is more deserving of nominal status, and *khayr* is more deserving of predicate status. When you say that the greater fitness of the predicate status is because the flow of the reasoning requires it, but he diverted to nominal status for the sake of emphasis, you will have freed yourself from many of the disputes.

Shaykh Khalil Efendi al-Amidi said to me, on the day I met him when I was young and he arrived in Baghdad, when a discussion arose about this noble verse: the syllogism derived from it is of the second figure, thus: Musa is strong and trustworthy; and the best one you hired is strong and trustworthy; it yields: Musa is the best one you hired. I said: The most evident objection to this is that the condition for the second figure to produce a conclusion, with respect to quality, is that its two premises differ in affirmation and negation, so that one is affirmative and the other negative; and this is absent in what you have mentioned. He fell silent and withdrew from the discussion, out of fear of disgrace.

You know that the proofs of the Qur'an do not require the order that the logicians established, for that is a technical discipline which God, exalted is He, spared the Arabs from. As for what was mentioned, that making *khayr* a subject serves to draw attention, this is what many have chosen. Al-Tibi allowed that its fronting and its being made a subject may be by way of inversion for emphasis. The apparent view is that the *al-* in *al-qawiyy al-amin* is generic, so Musa, peace be upon him, is included, and this is the point of the argument. The hiring is mentioned in the past tense, although the expected form would be the present tense, to indicate that it is a matter that has been tested and known. Al-Tibi also allowed that by *al-qawiyy al-amin* is meant Musa, peace be upon him, so that it is as if she said: The best one you hired is Musa. The first view is preferable.

Then, her words are a wise and comprehensive statement that cannot be improved upon, for when the two qualities, I mean sufficiency and trustworthiness, are combined in the one who manages your affairs, your mind is at ease and your purpose is accomplished. By sending forth this statement, whose context is that of a proverb and wisdom, she had no need to say: hire him for his strength and his trustworthiness. By my life, such praise from a woman for a man is more beautiful than specific praise, and more preserving of modesty, especially if she understood that her father's aim was to marry her to him. Her knowledge of his strength, peace be upon him, came from what she saw of his repelling the men from the water by himself until he watered for them both; and her knowledge of his trustworthiness came from his not approaching her with anything ugly, despite her being alone and weak.

It is related that when she said what she said, her father said to her: How do you know about his strength?

[Page 67]

She told him that he, peace be upon him, lifted a stone from the well that such-and-such could not lift, and it has already been mentioned in the hadith of Umar, may God be pleased with him, that it could not be lifted except by ten men. The reports about the number of those who could lift it are inconsistent. The least that they said is seven, and the most is one hundred. What indicates the status of the report regarding the lifting has already been mentioned. She also mentioned that he drew water alone with a bucket which forty men could not draw with. He said: How do you know about his trustworthiness? She mentioned what happened between him and her, namely his telling her to walk behind him, and that he lowered his head until she conveyed the message to him.

She put the description of strength first, although the trustworthiness of the hired man in guarding property is more important in the eyes of the employer. This was either because her knowledge of his strength, peace be upon him, came before her knowledge of his trustworthiness, or so that the mention of the description of trustworthiness after it would be by way of ascent from the important to the more important.

It was inferred from her saying *istajirhu* (hire him) that *ijara* (hiring) is lawful according to them, and it was likewise in every religious community, and it is among the necessities of human life and the interest of mutual dealing. This is in contrast to Ibn Aliyya and al-Asamm, who did not permit it. This is what consensus has been formed upon, and their dissent is a breach of it, so it is not to be heeded. This is strange of them, by my life, if they did not permit hiring at all. I have seen in *al-Iklil* that in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine on condition that you hire yourself to me﴾, etc., there is a refutation of those who forbade hiring connected with animals for ten years, because they usually change. So perhaps the hiring which they did not permit is similar to this kind of hiring. The matter in that is easier than the non-permission of hiring absolutely, as is not hidden.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 27:

﴿He said, "Indeed, I intend to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine"﴾. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani, a clause that answers an implied question), as if it were said: "What did her father say after he heard her words?" So it was said: "He said, 'Indeed, I...'" The emphasis of the sentence (by the particle inna) shows the great eagerness for what the sentence contains. In His saying ﴿these two﴾ (hatayn) there is an indication that he had other daughters besides them. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid that the two had four younger sisters. Al-Biqa'i said that he had seven daughters, as in the Tawrat (Torah), and we have already quoted this report. In al-Kashshaf there is evidence for this.

It has been objected that there is no indication in it of what was mentioned, since it suffices, for the need of pointing, that the addressee did not know that these were not the only ones he had. It was replied that, on this view, the anaphoric annexation (al-idafa al-ahdiyya, where the noun refers back to something already known) would suffice without the need for pointing. Thus this implies that the addressee also had knowledge of other daughters known to him, and the pointing is only to exclude the intention of other daughters from among his two other known daughters. Al-Khafaji rightly said: there is no point in disputing this, for such a thing is like a flower that cannot bear rubbing.

Warsh and Ahmad ibn Musa, from Abu Amr, read ﴿أنكحك احدى﴾ (ankihuka ihda) with the hamza removed. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿on condition that you serve me﴾ (ala an ta'jurani) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of ﴿I marry you﴾, meaning: stipulated upon you, or obligatory, or the like. It may also be a circumstantial clause from its subject, as Abu al-Baqa' said. Ta'jurani is from ajartuhu, meaning I became his hired worker (ajir), as in your saying abawtuhu, meaning I became his father. In this sense it takes one object. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿eight years﴾ (thamaniya hijajin) is an adverb of time for it. It may also be that ta'jurani means tuthibuni (rewards me), from the sense that God rewarded him (ajarahu Allah) for what he did, i.e., rewarded him, so it takes two objects, the second being here ﴿eight years﴾. The speech then involves the omission of the modified noun (al-mudaf) and the placing of the modifier (al-mudaf ilayhi) in its place, meaning: "you reward me with the fulfilment of eight years," i.e., you make them my reward and wage for the marriage. By this is meant the bridal gift (mahr).

On this meaning it is also permitted that it be an adverb of time for ta'jurani, with the object omitted, meaning: you compensate me with your service or work during eight years. It is reported from al-Mubarrad that one says ajjartu dari wa mamlukī (I let out my house and my slave), without the madd (elongation), and aajartu with the madd. The first is more common. On this view it takes two objects, the second being omitted, and the meaning is: "on condition that you hire yourself out to me." It may also take one object directly and the second with min, so one says ajjartu al-dara min Amr (I let the house to Amr). The apparent view of most scholars is that there is no difference between aajara with madd and ajjara without it. Al-Raghib said: one says ajjartu Zaydan when the action of one party is considered, and one says aajartuhu when the actions of both are considered, and both return to one meaning. It is said, as in al-Qamus: ajartuhu ajran, and aajartuhu ijaran and mu'ajara.

In Tuhfat al-Muhtaj: aajarahu with madd, ijaran; and with qasr, yajiruhu with kasra or damma of the jim, ajran. In it also: al-ijara (the lease), with the hamza having three vowels, and the kasra being the most eloquent in usage, is a noun for the wage, then it became famous for the contract. And al-hijaj is the plural of hijja with kasra, meaning a year. ﴿But if you complete ten﴾ (fa in atmamta ashran), in the service and work, ﴿then it is from you﴾ (fa min indika), meaning: it is then from you, by way of favour, not from me by way of obligation. ﴿And I do not intend to burden you﴾ (wa ma ureedu an ashuqqa alayka), by imposing the completion of the ten years and by scrutinising the observance of times and the exacting of works. The derivation of mashaqqa (hardship), which is what is difficult to bear, is from ash-shaqq (with a fatha on the shin), which is splitting a thing into two halves, for what is difficult for you splits your opinion about it, because of your hesitation over whether to bear it or not. ﴿You will find me, if God wills, of the righteous﴾ (satajidani in sha'a Allahu mina as-salihin), in good dealing, gentleness of manner, and fulfilment of covenant. What Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, intended by the exception is seeking blessing through it and committing his affair to God's granting of success, not making his righteousness conditional upon God's will, exalted is He, in the sense that if God wills, He makes him act righteously, and if He, mighty and majestic, wills, He makes him act otherwise, since this is not appropriate to the situation.

It has been said: because his righteousness, peace be upon him, is certain, so there is no sense in conditioning it. Similar to it is the saying of al-Shafi'i: "I am a believer, if God wills."

Page 68

﴿He said, "That is between me and you."﴾ *Dhalika* (ذَلِكَ) is the subject (mubtada') and *bayni wa baynak* (بَيْنِي وبَيْنَكَ) is the predicate (khabar). The meaning is: that which you proposed, and on which you made a covenant and set a condition with me, is established and binding between all of us. None of us may depart from it: I may not depart from what you stipulated for me, nor may you depart from what you stipulated for yourself.

As for His words, glory be to Him, ﴿whichever of the two terms﴾, that means the longer of the two or the shorter of the two. ﴿I fulfill﴾ means I will fulfill you by carrying out the service in it. ﴿Then there shall be no injustice against me﴾ is an explicit statement of the intended meaning and an affirmation of the matter of the option (khiyar): there shall be no injustice upon me in demanding an addition to what I have fulfilled of the two terms. The generalization of the negation of injustice to both terms, in the context of the stipulation, is made while the absence of injustice in the longer of them is already certain, in order to make both equal in the negation. That is: just as I will not demand an addition beyond ten, I will not demand an addition beyond eight. Or: whichever of the two terms I fulfill, there is no sin upon me, just as there is no sin upon me in fulfilling the longer, and no sin upon me in fulfilling the shorter, only.

Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] read *"ayyu al-ajalayni ma qadaytu"* (أيُّ الأجَلَيْنِ ما قَضَيْتُ). Here *ma* (فَما) is a superfluous particle (mazīda) for emphasis of the fulfilling: whichever of the two terms I am resolved to fulfill and have directed my determination toward. Likewise, in the first reading, it is superfluous for emphasizing the indefiniteness (ibhām) of the term, i.e., its generality. Making it a negative particle is open to objections that are not hidden.

Al-Hasan and al-Abbas, from Abu Amr, read *"ayma"* (أيْما) with the yā' vowelless and without shaddah, as in the words of al-Farazdaq:

*"I waited for Nasr and the two Simaks, which of them the rains, whose downpours began, poured upon me."*

Its original form is with shaddah, and the yā' was deleted for lightness. It is among those whose 'ayn is a wāw and whose lām is a yā'. Ibn Jinni explicitly stated that it is of the pattern of *awaytu* (أويْتُ) by analogy and derivation. Al-'Allamah al-Tibi has transmitted his words in explaining this in his commentary on al-Kashshaf, so whoever wishes may refer to it.

Abu Haywa and Ibn Qutaib read *"fa-la 'idwana"* (فَلا عِدْوانَ) with a kasra on the 'ayn. ﴿Allah is Witness over what we say﴾ regarding the conditions in force between us. ﴿A Guardian﴾ means a witness over what we say. This is what is narrated from Ibn Abbas. Qatadah said: *ḥafīẓ* (a Preserver). In al-Bahr [al-Muhit]: *al-wakil* is the one to whom the matter is entrusted. Since it is made to imply the meaning of "witness" and the like, it takes *'ala* (عَلى). From here it has been said: that is, a witness and a preserver. The intent is the confirmation of the covenant, and that neither of them has any way at all to depart from it. This is an explanation of what they resolved upon and agreed to establish in general terms, without addressing in detail the obligations of the two contracts of marriage and hiring (ijarah) in that law.

[Page 69]

The words of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed I wish to marry you…﴾ etc., clearly indicate that it was a presentation of his opinion to Musa, peace be upon him, and a request from him for the contract, not an actual conclusion (inshā') and its realization in action. Those who asserted the agreement of the two laws on this did not affirm the manner in which it occurred. It has been said: perhaps the marriage took place on a specific daughter with a dower other than the mentioned service, and the service was mentioned by way of a pledge (mu'āhadah), not a binding contract (mu'āqadah). So it is as if he said: "I wish to marry you one of my two daughters with a specific dower, if you hire me for eight years with a known wage. What do you say about that?" He agreed, and so he contracted with him for one specific one of them. Therefore it is not objected that indefiniteness regarding the woman being married is invalid. As for the service and the benefits of a free person, it is also so according to us, especially if it is said that its period is not specified, and it is also not for the wife but for her father. How then could it be valid as a dower?

It has been said: it is possible that it took place on a specific daughter with the mentioned service as dower, and there is no corruption in making the herding of sheep a dower. This is permissible according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and likewise according to the Hanafiyyah, as is understood from al-Hidayah. It is reported from the author of al-Madarik that he said: "Marrying on the condition of tending sheep is permissible by consensus (ijma'), because it is an undertaking of the matter of marriage, not pure service." Regarding the claim of consensus: if by it is meant the consensus of the imams absolutely, it is open to examination. In al-Muhit al-Burhani: if he married her on the condition that he would tend her sheep for a year, it is not permissible according to the narration of al-Asl. But Ibn Sama'ah related from Muhammad that it is permissible concerning the herding. In al-Intisaf, the position of Malik on this is in three views: prohibition, disapproval, and permissibility. It is said on the view of permissibility: the sheep belonged to the bride, not to her father. There is no indefiniteness in the term, since it is the eight years, and the additional period Musa, peace be upon him, promised to fulfill if it was feasible for him. Moreover, indefiniteness in the dower is permissible, as is explained in the books of furu' (branches of jurisprudence).

Some have said: it is possible that the laws differed in the matter of marriage. Perhaps the marriage of an unspecified daughter was permissible in the law of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and the determination would be for the guardian or for the husband. Likewise, making the service of the guardian a dower, and similar things that are not permissible in our law. It is not objected that what the earlier laws narrated without denial is a law for us, because that is not accepted in an absolute sense.

In al-Iklil, from Makki, he said: in the verse there are particularities regarding marriage. Among them: he did not specify the wife, nor did he set a limit for the start of the period; he made the dower a hire; and he consummated the marriage without executing anything. What the heart inclines to is the difference of the laws regarding the obligations of marriage. Perhaps support for this can be found in the twenty-ninth chapter of the first book of the Torah, that Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him, went to the land of the people of the East. Behold, there was a well in the wilderness, and over its mouth a great stone, and beside it three flocks of sheep. He said to its shepherds: "From where are you, my brothers?" They said: "From Haran." He said to them: "Do you know Laban son of Nahor?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Is he alive?" They said: "Yes, and this is Rachel his daughter with the sheep." Then he said: "This is not the time for gathering the livestock; water the sheep and go and pasture them." They said: "We cannot, until the shepherds gather and roll the stone away from the mouth of the well." While he was speaking to them, Rachel came with her father's sheep. When he saw that, he went forward and rolled the stone away and watered his uncle Laban's sheep. Then he kissed Rachel and wept and told her that he was the son of her paternal aunt Rebekah. She told her father, and he went out to meet him, embraced him, kissed him, and brought him into his house. Then Laban said to him: "Surely you are my bone and my flesh." He stayed with him a month. Laban said to him: "Although you are of my kin, I do not think it proper that you serve me for nothing. Tell me what wage you want." Laban had two daughters: the name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel. Leah's eyes were tender, and Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance. Ya'qub loved her, and said: "I will serve you seven years for Rachel." He said: "Giving her to you is better for me than giving her to another man. Stay with me." So he served him seven years for Rachel. Then he said: "Give me my wife, for my days are complete." Laban gathered the people of the place and made a feast for them. When evening came, he took his daughter Leah and brought her to him, and he went in to her. Laban gave his maidservant Zilpah to her to be her maid. When it was morning, behold, it was Leah. He said to Laban: "What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve you for Rachel?" He said: "Yes, but the younger is not to be married before the elder in our land. Complete the week of this one, and I will give you her sister Rachel also for the service which you will render me for seven more years." Ya'qub completed the week of Leah, and then he gave him his daughter Rachel as a wife, and gave her his maidservant Bilhah to be her maid. When Ya'qub went in to her, he loved Rachel more than Leah, and he served him seven more years. End of quotation.

And some of the People of the Book informed me that it is permissible for the father's service to be a dower for his daughter, and that the father is obliged to satisfy her with something if she is grown; that what he undertook of service need not be performed before consummation, and the undertaking and pledge suffice; that the dower in their view is everything that has value or what is in its ruling; and that the woman's surrender of herself to the husband, content with what she obtains from him of fulfilling desire and benefit, may stand in place of the dower. And that the permissibility of combining two sisters was specific to Ya'qub, peace be upon him. This last point is among what the scholars of Islam have mentioned. Allah the Exalted knows best the soundness of the rest of what was mentioned of these statements.

Now, the scholars have derived several rulings from the verse. In al-Iklil it says: in it is the recommendation for a man to present his marriageable female ward to people of goodness and virtue so that they may marry her; the consideration of a guardian (wali) in marriage; that blindness does not disqualify one from guardianship, for he, peace be upon him, was blind; and the consideration of offer (ijab) and acceptance (qabul) in marriage.

Ibn al-Gharas said: Malik derived from this verse that a father may marry off his adult virgin daughter without consulting her, because no consultation is mentioned in it. He said: some have argued for the permissibility of writing in the dower "I marry her to you," in opposition to one who chose "I marry her to him," saying: "He only possesses the marriage over her, not over him."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: the followers of al-Shafi'i used this verse to show that marriage is restricted to the wording of "inkah" (marrying off) and "tazwij" (wedding). He said: others used it to show the permissibility of combining marriage and hire in one transaction, so they extended it to every transaction combining two contracts and held them valid. He said: our scholars used it to show that wealth is not a consideration in equality (kafa'ah), for Musa, peace be upon him, was not wealthy at that time. He said: in His words, ﴿Allah is Witness over what we say, a Guardian﴾, there is sufficiency with the witness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, since He did not call any of the creation as a witness. This indicates that witnesses are not a condition in marriage. End of al-Iklil.

The Awza'iyyah used it to show the validity of a sale in which one says: "I sell you for a thousand in cash or two thousand on credit." End of what is in al-Iklil, with a little omitted.

It is not hidden what there is in these deductions of disputes and disagreements. Moreover, what was previously reported from Makki, that he, peace be upon him, consummated the marriage without executing anything, is also stated by others. It has also been narrated through the Imamiyyah (Twelver Shi'a) from Abu Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him. It has been said: he, peace be upon him, did not consummate it until he had completed the term.

It has come in some reports that when the two had completed the contract, Shu'ayb said to Musa, peace be upon them both: "Enter that house and take a staff from the staffs that are in it." There were the staffs of the prophets, peace be upon them. He entered and took the staff with which Adam descended from Paradise, and the prophets, peace be upon them, continued to inherit it until it came into the hands of Shu'ayb. Shu'ayb said to him: "Take another instead of this one." But nothing came into his hand except it, seven times. So he knew that it had a status.

And from Ikrimah, who said: Adam, peace be upon him, came out of Paradise with the staff. Jibril, peace be upon him, took it after his death, and it remained with him until he met Musa at night, and he gave it to him.

In Majma' al-Bayan, from Abu Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: Musa's staff was a rod of myrtle from Paradise. Jibril, peace be upon him, brought it to him when he set out toward Madyan.

Al-Suddi said: that staff had been deposited with Shu'ayb by an angel in the form of a man. He commanded his daughter to bring a staff. She went in and took the staff and brought it to him. When the elder saw it, he said: "Bring him another." She returned it seven times, but there came into her hand nothing other than it. So he gave it to him. Then he regretted, because it was a deposit. He followed him, and they disputed over it, and they agreed that the first one who appears in the morning would judge between them. Then the angel came to them and said: "Throw it down; whoever lifts it, it is his." The elder tried to lift it but could not, and Musa, peace be upon him, lifted it.

From al-Hasan: it was nothing but a staff of wood that he took up and handled.

From al-Kalbi: the tree from which he was called was the tree of the jujube (awsaj), and from it was his staff.

[Page 70 and 71 markers are incidental to the source; the text ends here.]

It is related that when he (peace be upon him) began working as a hired shepherd, Shu'ayb said to him: "When you reach the fork of the road, do not take the right-hand path, for although the pasture there is more abundant, there is a serpent (tinnin) in it, which I fear for you and for the sheep." When he reached the fork of the road, the sheep took the right-hand path, and he could not hold them back, so he followed their trail. Suddenly there was green pasture and lush growth the like of which he had never seen. He slept, and then the serpent came upon him. The staff fought against it until it killed it, and then returned to the side of Musa (peace be upon him), bloodied. When he saw it bloodied and the serpent slain, he was content. When he returned to Shu'ayb, he found the sheep full-bellied and abundant in milk. Musa (peace be upon him) told him what had happened, and Shu'ayb rejoiced and knew that Musa and the staff had a great matter. He said to him: "I have given you, from the offspring of my flock this year, every speckled and spotted (adra' and dar'a') animal." Then God Most High revealed to him in a dream: "Strike with your staff the watering-trough of the sheep." He did so and watered them, and not one ewe came to drink without giving birth to a speckled or spotted lamb. Shu'ayb fulfilled what he had promised him.

Yahya ibn Salam related that he (Shu'ayb) gave him every lamb born that was different in color from its mother. God Most High then revealed to Musa (peace be upon him) in a dream: "Cast your staff into the water from which the sheep drink," and he did so, and all of them gave birth to offspring differing from their parents' markings.

Ibn Majah, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and others related, from the hadith of Utba al-Sulami, traced back (marfu'an) to the Prophet (ﷺ): "When he (peace be upon him) wished to part from Shu'ayb, he told his wife to ask her father to give them some of his sheep to live on. He gave her what his flock bore that year of multicolored offspring, and his sheep were black and beautiful. Musa went to his staff and marked it at one end, then placed it at the lowest part of the trough and brought the sheep to drink. He stood facing the trough, and as each ewe came out, he struck her flank, one by one. They became excited and wagged their tails, and all of them gave birth to multicolored young, except one or two sheep, in which there was no (fashush), meaning wide in the udder's milk-flow; nor (dabub), meaning long-uddered, dragging it along; nor (ghazur), meaning narrow in the milk-flow; nor (tha'ul), meaning having no udder except something like two teats; nor (kamsha), which escapes the hand, meaning small of udder, which the hand cannot grasp."

The apparent meaning of this report is that the gift was to his wife (peace be upon him), and that this occurred when he wished to part from Shu'ayb (peace be upon them both). This is contrary to what the apparent meaning of what preceded it requires.

[72]

﴿When Musa had fulfilled the term﴾: i.e., he completed the appointed period that Shu'ayb had required of him. The term meant here is the other one, as Ibn Mardawayh reported from Miqsam, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both.

al-Bukhari and a group of scholars also reported from Ibn Abbas that he was asked which of the two terms Musa, peace be upon him, fulfilled. He said: "He fulfilled the greater and the better of them, for when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said something, he did it."

Ibn Mardawayh also reported through the chain of Ali ibn Asim, from Abu Haarun, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that a man asked him which of the two terms Musa fulfilled. He said: "I do not know until I ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." So he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "I do not know until I ask Jibril, peace be upon him." So he asked Jibril, and he said: "I do not know until I ask Mika'il, peace be upon him." So he asked Mika'il, and he said: "I do not know until I ask al-Rafi'." So he asked al-Rafi', and he said: "I do not know until I ask Israfil, peace be upon him." So he asked Israfil, and he said: "I do not know until I ask the Lord of Might, may His majesty be exalted." Then Israfil called out with his loudest voice: "O Lord of Might, which of the two terms did Musa fulfil?" He said: "The more complete of the two terms and the better of them, ten years."

Ali ibn Asim said: Abu Haarun, whenever he narrated this hadith, would say: "Abu Sa'id narrated to me from the Prophet (ﷺ), from Jibril, from Mika'il, from al-Rafi', from Israfil, from the Lord of Might, blessed and exalted is He, that Musa fulfilled the more complete of the two terms and the better of them, ten years."

As for the fa (ف) in the verse, it is said to be a fa of elaboration (fasiha), meaning: so he concluded the two contracts and Musa undertook what was required of him. When he had completed the term, ﴿and he set out with his family﴾. It is said that he set out toward Egypt, with Shu'ayb's permission, to visit his mother, his brother, his sister and his relatives. It seems that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, permitted him to do so because of the long period of his service and because he thought the matter of his offence had been forgotten. It is also said that he set out toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and this is further from gossip and idle talk.

﴿He perceived a fire from the side of the Tur﴾: i.e., he saw it from the direction facing the Tur, not from some part of it, as is the more obvious meaning. The root of ānasa (آنَسَ), it is said, is "to sense," so it is more general than "to see." al-Zamakhshari said: it is clear seeing about which there is no doubt, and from it comes insān al-ʿayn (إنسان العين, the pupil of the eye), because by it a thing is made clear. The word al-ins (الإنس, humankind) is so named because of their visibility, just as al-jinn (الجن) is so named because of their concealment. It is also said that ānasa means seeing what one is comforted by. Some scholars have maintained that what he saw was truly light, but it was described as fire in accordance with Musa's own belief, peace be upon him. Some of the knowers of God said: what he saw was in the form of actual fire, but its reality was beyond the reach of reason, though Musa, peace be upon him, supposed it to be ordinary fire.

﴿He said to his family: "Wait here"﴾: i.e., remain where you are. With him, peace be upon him, according to one view, were his wife and a servant, and the two are addressed in the plural form. According to another view, he also had two sons with him, the elder named Jirshum and the younger named Ilī'azar, who were born to him during his stay with Shu'ayb. This is consistent with the view that he, peace be upon him, had gone in to his wife before beginning what was required of him. But on the view that he did not go in to her until he had completed the term, this is only possible by assuming that he remained for years after that, and this has indeed been said. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid that he said: "Musa fulfilled ten years, then he stayed another ten years after that."

It is also reported from Wahb that a son was born to him on the road, on the night he perceived the fire. In al-Bahr it is said that he, peace be upon him, left with his family and property in the winter season and took a route other than the usual one, fearing the kings of Syria, while his wife was pregnant and did not know whether she would give birth by night or by day. He travelled in the wilderness without knowing its paths, and the journey brought him to the western side of the right bank of the Tur, on a dark, snowy and bitterly cold night. It is also said that, out of jealousy for his womenfolk, he would travel with a caravan by night and leave them by day. One day he lost the way, until night overtook him, and his wife's labour pains came upon her. He struck his flint, and it gave out no spark, so he looked and saw a fire shining from a distance. He said: "Wait here."

﴿"Indeed I have perceived a fire (ʾānastu nāran); perhaps I will bring you from it some news"﴾: i.e., news of the road, by finding there someone who will tell me of it. As you have heard, they had lost their way. The clause is a resumption that has the force of giving the reason for the command.

﴿"Or a brand"﴾: i.e., a thick piece of wood, whether or not it had fire at its tip. It is like the line of poetry:

*And he cast upon Qays a brand of fire, / its heat and its blaze fierce upon it.*

Or it may have had no fire, as in the line:

*The gatherers of wood went out in Layla's name, seeking / sturdy logs, not hollow nor rotten.*

For this reason it is specified, as some of the verifiers said, by the words ﴿from the fire﴾, and the brand itself is made into the fire itself for emphasis, as though, because fire had taken hold of it, it had turned into fire. al-Raghib said: al-jadhwah (الجذوة) is what remains of firewood after it has burned. Abu Hayyan's statement has the same sense: "a piece of wood in which there is fire without flame." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd that he said: "It is a piece of firewood in which there is fire." He and a group of others reported from Qatada that it is the base of a tree with fire at its end. It is said that on this view the min (مِن) is for origin, and the fire meant is the one he perceived.

Most readers recite jidhwatan (جِذْوَةً) with a kasra on the jim, while al-A'mash, Talha, Abu Haywa and Hamza read it with a damma. ﴿"So that you may warm yourselves"﴾: i.e., so that you may get warmth and be heated by it. This indicates that they had been struck by cold.

[Page 74]

Al-Alusi's commentary (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 28, verse 30:

﴿So when he came to it﴾, i.e., to the fire that he had sensed.

﴿He was called from the right side of the valley﴾, i.e., the call reached him from the right side with respect to Moses, peace be upon him, in his journey. So "al-ayman" (the right) describes the shore (*shati'*), and it is the opposite of "al-aysar" (the left). It is also permissible that "al-ayman" means "the one characterized by right (*yumn*) and blessing," the opposite of "al-asham" (the ill-omened). In that case it may be a description of either the shore or the valley. "Min" (from), according to what a group has chosen, denotes the inception of the end point (*ibtida' al-ghaya*), and it is connected to what comes after it. It is also permissible that it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the hidden pronoun of Moses, peace be upon him, in "nudiya" (he was called). The meaning would then be: he was called near the shore of the valley. It is also permissible, on the circumstantial reading, that "min" means "in," as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿What have they created from the earth?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 4]. The meaning would then be: he was called while being in the shore of the valley. His words, exalted is He, ﴿in the blessed place﴾, are in the position of a circumstantial clause from "the shore," or they are a complement to "nudiya."

"Al-buq'ah" is a portion of land that differs in form from what is adjacent to it, and its initial letter may be pronounced with a fatha, as in the *Qamus*. On this reading al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli and Maslama recited it. It is described as blessed because of the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His lights that it was singled out with.

It has been said: it is blessed because of the provisions and good fruits it contains, but this is not the case. His words, glorified is He, ﴿from the tree﴾, are a substitute (*badal*) for His words, exalted is He, ﴿from the shore﴾. Or, "the tree" in it is a substitute for "shore." The preposition is repeated because the substitution is with the repetition of the governing element, and it is a partial substitution (*badal al-ishtimal*), for the shore included the tree, since the tree was growing in it. "Min" here cannot be understood as meaning "in," as you have heard in the first "min." Yes, it is permissible in it that it is causal, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned﴾ [Nuh: 25]. It is connected to "the blessed," meaning: the blessed place because of the tree. It has been said that it is permissible for it to be connected to "the blessed" while still being for inception, meaning that the beginning of its blessing is from the tree.

This tree, according to what has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, was a jujube (*unnab*). According to what has been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, it was a samura tree. According to what has been narrated from Ibn Jurayj, al-Kalbi and Wahb, it was a thorny shrub (*'awsaja*). According to what has been narrated from Qatada and Muqatil, it was a bramble (*'ulayqa*), which is what is mentioned in the Torah today.

"An" in His words, exalted is He, ﴿O Moses﴾, may be explanatory (*tafsiriyya*), and it may be a lightened form of the heavy "an," the original being "bi-annahu," with the preposition connected to "nudiya." Calling may be connected to a preposition, and Abu 'Ali recited:

*I called by the name of Rabi'a ibn Mukdam, that the one who makes known his name, the trusted...*

The pronoun refers to the matter (*shan*), and the matter is explained by His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed I am Allah, the Lord of the worlds﴾. A group recited "anni" with a fatha on the hamza. This raised a difficulty: if "an" is explanatory, "inna" should be with a kasra, which is obvious. And if it is a verbal "an" with the pronoun of the matter as its subject, then likewise, since with a fatha it is made into a verbal noun together with what follows, and that cannot be a predicate of the pronoun of the matter. It was answered by holding that "an" is explanatory, and "anni" and what follows is in the sense of a verbal noun governed by an omitted verb. The estimated meaning is: "O Moses, know that indeed I am Allah," and so on.

It is mentioned in Surah Ta-Ha [11]: ﴿He was called, O Moses, indeed I am your Lord﴾, and in Surah al-Naml [8]: ﴿He was called: blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾. What is here is other than that, rather each one differs from the other, so this raised a difficulty.

[Page 74]

It was answered that the difference is only in wording, while in the intended meaning there is no difference. The Imam (al-Razi) held that He, exalted is He, related in each of these surahs some of what the call included, because the correspondence between what is in the three places requires some effort. The apparent meaning is that the call came from Him, Mighty and Majestic, without an intermediary angel. Moses, peace be upon him, heard, as the reports indicate, a verbal speech. It has been said that He created it in the tree without union or indwelling. It has been said that He created it in the air in the same way, and Moses, peace be upon him, heard it from the direction of the right side, or from all directions. Although everyone points to himself with "I," its meaning is not the place of its wording.

The Shaykh al-Ash'ari and the Imam al-Ghazali held that he, peace be upon him, heard the eternal, essential speech of Allah, without sound or letters. This, as you see, is His essence, Mighty and Majestic, without modality or quantity. Some of the gnostics (*'arifin*) mentioned that he heard His verbal speech, exalted is He, only with a sound, and that this was after His manifestation, Mighty and Majestic, through whatever manifestations He willed that wisdom requires. He, glorified is He, while manifesting in that way, remains upon His absoluteness, even beyond the restriction of absoluteness.

It has come in the authentic (*sahih*) reports that He, exalted is He, will manifest Himself to His servants on the Day of Resurrection in a form, and He will say: "I am your Lord," and they will deny Him. Then He will manifest Himself to them in another form, and they will recognize Him. Allah, exalted is He, and His attributes are behind the veils of might, greatness and majesty. So let thought not entertain the notion that it can attain a standing on the reality in any state whatsoever.

*A goal whose target the intellect falls short of reaching, and below its reach is a hand that does not perish.*

Some of the earlier scholars (*salafiyyun*) mentioned that he, peace be upon him, heard the verbal speech of Allah, exalted is He, only with the sound of one who denies manifestation in the manifestations, considering the saying of this to be among the greatest of abominations. Ibn al-Qayyim has a lengthy discussion in verifying this. We have already presented to you in the introductions what relates to this station, so remember it. Allah, exalted is He, is the Guardian of understandings.

Al-Hasan said: He, glorified is He, called Moses, peace be upon him, with the call of revelation (*wahy*), not the call of speech. The scholars of distinction did not accept this, because it contradicts the apparent meaning, and because the reason for his being specially named "the one who spoke with Allah (*Kalim*)" among the prophets, peace be upon them, does not become evident from it. The reason for the distinction is evident on the view that he heard the eternal speech of Allah, exalted is He, without letters and without apparent sound. Likewise on the view that he, peace be upon him, heard a sound indicating His speech, exalted is He, without the intermediary of an angel or a book, whether it came from one direction, but with a sound not acquired by the servants, as is the case with our hearing, or from all directions, because each of these involves a breach of custom. As for its reason according to those who hold that the hearing was after the manifestation in the appearance, it is likewise, if they say that this manifestation did not occur to any prophet, peace be upon them, other than Moses. Then, his knowledge, peace be upon him, that the One who called him was Allah, exalted is He, was obtained by necessity, by a creation from Him, glorified is He, in him. It has been said: it was by a miracle. The Mu'tazila (*Mu'tazila*, the rationalist school) required that its attainment be by it. Some of them specified it, and some did not specify it, claiming that the attainment of necessary knowledge contradicts moral obligation (*taklif*). There is discussion in this.

And ﴿Throw down your staff﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿O Musa﴾.
