The ﴿fa﴾ in His saying ﴿But when he saw it moving﴾ is the eloquent fa (fāʾ faṣīḥa), indicating omitted clauses, which were left out because the situation points to them and to show how quickly what they signify came about. The sense is: "So he threw it, and it became a serpent and moved. When he saw it moving and writhing, ﴿as if it were a jann﴾." It was a serpent, black-eyed (kaḥlāʾ al-ʿayn), harmless, and quick in its movement (kathīra fī al-dawr). The comparison with it is in terms of the speed of its motion and its agility, not in its form or bulk. It cannot be said that when he threw it, it became a huge serpent (thuʿbān), so how can it be likened to a jann? Some have said: it is permissible that the intended meaning is likening it to the jann in form and bulk, and there is no difficulty in that, because the serpent has varying states in which it becomes thinner or thicker. It has also been said that jann is applied to large serpents, so when it is likened to them in this respect, that is intended. But the first explanation mentioned is preferable.

﴿He turned back in flight﴾, retreating in fear of it. ﴿And did not return﴾, that is, did not come back. ﴿O Musa﴾, that is, he was called, or it was said: "O Musa!" ﴿Come forward and do not fear; indeed you are among the secure﴾, safe from dangers, for ﴿the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾.

Page 75

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 32:

﴿Insert your hand﴾, i.e., put it ﴿into your pocket (jayb)﴾, which is the opening of the robe through which the head comes out. ﴿It will come out white, without harm (su')﴾, i.e., without a defect. ﴿And draw your wing (janah) to yourself against fear (al-rahb)﴾, i.e., because of dread. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: He (glorified is He) commanded him to press his upper arm and forearm, which is the "wing," to his side, so that his fright would be lessened by this, and it is part of human nature that when a person does this at the time of fright, his heart grows stronger. Al-Thawri said: Musa (peace be upon him) feared that some harm had befallen him, so He (glorified is He) commanded him to return his hand to his side so that it would return to its first state, and he would know that this was not a harm but a sign from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Close to this is what has been said: The meaning is that if a matter terrifies you because of the brilliance that overpowers you from it, then press it to yourself and your fear will subside.

In al-Kashshaf there are two meanings to this. The first is that when Allah the Exalted turned the staff into a serpent, Musa was alarmed and agitated, and he shielded himself with his hand, as a frightened person does from something. He was told: Your shielding yourself with your hand carries a shame before the enemies. So when you throw it down and it turns into a serpent, put your hand under your upper arm in place of your shielding yourself with it, then bring it out white, so that two things are achieved:

avoiding what is a shame for you, and displaying another miracle. The "wing" here means the hand, because a person's two hands are like the two wings of a bird; and when he puts his right hand under his left upper arm, he has drawn his wing to himself. The second meaning is that by drawing his wing to himself is meant his steadiness, self-control and firmness when the staff turned into a serpent, so that he would not be agitated or fear, a metaphor taken from the action of a bird, because when it is afraid it spreads its wings and lets them droop; otherwise its wings are folded against it and tucked in.

The meaning of "min al-rahb" (against fear) is "because of the fear," i.e., when the dread overtakes you at the sight of the serpent, then draw your wing to yourself. He made the dread that used to afflict him a cause and reason for what he was commanded to do, namely drawing his wing to himself. The meaning of ﴿draw your wing to yourself﴾ and His statement (exalted is He) ﴿insert your hand into your pocket﴾ is one and the same according to one of the two interpretations, but the two expressions differ. He repeated the one meaning only because the purposes differ: the purpose of the first is the hand coming out white, and the purpose of the second is the concealing of the fright. (End of quotation.) Drawing the wing, according to the second interpretation, is a metonymy (kinayah) for steadfastness and self-control, like the saying:

"Tighten your belly-bands for death, for death will meet you."

This is taken from the action of a bird when it is secure after fear. It was originally a metaphor from the bird's action in this state, then its use became common for steadfastness and self-control until it became a proverb for it and a metonymy for it. On this reading it serves as a completion (tatmim) for the meaning of ﴿Indeed you are among the secure﴾. This is taken from the words of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, who said: This is a command from Him (glorified is He) to resolve upon what He wants from him and an urging to diligence in it, lest the diligence that overtakes him at some times prevent him from proceeding with what he was commanded to carry out.

The intended "drawing" is not the drawing that removes the gap between two things, and this is further from disputation than what al-Zamakhshari mentioned. Similar in avoiding disputation is what al-Biqa'i said: that by drawing his wing to himself is meant his steadiness and self-control when his hand came out white, so that he would not be wary or be agitated from fear. By one of the two interpretations he meant the first aspect, since the meaning on it is: insert your right hand under your left upper arm.

Some have said: the meaning is: draw your two outstretched hands together, by inserting the right under the left upper arm and the left under the right, or by inserting both into the pocket. Its apparent sense is that by "the wing" is meant the two wings, and al-Tabarsi clearly stated this in something like what was mentioned, and said: The singular has indeed come meaning the dual, as in his saying:

"Your two hands are one hand, one of which is all generosity,
And your left palm is a spear that you plunge into danger."

The meaning is "your two hands are two hands," as shown by his saying "one of which." In al-Kashshaf there is also, among the innovated interpretations (bida' al-tafasir), that "al-rahb" means the sleeve in the dialect of Himyar, and that they say: "Give me what is in your rahb," i.e., in your sleeve. I wonder how this is established in the language, and whether it has been heard from the reliable authorities whose Arabic is accepted? Then I wonder how it fits in the verse, and how it applies in detail as the other words of revelation do? Moreover, Musa (peace be upon him) on the night of the discourse wore nothing but a woolen cloak with no sleeves. (End of quotation.) What he pointed out, that this does not match the eloquence of the revelation, is beyond doubt, for those who held this view said: The meaning according to it is: ﴿and draw to yourself your hand, brought out from the sleeve﴾, because his hand had been in the sleeve. This is a meaning, as you see, and its wording is shorter in conveying it.

As for the matter of hearing it from reliable authorities, it has been challenged in al-Bahr by the fact that it is related from al-Asma'i, who is trustworthy and reliable. Al-Tibi said: Muhyi al-Sunnah said: al-Asma'i said: I heard some of the Bedouins saying: "Give me what is in your rahb," i.e., what is in your sleeve. Some claim that the use of rahab for the sleeve is also the dialect of Banu Hanifah, and it is so among them and likewise among Himyar, with the vowel of the ra' and ha' being fatha. In my view, there is no certainty about the existence of this dialect. Even if it is established, it is not proper to interpret the noble revelation by it.

The apparent view is that "min al-rahb" is connected to "ḍummu" (draw). Abu al-Baqa' said: it is connected to "wallā" (he turned), and it has been said: to "mudbiran" (retreating), and it has been said: to an omitted word: i.e., be calm from the fear. It has also been said: to "ḍummu." There is no hiding what is in its connection to other than "ḍummu," though it indicates connection to "wallā" or "mudbiran." The statement of Ibn Jurayj, as transmitted from him by Ibn al-Mundhir, makes the verse one of hyperbaton (taqdim wa ta'khir), where the meaning is: he turned back, retreating, from the fear. The Two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr?) and the Meccan and Medinan readers recited "min al-rahab" with fatha on the ra' and ha'. Most of the Seven Readers recited it with damma on the ra' and sukun on the ha'. Qatadah, al-Hasan, 'Isa and al-Jahdari recited with damma on both, and all are dialects.

﴿Those two (fa-dhanika)﴾, i.e., the staff and the hand. The masculine form is used out of regard for the predicate, which is His statement (exalted is He): ﴿two proofs (burhanan)﴾. It has also been said: the reference is to the turning of the staff into a serpent after it was thrown down, and the bringing out of the hand white after it was inserted into the pocket. The masculine usage is then evident. "Burhan" means a clear proof. It is on the pattern fu'lan, from their saying "abarra al-rajul" (the man produced a proof) from "barra al-rajul" (the man became white). A white woman is called "burha'" and "burhardhah."

Some have said: it is fu'lan from "al-barh," meaning cutting, so it is explained as a decisive proof. It has also been said: it is fu'lan from their saying "barhana" (to prove). It is reported from most that "barhana" is a later coinage derived from the word "burhan."

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir recited "fa-dhannaka" with shaddah on the nun, and this is a dialect of it. It was said that it is a substitute for the omitted alif of dha in the dual, where its alif became a nun and was assimilated. Al-Mubarrad said: it is a substitution for the lam of dhalika, as if they inserted it after the dual nun, then the lam was changed to a nun because of the nearness of the articulation point and assimilated; and the analogical expectation was to change the first, but the sign of the dual was preserved.

Ibn Mas'ud, 'Isa, Abu Nawfal, Ibn Hurmuz and Shibl recited "fa-dhaniyka" with a ya' after the kasrah nun. This is the dialect of Hudhayl. It has also been said that it is rather the dialect of Tamim. Shibl transmitted it from Ibn Kathir, and also from him: "fa-dhanayka" with fatha on the nun before the ya', according to the dialect of those who make the dual nun fatha, as in his saying:

"Upon two swift ones (ahwadhayn), they departed one evening,
And it was but a glance, and they disappeared."

From Ibn Mas'ud it is also reported that he recited with shaddah on the nun, kasrah, and a ya' after it. It is said this is the dialect of Hudhayl. Al-Mahdawi said: rather, their dialect is to lighten it.

"From your Lord (min rabbika)" in His statement ﴿from your Lord﴾ is connected to an omitted word, which is an attribute of "two proofs," i.e., existing from your Lord. "To (ila)" in His statement (glorified is He) ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ is also connected to an omitted word. According to what the apparent sense of some of them requires, it is an attribute following an attribute of it, i.e., reaching them. According to what the apparent sense of others requires, it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from it, i.e., "sent with them to them."

In al-Bahr it is said that it is connected to an omitted word indicated by the meaning, its estimated form being: "Go to Pharaoh ﴿for they were a corrupt people (qawman fasiqin)﴾," i.e., they had gone outside the bounds of injustice and transgression, so they were deserving that We send you to them with these two dazzling miracles. The discussion of "kanu" (they were) is known from what preceded in its parallels.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 28, verses 33–34:**

[Page 78]

﴿He said, "My Lord, I killed a soul among them, so I fear that they will kill me"﴾ for that reason, ﴿that they will kill me﴾ in retaliation for it. The purpose of this statement is to seek protection and support so that he may convey the message in the most complete manner, not to seek to be excused from being sent. The Jews claimed that he (peace be upon him) asked his Lord, glorified is He, to be excused from this. In the Torah that is in their hands today, he is reported to have said: "O Lord, send whom You will send." He reinforced his request for support with his saying: ﴿And my brother Aaron, he is more eloquent in speech than I, so send him with me as a helper (ridan)﴾, meaning an aide, as narrated from Qatada, and Abu Ubayda adopted this view and said: "It is said: radatuhu ʿalā ʿaduwwihi, meaning I helped him against his enemy."

Abu Hayyan said: al-ridd is the helper by whom the matter is strengthened. It is a verb in the sense of a passive participle (fiʿl bi-maʿnā mafʿūl), so it is a noun for what one is aided by, just as al-difʾ (warmth) is a noun for what one warms oneself with. Salama ibn Jandal said:

*"And my ridʾ is every white Musharrafi sword, of sharp edge, keen, with nicks."*

It is also said: radaʾtu al-ḥāʾiṭa arduʾuhu, when you prop up the wall with a piece of wood so that it does not fall.

As for His saying ﴿more eloquent than I﴾, it indicates that he (peace be upon him) also had eloquence, but the eloquence of his brother is greater than his. Abu Jaʿfar, Nafiʿ and the two Medinans recited *ridan* with the hamza dropped and its vowel transferred to the dal. The well-known reading of Abu Jaʿfar is that he recited with the transfer, without hamza and without tanwin. Its basis is that he treated the connected form as if it were the pause form (wasl treated as waqf). With the lighter reading, *ridan* may also be considered a defective noun (manqūṣ) in the sense of an increase, from radaytu ʿalayhi, when I added to it. ﴿He will confirm me (yuṣaddiqunī)﴾, meaning he will clarify the truth with his tongue, expound the matter, and dispute with the disbelievers by it. So *taṣdīq* (confirmation) is a metaphor for the aforementioned clarification, which brings about confirmation, because he is like a witness to his speech. Ascribing it to Aaron is literal, and this is indicated by ﴿And my brother Aaron...﴾, etc., because the excellence of eloquence is only needed for what has been mentioned, not for the saying "You have spoken truly" or "My brother Moses is truthful," for Sahban and Baqil are equal in that. Alternatively, the wing of my speech joins with clarity, so that the people whose denial I fear will confirm me. Then *taṣdīq* is in its literal sense, and it was ascribed to Aaron (peace be upon him) because by his clarification he brought about the people's confirmation. This is supported by His saying ﴿Indeed I fear that they will deny me﴾, since it indicates that the confirmation is in the literal sense.

It was also said: the confirmation of another means making his truthfulness apparent. Just as it can occur by saying "He is truthful," it can also occur by supporting him with proofs and the like, such as God's confirmation of the prophets (peace be upon them) through miracles. What is meant here is confirmation by means of proofs, so the meaning is: my truthfulness will become apparent through the establishment of proofs and the refutation of doubts, ﴿Indeed I fear that they will deny me﴾, while my tongue will not obey me during argument. According to this, there is no need to claim metaphor either in the verb or in the ascription.

It has been objected that his truthfulness means either that he said "He is truthful" or that he said to him "You have spoken truly." Therefore, applying it to another is apparently metaphorical. The clause *yuṣaddiqunī* may be a qualifier of *ridan*, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or a resumptive new clause (istiʾnāf).

Most of the Seven Readers recited *yuṣaddiqnī* with jazm, as an answer to the imperative (jawāb al-amr).

Some claimed that on the reading with raf', the answer is elided; it is objected that an imperative does not necessarily require an answer, so there is no need to claim elision.

Ubayy and Zayd ibn ʿAlī, may God be pleased with them, recited *yuṣaddiqūnī* with the plural pronoun. It refers to Pharaoh and his chiefs, not to Aaron, and the plural is for honor, as has been said. According to what is reported from Ibn Khalawayh, the verb is jussive. He took this reading as evidence for those among the Seven who read *yuṣaddiqnī* with jazm, and said: "For if it were in the raf' form, it would be *yuṣaddiqūnanī*." Abu Hayyan, after reporting that the jazm is as an answer to the imperative, and that the meaning of *yuṣaddiqūnī* is "hope for their confirmation of me," said: "So reflect."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 35:

﴿He said: "We will strengthen your arm through your brother."﴾ This is a response to Moses' request, and according to what has been said, it refers back to his words ﴿So send him with me...﴾ and so on. The meaning is: "We will strengthen you through him and help you." The phrase شَدُّ عَضُدِهِ (shaddu 'adudihi, "tightening his arm") is a talwihi kinayah (an allusive metonymy, where the expression indirectly points to its meaning) for strengthening him, because the hand becomes strong when the upper arm (عَضُد, 'adud, the part between the elbow and the shoulder) is strong, and the whole body is strengthened when the hand is strengthened. There is no obstacle to taking the expression literally, since "through your brother" is not included in what was made a metonymy. Alternatively, this may be an isti'arah tamthiliyyah (a figurative representation, in which a whole scene is likened to another), where the state of Moses, peace be upon him, being strengthened by his brother is likened to the state of the hand being strengthened by a strong upper arm. It is also permitted that there is a majaz mursal (an unrestricted metonymy, where a word is used for something related to it) of the type of using the cause for the effect, on two levels, so that the original is: "We will strengthen you through him, then We will support you, then We will tighten your arm through him."

Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-Hasan read عُضُدَكَ (‘ududaka) with two damma vowels. It is also reported from al-Hasan that he read it with a damma on the ʿayn and a sukun on the ḍād. ʿĪsā read it with a fatha on both. Some read it with a fatha on the ʿayn and a kasra on the ḍād. It is also said عَضْدٌ (‘aḍd) with a fatha on the ʿayn and a sukun on the ḍād, but I do not know of anyone who read it that way.

﴿And We will give you both authority (sultan)﴾, that is, a great domination and superiority. According to what has been said, this also refers back to his words ﴿Indeed I fear that they will deny me.﴾

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So they will not reach you﴾ is a consequence of what has been achieved from his request, meaning: they will not reach you by overpowering you or by argument ﴿through Our signs﴾. The phrase بِآياتِنا (bi-ayatina, "through Our signs") is connected to a deleted element, which has been made explicit in other places, meaning: "Go with Our signs," or it is connected to نَجْعَلُ (naj'alu, "We will give"), meaning: "We will empower you through Our signs," or to سُلْطانًا (sultanan, "authority"), because it contains the meaning of domination and superiority, or it is connected to the meaning of لا يَصِلُونَ (la yasiluna, "they will not reach"), meaning: "you will be protected from them by them," or it is connected to the negative particle according to the view of some who permit the prepositional phrase to be connected to it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permitted that this is an oath whose answer is لا يَصِلُونَ (la yasiluna), placed before it, or it is one of the oaths that come in the middle of speech and are inserted into it merely for emphasis, so it needs no answer at all. It is objected to the first view that the answer of an oath does not precede it, nor is it joined with the particle of consequence (fa’) either. Perhaps he meant that this indicates the answer, while the answer itself is deleted, but he was lax in the expression.

It is also permitted that بِآياتِنا is a complement (silah) of a deleted element which is explained by the word الغالِبُونَ (al-ghalibuna, "the victors") in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿You two and whoever follows you are the victors﴾. Or it is a complement of it, with the definite article in الغالِبُونَ being the definite article of definiteness and not in the sense of الَّذِي (alladhi, "who"), or in its sense according to the view of those who permit placing what is in the complement's domain before the relative pronoun, either absolutely or when the placed element is an adverbial phrase. Its placement is either for the sake of the verse's ending (fasilah) or for restriction (hasr).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 36:

﴿So when Moses came to them with Our clear signs﴾ i.e., signs clear in their indication of the truth of his prophethood, peace be upon him, from Him, the Mighty and Majestic. The apparent meaning is that by "the signs" are meant the staff and the hand, since these are the two that Moses, peace be upon him, displayed at that time. The reason for expressing them in the plural form has already been discussed in Surah Ta-Ha (sirr al-ta'bir, the secret of the expression). (They) said, "This is nothing but ﴿fabricated magic﴾" i.e., magic that you have invented, the like of which was not done before him, so that iftira' (fabrication, from al-iftira', "invention") is in the sense of ikhtilaq (inventing), not in the sense of kadhib (lying). Or it is magic that you learned from someone else and then falsely attributed to God Most High, so that iftira' is in the sense of kadhib (lying), not in the sense of ikhtilaq (inventing). The qualifier, on these two interpretations, is restrictive. It has also been said:

The intended meaning of iftira'
is tamwih (deception), i.e., it is magic that deceives, having no reality, like all other kinds of magic. In this case the qualifier is emphatic, and iftira' is not in its literal sense as in the first interpretation. The truth is that among the kinds of magic there are some that have a reality, so the qualifier is restrictive here too. ﴿And we never heard of this﴾ i.e., of this kind of magic, or of what came from Moses, peace be upon him. The speech is according to an elided noun (taqdir mudaf), i.e., "of the like of this." Or the reference is to the claim of prophethood, and their denial of hearing such a thing is a deliberate lie, for Joseph, peace be upon him, had come to them before with clear signs, and [they said] "and you have not been in doubt about what he brought until, when he died, you said, 'Allah will not send after him a messenger.'" It is also possible that they meant to deny having heard the claim of prophethood made in truth, since they denied the very principle of prophethood and did not affirm the validity of any of them, like the Brahmins and many of the Europeans and whoever licks their filth today. The bi' (ba') in this phrase, as in Majma' al-Bayan, is either in its original sense or is extra, i.e., "we did not hear this." ﴿In the time of our forefathers, the earliest ones﴾ i.e., occurring in their days. So the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "this," with an elided noun, and its governing element is "we heard."

It is also permitted that bi-hadha be taken as tagged to the occurrence of "this," so that the prepositional phrase is attached to that elided element. By describing their forefathers as "the earliest ones" they indicated the absence of this for a long time.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 37:

﴿And Moses said, "My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him."﴾ He, peace be upon him, intends by the relative clause (al-mawsul) himself. Ibn Kathir read "qala" (said) without the waw, and that is because it is a response to their saying, "It is nothing but magic," and a response is not conjoined with a waw or any other particle. The reason for the conjunction in the reading of the rest of the seven readers is that the intent is to relate both statements, so that the listener may weigh the two statements reported to him and distinguish the sound of them from the corrupt.

﴿And whoever will have the good outcome of the [final] abode﴾, that is, the praiseworthy outcome in the abode, which is the world, and its outcome is that the person is concluded with that which leads him to Paradise, by the grace and generosity of Allah the Exalted. The reason for understanding "the praiseworthy outcome" from the absolute term "outcome" is that it is what Allah the Exalted called His servants to, and He equipped them with intellects that do not guide them to it by themselves, enabled them to it, removed its obstacles, provided its motives, and urged them toward it. Thus it is, for that reason, the one intended from all the servants and the purpose of their creation. This is what Ibn al-Munir chose, in agreement with what the majority hold. He related that some people said to him: "What prevents you from saying that 'them' [in the sense of 'theirs'] is the outcome of good, since the outcome is attributed to its possessors with the lam, as in this verse, and the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the disbelievers will know to whom belongs the outcome of the abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 42], and the saying of the Glorified: ﴿and the outcome is for the God-fearing﴾ [al-A'raf: 128; al-Qasas: 83], since the outcome of good is what belongs to them, whereas the outcome of evil is upon them, not to them?" He said to him: "I would have had a statement on that, were it not that it has come in the words of those (who say): ﴿for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode﴾, and it did not say 'upon them'. The use of the lam in the place [of 'upon'] is an indication that the argument from the lam for intending the outcome of good has been nullified."

It may be said: the lam is apparent in benefit, and that suffices for understanding that the intended outcome is the outcome of good. In verses like the one Ibn al-Munir cited, one is obliged to say that they are of the mode of mockery (tahakkum), and this is similar to what they said: that good tidings (bishara) are for good, and "give them good tidings of a painful punishment" is of the mode of mockery.

Al-Tibi said, also defending the one side: I say: the verse does not preclude that. For the context of the curse and evil precludes the intent of good. He used "for them" only to signal that these two are true, established for them, and necessarily attached to them, and the fronting (taqdim), which conveys exclusivity, supports this, so reflect.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "yakun" with the yaa' (third person masculine), because the noun in the nominative is metaphorically feminine and is separated from its governing verb.

﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾, that is, they will not attain what they seek, nor be saved from what they fear. The essence of Moses' words, peace be upon him, is: "My Lord knows better than you the state of the one whom He, the Glorified, has qualified for the greatest success, in that He made him a prophet, sent him with guidance, and promised him the good end. Were he as you claim, a liar, a sorcerer, a fabricator, He would not have qualified him for that, for He is Rich and Wise, who does not send liars nor appoint sorcerers as prophets."
Page 80
And the wrongdoers do not succeed in His sight.

[Ruh al-Ma'ani] ﴿And Pharaoh said, "O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself."﴾ The accursed one said this after he had gathered the magicians and set himself to oppose (Moses). The apparent meaning is that he intended the literal sense of what his words indicate, namely the negation of his knowledge of any god other than himself, not the negation of its existence. Failing to know a thing does not indicate its non-existence. He did not affirm non-existence by saying, "There is no god for you other than me." Yet both this statement and what he said are false, because the apparent meaning of Moses' words to him, "You know well that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear evidences" (Q. 17:102), indicates that he knew their god was other than him. His leaving that statement aside is more apparently consistent with his intent of keeping his people away from following Moses, choosing a satanic stratagem: showing that he was fair in general, so that through this he could win their acceptance of what he would later tell them about the matter of God, and their submission to him, relying on the fairness they had seen in him. It is as if he said, "I know of no god for you in past times other than myself, as Moses says." The matter is open to possibility, and I will verify this for you.

﴿So kindle for me, O Haman, over the clay﴾, that is, make bricks for me. ﴿Then make for me﴾ from them ﴿a tower (sarh)﴾, that is, an exposed, high structure, from "sarraha al-shay'" when a thing became manifest. ﴿That I may look upon﴾, that is, that I may look upon and ascend. Here the form (iftaʿala, "ittalaʿa") is used with the meaning of the bare verb, as in al-Bahr and others.

﴿To the god of Moses﴾, whom he claimed to be his god and the god of the worlds. It is as if he gave his people to understand that, if God were as Moses says, He would be a body in the heaven, since bodies in it can be reached by ascent. Then he said: ﴿And indeed I think him among the liars﴾ regarding what he mentions. This is an emphasis of what he intended, and an indication that his hope of ascending to the god of Moses (peace be upon him) is not because he is certain that He is there. The command to make the tower and build it does not indicate that it was built. There has been disagreement on this. It was said: he built it, and of its description is what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows best. It was also said: he did not build it. On this view, his statement and his command were for confusing his people and giving them the impression that he was about to verify the matter. What he mentioned would then be a mention of one of the ways of verification, so that he could afterwards say, "I verified the matter by another way, and so I know that there is no god for you other than me, and that Moses is lying in what he says." On the first view, it is possible that he ascended the tower alone, or with someone he trusted with his secret, and remained there for as long as he remained, then came down to them and said: "I ascended to the god of Moses, and I verified that the matter is not as he says, and I know that there is no god for you other than me."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, who said: "When the tower was built for him, he climbed to its top and ordered an arrow, which he shot toward the sky. It came back to him stained with blood, and he said: 'I have killed the god of Moses.'" If this is sound, it is by way of mockery through action, but I do not think it is sound. In any case, the people were in extreme stupidity, ignorance, excessive blindness and dullness, for otherwise they would not have accepted such nonsense. Allah, Exalted, has special properties in times, places and persons, and it is not far-fetched to say: among them there were people of intellect who knew his deception and trickery and believed his nonsense in what he said, but they placed themselves among the ignorant and did not show any opposition to what the accursed one was upon, in any state, either out of desire for what was with him or out of fear of his tyranny and aggression against them. How many have we seen of intelligent and learned men who agree with tyrannical oppressors and confirm them in what they say, even if it is impossible or unbelief in the Hereafter?

The accursed one's statement to Moses (peace be upon him), "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned" (Q. 26:29), was possibly said after this statement related here, and followed by informing them with certainty that they have no god but him. Then he threatened Moses with prison if anything from him indicated opposition. This is a reading of the verse that is not devoid of subtlety, though there is some obscurity in it. There are other readings of the verse:

The first: he intended by his words "I know of no god for you other than me" the negation of knowledge, not of existence, as in the previous reading, except that he did not negate existence because he did not have what required a definite judgment of non-existence. By his words "And indeed I think him among the liars" he intended: "I think him a liar in his claim to be a messenger from Allah, Exalted." By his words "O Haman, kindle for me over the clay," etc., he intended to inform people of the falsity of that claim, on the basis of his supposition that God, if He is in the heaven, is reached by one who is a messenger from Him, and that this is by ascent to Him, which is beyond human ability, so it is impossible in relation to Him. Thus what is built upon it, namely the messengership from Him, is likewise. So his statement "Then make for me a tower" is to show the impossibility of the ascent on which the validity of the claim to messengership depends in his opinion. Perhaps this is by way of mockery.

The second: he also intended the negation of knowledge, not of existence itself, but in negating knowledge he was confusing his people and lying in it, since he knew that they had a god other than him, who is the god of all creation, namely Allah, Mighty and Majestic. By his words "And indeed I think him..." etc., he intended: "I think him a liar in his claim to messengership," as in the preceding reading. By his words "O Haman..." etc., he sought to have made for him something that would remove his doubt about the messengership, namely that he should build for him an observatory in a high place from which he could observe the states of the stars, which in his opinion indicate worldly events, and see whether there is in them anything indicating that Allah, Exalted, sent him.

It has been objected that this does not fit his words "that I may look upon the god of Moses," unless it is meant "that I may look upon the rule of the god of Moses through the arrangements of the stars and consider them, to see whether Moses was sent as he claims or not." On this reading the speech would be by way of an omitted modifier, with "ila" (to) meaning "ʿala" (upon). It was also allowed on this reading that by "the god of Moses" he meant the stars, so that it is as if he said, "Perhaps I will ascend to the stars which are the god of Moses, and look whether there is in them anything indicating that they sent him," or "Perhaps I will look upon the rule of the stars which are the god of Moses in the matter of his messengership," and this, as you see, is weak. In general, this reading is not worth paying attention to.

The third: he intended by negating his knowledge of another god the negation of its existence, and by his supposing (him) a liar, he supposed him a liar in affirming a god other than himself. "Supposition" is interpreted as "certainty," as in the words of Durayd ibn al-Simma:

"I said to them: suppose (that) with two thousand armored men, their chiefs, in coats of mail woven of Persian rings."

Affirming the supposition mentioned does not remove the intent of that negation. Some allowed it to remain on its apparent meaning and, to remove the contradiction, said: "It is possible to say: the apparent meaning is that his first statement was a deception and confusion for the people, and the second was an agreement with the confidant of his secret, Haman. So affirming supposition in the second does not preclude that knowledge in the first was the negation of the known." But it is objected that the context of the verse rejects this, and that his command to build the tower, hoping to ascend to the god of Moses (peace be upon him), with the particle "fa" in "So kindle for me," was intended as mockery, as if he attributed to Moses the claim that his god is in the sky, and so said: "O Haman, build for me a tower (sarh)..." (Q. 40:36), "that I may ascend to the god of Moses," mocking him. This is similar to when someone informs you that Zayd is alive and in his house, while you know otherwise, and you say to your servant, after mentioning your knowledge of what contradicts his claim, mocking him: "O servant, saddle the mount for me, that perhaps I may go to so-and-so and keep him company." Indeed, what Pharaoh said is more evident as mockery than what was mentioned. So on this basis, his request to build the tower does not contradict what he claimed at first and last of knowledge and certainty.

Another said, to answer what was said about the contradiction: it would be contradictory only if his words "that I may look upon..." etc. were not said by way of supposition and concession. Another said regarding this: the accursed one was a polytheist who believed that whoever possesses a land is its god and the object of worship of its people. So what he affirmed in his words "that I may look upon" was a god for other than his kingdom, and what he negated was the god of his kingdom, as his words "for you" indicate. This does not escape discussion.

In al-Kashshaf, the view is that there is contradiction between the building of the tower and what he claimed of knowledge and certainty, except that he said: "It was hidden from his people because of their dullness and foolishness, or it was not hidden from them, but each of them feared for himself his whip and his sword." If this door is opened, it is permissible to leave the supposition on its apparent meaning without any need to remove the contradiction. But in my view, the better course is to strive to remove the contradiction. If that is not possible, the forsaken one's committing of this is attributed to his ignorance or foolishness, and his indifference to the people because of their dullness, or their fear of him, or the like.

The view that he intended by negating his knowledge of another god the negation of its existence has been objected to. In al-Tahqiq, and also in others, it is said: "It is not sound, for the lack of knowledge of a thing does not indicate its non-existence, especially the lack of knowledge of one person." Al-Qadi al-Baydawi said: "This is correct for active knowledge (al-ʿulum al-fiʿliyya), because it is necessary for the realization of its objects, so the absence of the knowledge entails the absence of the objects. But this is not the case for receptive knowledge (al-ʿulum al-infiʿaliyya)." It was answered: The purpose of the one who says this is that the non-existence of the object is a cause of the non-knowledge of its existence in general, and there is no doubt that it is so. So the effect (musabbab) is used and the cause (sabab) is intended. There is not a total necessary connection between them. Moreover, since it is among the strongest causes of non-knowledge, because it is the constant one, it is permissible to use it and intend by it the non-existence. For the art of eloquence does not require rational necessity, but customary and conventional necessity is also sufficient. One of us may say, "I do not know that," meaning: if it existed, I would know it, when a sign is present. This usage is common in the customs of the Arabs and non-Arabs, among the common people and the elite. From it is the statement of the examiner of witnesses when asked about the uprightness of the witnesses: "I do not know how..." And the forsaken one claimed divinity.

Then the apparent meaning is that, on the assumption that the intended sense is the negation of existence, the speech is a kinaya (metonymy), not a majaz (figurative usage). In sum, what has been mentioned is a plausible view, and the determination of the most probable view is left to your understanding. Allah, Exalted, is the Granter of success.

Some who say that Allah, Exalted, is in the heaven, in the sense that He, glorified is He, intended in His words, Mighty and Majestic, "Are you secure from the One who is in the heaven?" (Q. 67:16), as the Salaf (early predecessors) say regarding this verse, argue as follows: if Pharaoh had not heard from Moses (peace be upon him) that his god is in the heaven, he would not have said, "So make for me a tower, that I may look upon the god of Moses." So his saying that is evidence of having heard it. However, he erred in understanding the intended meaning of what he heard, and he supposed that God's being in the heaven is by way of containment, settledness and the like, which belong to bodies. You know that this argument is extremely weak, and establishing the doctrine of the Salaf does not need to be supported by such things.

In the statement of the forsaken one, "kindle for me over the clay," the intended meaning of "clay" is mud-brick (libn), not "make bricks for me" (ājurr). This indicates that Haman did not have knowledge of the craft of baked bricks, so he was commanded to make them in a way that includes teaching. There are reports that support this. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "Pharaoh was the first to order the craft and building of baked bricks." He and a group related from Qatada, who said: "It reached me that Pharaoh was the first to bake bricks and make a tower for himself." And from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him): when he traveled to al-Sham and saw the palaces built with baked bricks, he said: "I did not know that anyone built with baked bricks except Pharaoh."

In his command to him, though Haman was his vizier and his companion riding behind him, to do the work of the lowly, namely kindling over the clay, addressing him by his name without kunya or title, with "O" (yā), which indicates nearness, in the middle of the speech and not at its beginning, there is evident indication of his tyranny and self-exaltation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 39:

﴿And he and his soldiers were arrogant﴾, meaning: they regarded everyone other than themselves as contemptible in comparison to themselves. They saw greatness and majesty only in themselves, so they looked upon others the way kings look upon slaves. ﴿in the land﴾: most scholars hold that this means the land of Egypt. It was also said that it refers to the physical realm known as the earth, as opposed to the heavens. Specifying it this way is a condemnation of them, since they were arrogant about what is the lowest of physical bodies, and it would have been fitting for them to consider their own place and its lowliness, so that they would not have been arrogant. ﴿without right﴾: that is, without entitlement. Their view was false, since regarding everyone as contemptible in relation to the one who sees is not true, and seeing greatness and majesty as belonging to oneself alone, to the exclusion of others, is not a real right except for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "Arrogance with right belongs only to Allah, exalted is He, and every other arrogant person apart from Him, Mighty and Majestic, is arrogant without right." In the hadith qudsi (a saying of the Prophet ﷺ in which Allah speaks in the first person, though it is not part of the Qur'an): "Majesty is My cloak and greatness is My garment, so whoever contends with Me over either of them, I will cast him into the Fire."

Page 83

﴿And they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾: for resurrection and recompense. Regarding the word "thought" (ẓann), it was said that it is either meant in its literal sense, or it expresses their conviction, to belittle them and to give them respite. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i and Nafi' read لا (يَرْجِعُونَ) with a fatḥah on the yā' and a kasrah on the jīm, i.e., (yarji‘ūn), making the verb active rather than passive.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 40:

﴿So We seized him and his hosts, and We cast them into the sea.﴾ That is, We threw them down and drowned them in it. The details of this have already passed. In the use of "nabdh" (casting away), which is the throwing and tossing of a worthless thing because of the little regard given to it, the poet says:

I looked at its title and cast it aside, as you cast away a worn-out sandal from your sandals.

This is a belittling of them. In the expression, according to what has been said, there is a metaphor (isti'arah) that is both implicit (makniyyah) and imaginative (takhyiliyyah). This is because they were likened in worthlessness to worn-out sandals, the name of sandals was borrowed for them, then the borrowed term was omitted and the thing borrowed for remained, and "casting away" was made a clue that the usage is literal, while the figurative element lies in the "attachment," along the lines of what is said about the claws of death having sunk into so-and-so. Some of them said: "seizing" (akhdh), which is literal in the sense of taking hold, is figurative for creating in them the motive to set out toward the sea, and "casting" (nabdh) is figurative for creating in them the motive to enter it. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is said that it is a kinayah (metonymy) for making them enter it. The better view is that the statement is in the mode of tamthil (extended analogy), as if He, Mighty and Majestic, in what He did to them, seized them together with their multitude in one palm and cast them into the sea. The apparent view is that the first "fa" (fa') is causal (sababiyyah) and not merely for sequence, while the second "fa" is for sequence if "seizing" is kept in the sense of taking hold, or if it is intended as creating the motive to set out or something similar. But if "seizing" is intended as destruction, then it is for explanation (tafsir), as in "fa-istajabna lahu fa-najjaynahu" and similar. ﴿So look﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿at how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾, and He made it clear to people so that they might take warning from it.

﴿And We made them﴾, that is, We created them, ﴿leaders﴾, exemplars of misguidance, because they led others to misguidance, as His words indicate: ﴿calling to the Fire﴾, that is, calling to what necessitates it of disbelief and sins. This is on the basis that "the Fire" is a metaphor for that, or on the basis of an omitted modifier, so that the meaning is that We made them misguided and misguiding. The "making" here is similar to His words: ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. The verse is clear in support of the position of Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni school) that good and evil are both created by Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) interpreted it, in one way, by saying that "making" here means "naming," similar to His words: ﴿And they made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19], that is, We named them among the nations after them as callers to the Fire. In another way, they said that making them so means abandoning them and withholding from them the grace and the success toward guidance. The first is related from al-Jubba'i, and the second from al-Ka'bi. From Abu Muslim: the meaning is that We made them, by hastening punishment for them, leaders, that is, those who precede those among the disbelievers who come after them to the Fire. This is in the extreme of far-fetched interpretation, as is not hidden. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾, that is, they will not be given relief from the punishment in any way.

﴿And We made them follow a curse in this world﴾ which had deluded them, [meaning] expulsion and banishment, or a curse from those who curse, since the angels, peace be upon them, continue to curse them, and so do the believers, generation after generation. This is either because they are included among the wrongdoers whom they curse, or because they are named explicitly, as in God Almighty's curse upon Pharaoh and his hosts. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the reviled﴾, that is, among the expelled and banished. It is said: "God has reviled him" (qabahahu Allah), with the verb lightened, meaning He removed him and distanced him from every good, as al-Layth said. It is not repeated with the curse mentioned earlier. It is said that this is because its meaning also includes expulsion; the earlier one is in this world, and this one is in the Hereafter. Or, the earlier one is expulsion from His mercy that is in this world, and this one is expulsion from Paradise. Or, according to this, what is meant by the curse mentioned earlier is what comes later. Moreover, "among the expelled" means that they belong to the group known for this, which is more eloquent and more specific. Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: "among the reviled" means among the destroyed. From Ibn 'Abbas, it means among those disfigured in their creation by blackness of faces and blueness of eyes. This meaning is the one that comes first to mind, except that the verb qabuha (to be reviled) in it is intransitive (lāzim), so forming the passive participle from it is not evident. It may be said: if this interpretation is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas, then it must be held that he also heard it [from the Prophet]. It is also permissible that this is an explanation by something that is necessarily associated with it in general. ﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾ is related to "the reviled", or to an omitted word that this explains, as you have learned just now regarding its parallel. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj, and 'Abd ibn Humayd from Qatadah, something that clearly indicates that it is coordinated with "in this world". This is coordination with the position (ma'tuf 'ala al-mahall). The report from Ibn Jurayj is more apparent in this regard. Both are in al-Durr al-Manthur. What you heard first is the apparent meaning.

This verse is the clearest evidence that Pharaoh will not be saved on the Day of Resurrection, and that he is cursed and distanced from the mercy of God Almighty both in this world and in the Hereafter, for the plural pronouns in it refer to Pharaoh and his hosts. And it almost includes whoever holds that they refer to the hosts, in the hosts.

In al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyya by the scholar Ibn Hajar, it is related that 'Adi and al-Tabarani reported from Ibn Mas'ud that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God Almighty created Yahya ibn Zakariyya in his mother's womb as a believer, and He created Pharaoh in his mother's womb as a disbeliever."

Ruh al-Ma'ani (al-Alusi) on Surah 28 (al-Qasas), verse 43:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾, that is, the Torah, which, as Abu Hayyan said, is the first book in which the rulings were detailed, ﴿after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾, namely the peoples of Noah, Hud, Salih and Lot, peace be upon them. The mention of the giving of it after their destruction serves to indicate that it was sent down after the need for it had arisen, as a preface to what follows concerning the need that calls for the sending down of the Noble Qur'an upon the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. For the destruction of the earlier generations is among the causes of the effacement of the landmarks of the sacred laws and the obliteration of their traces, which lead to the disruption of the order of the world and the corruption of the conditions of nations, and these call for a new legislation that establishes the principles which endure throughout the ages, arranges the branches which change with the changing eras, and reminds of the conditions of past nations, which necessitates reflection. Whoever overlooks this said:

"It is better to interpret 'the earlier generations' as those who did not believe in Moses, peace be upon him, and its counterpart would be 'the later', namely those who believed in him, peace be upon him." It was also said:

"What is meant by them is that which includes those who did not believe in Moses, such as Pharaoh and his hosts, and the peoples destroyed before them." But this is not the right view. The word "ma" here is a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, meaning: We gave him that after Our destruction of the earlier generations. ﴿As insights for mankind﴾, that is, lights for their hearts by which they perceive the realities and distinguish between truth and falsehood, given that they had been completely blind to understanding and perception. For insight (basirah) is the light of the heart by which one gains insight, just as sight (basar) is the light of the eye by which one sees. It is also applied to the eye itself, and its plural is absar; the first (basirah) is pluralized as basa'ir. By "mankind" is meant, it is said, his community, peace be upon him; and it is also said that it includes them and those after them. That the Torah was insights for those to whom our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was sent is because it contains what guides them to the truth of his mission, peace and blessings be upon him, or increases them in knowledge beyond their knowledge. It has been objected that this implies encouragement to study the Torah and to know what is in it,

and it is authentically reported that "Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for permission regarding some compilations he had written from the Torah, so that he might read them and increase his knowledge beyond his own. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, became angry until it was seen in his face, then said: "Had Moses been alive, he would have had no choice but to follow me." So 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, threw them from his hand and regretted doing so."

It is answered that his anger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was due to the fact that the Torah in the hands of the Jews at that time was corrupted, containing additions and omissions, and was not the very Torah that was revealed to Moses, peace be upon him; and the people were recent converts from disbelief. So if the door to consulting the Torah and studying it had been opened at that time, it would have led to great corruption. Thus the prohibition of reading it, when Islam was recent and departure from disbelief was new, does not indicate that it is in itself not insights containing what guides to the truth of his mission, peace and blessings be upon him, and increases knowledge of the soundness of what he brought. Among what indicates the permissibility of returning to it in general is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93]. Believers among the People of the Book, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam and Ka'b al-Ahbar, used to transmit from it what they transmitted of reports, and no one from the pillars of Islam denied that or disapproved of hearing it; and there is no difference between hearing what they related from them and reading it in the Torah and taking from it. Many scholars have also returned to it in order to confront the Jews and argue against them with some of its expressions, to establish the truth of his mission, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. What I incline to is that the intended meaning of "mankind" is the Children of Israel, for this is what the context requires.

As for the study of the Torah, the discussion of it is lengthy. In Tuhfat al-Muhtaj of the learned master Ibn Hajar, may Allah have mercy on him, it is stated: it is forbidden for anyone other than a thorough scholar to study the likes of a Torah whose alteration he knows of or doubts, and this is closer to verification. Whoever examines the Torah that is in the hands of the Jews today finds most of it altered, with no agreement at all between it and what is in the Great Qur'an, and the Qur'an is what is relied upon. ﴿And guidance﴾, that is, to the sacred laws, which are the paths leading to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; ﴿and mercy﴾, in that whoever acts by it attains the mercy of Allah, Exalted, according to His promise, glory be to Him. Thus the general scope of His mercy in this sense does not contradict that some people disbelieve in it and are not shown mercy. The accusatives of the coordinated terms are in the circumstantial position relative to "the Book", either because they are themselves the insights, guidance and mercy, or by the omission of a modifier, meaning "possessing insights," etc. Abu al-Baqa' permitted their being in the accusative of cause, meaning: We gave him the Book for insights, guidance and mercy. ﴿So that they may remember﴾, that is, in order that they may remember, on the basis that la'alla here denotes causation. Ibn Abi Hatim related through al-Suddi from Abu Malik that he said: "La'alla in the Qur'an means 'in order that' in more than one verse, such as [Ash-Shu'ara: 129] ﴿so that you may live forever﴾." Al-Waqidi related from al-Baghawi that he said: "Everything in the Qur'an with la'alla is causal except ﴿la'allakum takhludun﴾, where it is for comparison." The well-known view, however, is that it denotes hope. Since hope is impossible for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, some have made the statement a figure of speech, meaning: We gave him that so that they would be in a state receptive to remembrance, like the state of one from whom good is hoped. Others directed the hope to the addressees, so it is from them, not from Him, Exalted. Al-Zamakhshari took this as a metaphor of subsequent type, likening will to hope since each of them seeks occurrence. It was objected that this entails the non-fulfilment of Allah's will by His will, since not all remember, unless it is by way of ascribing to the whole what belongs to some. You know that will, according to the Mu'tazilah, is of two kinds: permissive (tafwidiyyah), whose object may fail to occur, and compelling (qasriyyah), whose object never fails to occur at all. So if the first kind is intended here, the difficulty disappears; yet the said division contradicts the correct school.

*Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 44:*

﴿And you were not on the western side﴾ This begins an explanation that the revelation of the Noble Qur'an also took place at a time when the need for it was pressing and wisdom absolutely required it. It includes establishing that it is a truthful revelation from God, Exalted, by showing that knowledge of the circumstances that were detailed cannot be attained except through witnessing them or learning from one who witnessed them. Since neither of these two was the case, it became clear that it came by revelation from the Knower of the Unseen, without doubt. So it has been said.

It is not hidden that establishing that it was by revelation is not complete except by negating that it was by transmission from many sources (*istifada*) and that it was by learning from some of the People of the Book who were contemporaries of him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, as the polytheists said: ﴿Only a human teaches him﴾ (An-Nahl: 103). Perhaps the reason it did not address negating that, but addressed negating what is more evidently absent, is to indicate that the absence of that is evident, and to emphasise the claim of it, since it signals that what needs to be told of its absence are those two matters and not that one. Moreover, He, Mighty and Majestic, has negated in another place that it was by learning from some of the People of the Book, and perhaps it may be known from that that it was not by transmission from many sources. Even if we say that it is not known, its proof is very clear. For this reason, none of the polytheists claimed that one stood there. So reflect.

The meaning according to what some of them held: "You were not present at the western side of the mountain, or the western place where the appointed time occurred and where God, Exalted, gave Moses, peace be upon him, the tablets of the Torah." The discourse on this is from the type of omitting the qualified noun and placing its adjective in its position. According to some, it is from the type of *idafa* (construct phrase) of the qualified noun to the adjective, which the Kufans permitted, as in *masjid al-jami'* (the congregational mosque). The original form is "the western side," so the side and the western become one on this view, and it is a part of the western on the first view.

﴿When We decreed to Moses the command﴾ That is: We charged him, and We confirmed the matter of his prophethood by revelation and the giving of the Torah.

﴿Nor were you among the witnesses﴾ That is: among those present for the revelation to him, or among the witnesses to the revelation to him, peace be upon him. They are the seventy chosen men for the appointed time, so that you might witness what happened to Moses at his appointed time and then inform the people. So "witness" (*al-shahid*) is from testimony (*al-shahada*), either in the sense of presence or in its well-known sense. It has been objected that taking the first meaning leads to repetition, since He has already negated presence first in His saying: ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾. Likewise, taking the second meaning leads to something similar, because negating presence requires negating being among those who testify in that sense. From here it has been said: the intended meaning of the first is the negation of his, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, being present in person for some purpose, and of the second is the negation of his, peace and blessings be upon him, being among a group who were brought to attend and witness what took place there for Moses, peace be upon him, because the intended "witnesses" are a known group whose condition was that.

It has also been said: the intended "witnesses" are the angels, peace be upon them, for "witness" has come as a name for an angel, as in the *Qamus* (dictionary). So it is as if it were said: "You were not present at the western side when We decreed to Moses the matter of his prophethood by revelation, and you were not among the angels who descend and ascend by the command and revelation of God, Exalted, to His prophets, peace be upon them, and who have knowledge of events that is not available to other humans, so that you would have knowledge of what happened to Moses, peace be upon him, and then inform the people of it."

Ibn 'Abbas said, as in *al-Tafsir al-Kabir* and *al-Bahr*: the meaning is "You were not present at that place, and even if you had been present, you would not have witnessed those events, for it is possible that one could be there and not witness or see." It has also been said, and this is the choice of Abu Hayyan, that the meaning is "You were not among the witnesses to all that We informed you of," so it is a negation of his, peace and blessings be upon him, witnessing all that happened to Moses, peace be upon him, and thus it is a general statement after a specific one. It has also been said: the intended meaning is "You were not among the witnesses of that time," and so it is a negation of his presence, and witnessing that time is more general than being on the western side or elsewhere. Its outcome is the negation of his physical existence at that time, so this is an escalation in the negation.

It has also been said: the intended meaning of "And you were not" at that time is being included in the category of those who are characterised by testimony, namely those who exist in physical existence wherever they may be. Its result is like the result of what came before, even though the two differ in the way of intending the meaning. The sense of testimony in what came before is determined to be presence. Perhaps what came before is more evident than this, and indeed, if someone claims that it is more evident than all that has been said, that is not far-fetched. Your awareness of those views and what is in them of debate and dispute is not hidden from you. And in the heart there is something about the soundness of attributing to Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, what has been narrated from him, so reflect on all of that. May God, Exalted, guide you.

[p. 86]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 45:

﴿But We produced generations﴾, that is, but We created many generations between your time and the time of Musa, ﴿so the lifespan lengthened for them﴾, and the period extended, so the laws and rulings changed and the reports became obscure to them.

Page 87

Especially concerning the last of them, among whom you are, so wisdom required new legislation and the narration of the reports as they truly were. Thus ﴿We revealed to you﴾ and ﴿We related to you the reports﴾ — the omitted supplementary element here is "We revealed," which has been dropped, relying on the mention of what necessitates it and indicates it: the producing of generations and the lengthening of the period. The summary of the meaning is: you were not present to learn this, but you knew it through revelation, and the cause of it was the lengthening of time until the laws changed and the reports became obscure. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You were not dwelling﴾, that is, residing ﴿among the people of Madyan﴾, namely Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) and the believers, is a negation of the possibility that the Prophet's (ﷺ) knowledge of some of what preceded in the story was through hearing it from one who witnessed it. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿reciting to them﴾, that is, reading to the people of Madyan by way of learning from them, as a student reads the lesson to his teacher, ﴿Our verses﴾, the clear ones concerning what happened to Musa (peace be upon him) among them and what happened to them with him. It is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun hidden in "dwelling" (thāwiyan), or a second predicate (khabar) for "kunta." ﴿But We were sending messengers﴾ to you, and revealing to you those verses and their like. The istidrak (correction) here is like the previous istidrak, except that there is no omission in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 46 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And you were not on the side of the Mount when We called,﴾ that is, at the time of Our calling Moses, "Indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds," and of Our making him a prophet and Our sending him to Pharaoh. ﴿But it is a mercy from your Lord﴾ that is, but We sent you with the Qur'an, which speaks of what was mentioned and other things, as a mercy from Us to you and to mankind.

It is said: that is, We taught you as a mercy. The word "mercy" (raḥmah) is the second object of "taught" (ʿallama), and what is meant by it is the Qur'an. It is not an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu). The second object is the story that was mentioned, as you will soon know, God willing. As for making it accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) for a deleted verb, its status is clear and needs no explanation. The turn to the name "Lord" (al-Rabb) serves to indicate that this is among the effects of lordship, and it honours him (peace be upon him) by attributing it to him. Here he has dispensed with mentioning what is implied by what is absent by mentioning what necessitates it from God's side, just as in the first part he dispensed with mentioning what necessitates it from the side of people. He stated it explicitly between the two, to make clear what is intended and to indicate that it is also meant in both. How wonderful is the arrangement of the revelation, belonging to God!

His words, glorified is He: ﴿so that you may warn a people﴾ are connected to the verb that is given as the reason, namely mercy. This requires that the sending was with the Qur'an, or something of its meaning, such as teaching the Qur'an, and not teaching the story that was mentioned, since its being a cause for warning does not clearly appear. It has also been permitted that it be connected to the three contrasting clauses by the principle of competition (tanāzuʿ).

ʿĪsā and Abū Ḥaywah read "raḥmatun" in the nominative, as the predicate of a deleted subject, and the estimate is: "But it is he, or this, or she, or this one, is a mercy." The pronoun or demonstrative is said to refer to the sending that is understood from the speech. The masculine and feminine forms are used in accordance with the referent and the predicate. The disagreement about the first is well known. Abū Ḥayyān permitted that the estimate be: "But you are a mercy," and "so that you may warn" according to this reading is connected to what is a qualifier of "mercy." His words, majestic and exalted: ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner has come before you﴾ — the phrase "to whom no warner has come" is a qualifier of "a people." The first "min" (from) is extra, for emphasis. His words, exalted: ﴿so that they may remember﴾ (46), that is, they may be admonished by your warning. This is a reason for the warning according to the view that "laʿalla" indicates causation. But according to the view that it indicates hope, whether literally or figuratively, it is said that it is in the position of a qualifier, with the verb "say" implied, meaning: "so that you may warn a people about whom it is said, 'perhaps they will remember.'" The people here is said to be the Arabs. The apparent meaning of the verse is that no messenger was sent to them before our Prophet (peace be upon him) at all. This is not the intended meaning, because there is agreement that Ismāʿīl (peace be upon him) was sent to them. It seems that this is because of the long time between his mission (peace be upon him) and the mission of our Prophet (peace be upon him), for there are more than two thousand years between them, and his law was obliterated, and most people in most of this period did not know its reality. It has been said that this is so. It has also been said that this is because they stated that the ruling of Ismāʿīl's mission ended with his death, and that no prophet was sent to them after him except our Prophet (peace be upon him). Al-ʿAllāmah Ibn Ḥajar said in al-Minaḥ al-Makkiyyah: "It is established that no messenger was sent to the Arabs after Ismāʿīl (peace be upon him), and that Ismāʿīl's mission ended with his death." He claimed, just before this consensus, that Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) and those after him, that is, other than Ismāʿīl (peace be upon him), were not sent to the Arabs, and that Ismāʿīl's mission to them ended with his death. End of quotation. So it seems that because Ismāʿīl (peace be upon him) remained among them only a short time, and the ruling of his mission ended after his death among them, and they remained a long time without a messenger sent among them, the arrival of a warner to them from before him (peace be upon him) was denied.

Al-ʿAllāmah Ibn Ḥajar also mentioned in al-Minaḥ something that indicates that every messenger other than our Prophet (peace be upon him) has his mission end with his death, and that this is not specific to Ismāʿīl (peace be upon him). What is understood from the words of al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salām in his Amālī is that this ending is not absolute. He said: "A benefit: every prophet was sent only to his people, except our master Muḥammad (peace be upon him). Accordingly, those other than the people of each prophet who lived in a period of interval (fatrah, a time without prophets), except the descendants of the earlier prophet, are addressed by the mission of the earlier one, unless the law of the earlier one has been obliterated, in which case all of them become people of the interval." End of quotation. This, and also what we have quoted from al-ʿAllāmah Ibn Ḥajar, is now with me subject to acceptance and rejection. Perhaps God will open my heart later to establish the truth in this matter.

It has been said: just as Mūsā and ʿĪsā (peace be upon them both) were sent to the Children of Israel, they were also sent to the Arabs. So what is meant by the denial of this arrival is the interval (fatrah) between ʿĪsā and our Prophet (peace be upon them both). According to what al-Bukhārī narrated from Salmān al-Fārisī (may Allah be pleased with him), it was six hundred years; in many books it is said to be five hundred and fifty years. The denial of the arrival of a prophet between the time of our Prophet and the time of ʿĪsā (peace be upon them both) is what a group of scholars authenticated, based on the ḥadīth: "There is no prophet between me and ʿĪsā." Some said that between them there were four prophets: three from the Children of Israel and one from the Arabs, who is Khālid ibn Sinān. It has been said otherwise. Some chose that what is meant by these people are the Arabs contemporary with him (peace be upon him), since they are the ones for whom his warning to them can be imagined, not their ancestors who passed away. This is probably the most apparent view. The non-arrival of a warner to them before him (peace be upon him), according to the view that the ruling of the mission of a messenger other than our Prophet (peace be upon him) ends with his death, is clear. But if it is said that it does not end with that, and the ruling of the messenger's mission remains in effect, then whoever among the descendants of those to whom he was sent knows it must act upon it, insofar as it is one of that messenger's rulings, until another messenger comes. He acts upon it insofar as it is one of his rulings, or in the manner in which he commands it, in relation to him or in relation to the one before him. Or it is abandoned if the second comes abrogating it. So the meaning of the non-arrival of the warner to them is that what he brought did not reach them in reality. It is impossible for "these people" to mean the Arabs absolutely, and to say that no one at all was sent to them before the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him). This is evidently false and contradicts His words, exalted: ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fāṭir: 24], and the Arabs are the greatest of nations. Likewise, it contradicts His words, exalted: ﴿so that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 6], on the basis that "mā" in it is not negating. On the view that "mā" in it is negating, it requires interpretation by taking "the fathers" to mean the nearest fathers. What is permitted in "mā" here is not what was permitted there in the possibility in the verse of Yā-Sīn. Rather, the negation is definite and only that. Forcing other interpretations that do not befit the Book of Allah is not appropriate. "Nadhīr" means "mundhir" (warner). The possibility that it is a verbal noun meaning "warning" is something one should not pay attention to. And the change in the sequential order between "the decree" in the sense of settling the matter of Mūsā's prophethood by revelation, and the giving of the Torah, and his dwelling among the people of Madyan, referred to by His words, exalted: ﴿And you were not dwelling among the people of Madyan﴾, and the call (nidā') is to draw attention to the fact that each of these is an independent proof that his narration of the story (peace be upon him) is by way of divine revelation. Had the sequential order been observed, he would first have denied dwelling among the people of Madyan, then secondly denied presence at the call, and thirdly denied presence at the settling of the matter. Otherwise it might be supposed that all of these are one proof for what was mentioned, as passed in the story of the cow.

Some people interpreted "the settling of the matter" as the appointment as prophet, and "the call" as the call for taking the Torah, based on His words, exalted: ﴿Take the Book with strength﴾ [Maryam: 12], in observance of the sequential order between them. This was criticised on the grounds that it loses the aforementioned indication, and that even with this, the sequential order between the connected items is not entirely removed, because dwelling among the people of Madyan actually precedes the decree and the call. And it was placed in the middle between them in the noble arrangement. Also, the interpretation of each of "the decree" and "the call" in the way that is more suitable to the contrasting clause that follows is more appropriate. It is strange that some who interpreted what was mentioned in a way that agrees with the actual sequential order interpreted "the witnesses" as the seventy chosen men for the appointed time. This cannot easily fit, because they were with Mūsā (peace be upon him) only when he was given the Torah, so he should have interpreted it otherwise. Several interpretations have already passed for you, none of which rejects interpreting what was mentioned in a way that agrees with the actual sequential order.

It has been permitted, according to the interpretation that agrees with it, that the intended "witnesses" are the angels (peace be upon them) who were around the fire, for the reports speak of their presence around it when Mūsā (peace be upon him) came to it. Likewise His words, exalted: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾ [al-Naml: 8], according to one view. This is so. Other interpretations of the verses exist. Al-Farrāʾ said, regarding His words, exalted: ﴿And you were not dwelling﴾ etc.: that is, you were not residing among the people of Madyan with Mūsā (peace be upon him), so that you saw him and heard his speech, yet here you are reciting to them, that is, to your community, Our signs. So it is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ). End of quotation. Similar to this is what was narrated from Muqātil regarding it: the meaning is that you did not witness the people of Madyan, so that you could recite to the people of Makkah their news. But We sent you to the people of Makkah and sent down to you these reports, and had it not been for that, you would not have known them. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: Allah says: O Muḥammad, you were not the messenger to the people of Madyan, reciting to them the verses of the Book. Rather, it was someone else. But We were sending messengers in every age: We sent Shuʿayb to the people of Madyan, and We sent you to the Arabs, to be the seal of the prophets. End of quotation. It is not hidden that what we presented earlier is more worthy of consideration.

A group went to the view that the call in His words, exalted: ﴿And you were not on the side of the Mount when We called﴾ was a call concerning this Muḥammadan community, may the best of blessings and the most complete greetings be upon its Prophet. They mentioned several reports that indicate this.

Al-Firyābī, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil all together narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said concerning this: "They were called: O community of Muḥammad, I have given you before you ask Me, and I have answered you before you call upon Me."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it by another route from Abū Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (peace be upon him).

He also narrated, and Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil, Abū Naṣr al-Sijzī in al-Ibānah, and al-Daylamī narrated from ʿAmr ibn ʿUyaynah, who said: "I asked the Prophet (peace be upon him) about His words, exalted: ﴿And you were not on the side of the Mount when We called, but it is a mercy from your Lord﴾: what was the call, and what was the mercy?" He said: "A Book which Allah wrote before He created His creation by two thousand years. Then He placed it upon His Throne. Then He called: O community of Muḥammad, My mercy has preceded My wrath. I have given you before you ask Me, and I have forgiven you before you seek forgiveness from Me.
