Whoever among you meets Me testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is My servant and My messenger, truthfully, I will admit him into Paradise."

Al-Khutli in al-Dibaj narrated it likewise, marfu', from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When God brought Musa near to Mount Sinai, as one who confides in Him, he said: 'O my Lord, is there anyone You have found more honoured by You than me? You brought me near as one who confides, and You spoke to me directly.' He said: 'Yes. Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, is more honoured by Me than you.'

Page 90

He said: 'If Muhammad (ﷺ) is more honoured by You than me, then is the community of Muhammad more honoured than the Children of Israel? You split the sea for them, rescued them from Pharaoh and his deeds, and fed them manna and quails.' He said: 'Yes. The community of Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, is more honoured by Me than the Children of Israel.' He said:

'My God, show them to me.' He said: 'You will not see them, but if you wish I will let you hear their voices.' He said: 'Yes, my God.' So our Lord called out to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ): 'Answer your Lord!' He said: They answered, while they were in the loins of their fathers and the wombs of their mothers until the Day of Resurrection, and they said: 'Labbayk, You are truly our Lord, and we are truly Your servants.' He said: 'You have spoken truly. I am truly your Lord, and you are truly My servants. I have pardoned you before you call upon Me, and I have given you before you ask Me. Whoever among you meets Me bearing witness that there is no god but God, will enter Paradise.'"

Ibn 'Abbas said: When God sent Muhammad (ﷺ), He wished to bestow upon him a favour by what He had given him and by what He had given his community, and so He said: "O Muhammad, you were not at the side of the mount when We called out" (Qur'an 28:46). This has been regarded as problematic, since this meaning does not suit the context, and the verses cannot easily be connected in light of it. For the soundness of these reports a proof is necessary, and al-Hakim's authentication (tashih) is of doubtful status.

Some have said: It may be said that, assuming the reports are sound, the intended meaning is "You were not present with Musa, peace be upon him, at the side of the mount so that you would witness his circumstances and report them to people. But We sent you with the Qur'an which speaks of that and of other things, as a mercy from Us to you and to people." The specification by the calling out to his community is not because what was reported is what occurred in that regard; rather, it is to bring joy to him, upon him be blessings and peace, regarding what returns to him and to his community. It also contains consolation for him, may God bless him and grant him peace, for what will occur from the community of the call (ummat al-da'wa) of disbelief in him, upon him be blessings and peace, and refusal of his law, and it alludes to the content of God's words: "If these disbelieve in it, We have entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it" (Qur'an 6:89). Then the verses are connected to one another in an evident way. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 47:

﴿And if not that a calamity should befall them﴾, i.e., a punishment, which, as related from Abu Muslim, is the punishment of this world and the Hereafter. It is said: the punishment of annihilation. ﴿for what their hands have sent forward﴾, i.e., for what they have committed of disbelief and sins. It is expressed as "hands" for all deeds, even if they do not proceed from the hands, by the commission of the hands and the sending forward of the hands, since most deeds are carried out by them. ﴿and they would say, "Our Lord, if only You had sent to us a messenger"﴾, i.e., why did You not send to us a messenger supported by You with signs ﴿so that we would follow Your verses﴾, the manifest ones shown through his hand, ﴿and be among the believers﴾ (47) in what he brought.

"Law la" (if not) the second is hortative (tahdidiyya), as we have indicated. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿fa-nattabi'a﴾ ("so that we would follow"), is its answer. Since the hortative is a demand like a command, it is answered in the manner in which commands are answered. As for the first, it is counterfactual (imtina'iyya), and its answer is omitted, relying on the context to indicate it. The estimate is: "if not that We had sent You" (lima arsalnaka). The "fa" in ﴿fa-yaqulu﴾ ("and they would say") is conjunctive, linking "yaqulu" to "tusibuhum" (a calamity befalls them). The intended causality, given the absence of the answer, and its essential pillar, is their saying that when a calamity befalls them: "Why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we would follow him and be among the believers?" Its meaning is: were it not for their saying, when they are punished for what they have committed, "Why did You not send to us a messenger that we would follow," then "We would have sent You to them." The sum of this is the causality of the said saying for the sending of him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, to them, cutting off their excuses entirely. But since the punishment was the cause of the saying, and its existence was tied to its existence, it is treated as though it were the cause of the sending through the intermediary of the saying. Thus "law la" is placed before it, and the saying is brought joined to it by "fa," which conveys the meaning of causality. The point of choosing this style, rather than making the punishment a mere condition, is that had they not been punished, for example, for their disbelief, despite having witnessed what compelled them to certain knowledge, they would not have said, "Why did You not send to us a messenger?" The cause of this saying is only the punishment and nothing else, not regret over what they missed of faith in their Creator. In this there is, as is not hidden, strong testimony to the firmness and deep-rootedness of their disbelief, like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And if they were returned, they would certainly return to that which they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28]. This is what the author of al-Kashshaf intended, and there is no need in the statement for an estimated omitted noun (mudaf), as appears to be the case.

Some have held that the statement is according to an estimated omitted noun, i.e., "lest a calamity befall them," etc. Thus the cause of the sending is only the aversion to that, because of what it contains of establishing the proof against them, and to Allah belongs the conclusive proof. This aversion is undoubtedly realized, which is what "law la" requires. They dismissed, by this estimate, the necessity of the realization of the befalling and of the said saying, and the negation of the non-sending as "law la" demands. In that there is what there is.

Ibn al-Munir said: "The verification in my view is that 'law la' is not, as the grammarians say, indicating that what follows it exists, or that its answer is impossible. The precise statement of its meaning is that it indicates that what follows it prevents its answer, the reverse of 'law.' Then the preventing thing may be existing, or may be supposed. What is in the verse is of the second kind, so there is no difficulty in it." The verse has also been cited as evidence that the saying of one to whom no messenger was sent, if he is punished, "My Lord, if only You had sent to me a messenger," is something fit for argument; otherwise it would not be fit to be a cause for the sending. In that is an indication that reason does not suffice without the Messenger. The discussion of this is well known, and the speech on it is abundant.

[Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 28, verse 48]

﴿Then when the truth came to them from Us⦆ — ﴿فَلَمّا جاءَهُمُ﴾: that is, those people; and what is meant by them here is the people of Makkah who were present at the time of the mission (ba'tha). All the plural pronouns that follow refer back to them.

﴿The truth from Us﴾ — ﴿الحَقُّ مِن عِنْدِنا﴾: that is, the true matter, which is the Qur'an revealed to him, upon him be blessings and peace. ﴿They said﴾ — ﴿قالُوا﴾: out of obstinacy and by way of demand. ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa﴾ — ﴿لَوْلا أُوتِيَ مِثْلَ ما أُوتِيَ مُوسى﴾: meaning him, upon him be blessings and peace, [they mean] the Book revealed all at once, upon Musa, peace be upon him.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Musa before?﴾ — ﴿أوَلَمْ يَكْفُرُوا بِما أُوتِيَ مُوسى مِن قَبْلُ﴾: this is a refutation of them and a demonstration that what they said was pure obstinacy, not a request for that which would guide them to the truth. ("Before") — ﴿مِن قَبْلُ﴾ — is connected to "they disbelieved" (يَكْفُرُوا). Its connection to "was given" (أُوتِيَ) does not have a clear meaning, since it would be a restriction without benefit, because it is known that what was given to Musa, peace be upon him, was before Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, or before these disbelievers. Yes, the matter of the refutation remains as it is, i.e.: did they not disbelieve, before this statement, in what was given to Musa, peace be upon him, just as they disbelieved in this truth?

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said﴾ — ﴿قالُوا﴾: is a resumptive clause, brought to affirm their disbelief implied by the preceding denial, and to explain its manner.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Two sorceries﴾ — ﴿سِحْرانِ﴾: is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they [i.e., the two Books] — they mean what was given to our Prophet and what was given to Musa, upon both of them be blessings and peace — are two sorceries. ﴿Supporting one another﴾ — ﴿تَظاهَرا﴾: that is, they cooperated, each confirming the other and supporting him. The reason for this is that the people of Makkah sent a group of their men to the rabbis of the Jews at one of their festivals, and they asked them about his affair, upon him be blessings and peace. They said: "We find him in the Torah by his description and attributes." When the group returned and informed them of what the Jews had said, they said that.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said: Indeed we are, in each of them﴾ — ﴿وقالُوا إنّا بِكُلٍّ﴾: that is, in each one of the two Books — ﴿disbelievers﴾ — ﴿كافِرُونَ﴾: an explicit statement of their disbelief in both of them, and an emphasis on their disbelief implied by calling them sorcery; this is due to the utmost of their defiance and their persistence in disbelief and transgression.

Al-Akthar read ﴿ساحِرانِ﴾ ("two sorcerers"), and the disbelievers intended by them our Prophet and Musa, upon them both be blessings and peace.

Talha and al-A'mash read ﴿(أظّاهَرا)﴾ with a hamzat al-wasl and a shaddah on the ẓā', and it is likewise in the codex of Abdullah. Its origin is ﴿تَظاهَرا﴾; when the tā' was changed into ẓā' and assimilated, it was made sukun, so a hamzat al-wasl was brought in to begin with a sakin. Maḥbub from al-Ḥasan, Yaḥyā ibn al-Ḥārith al-Dhimārī, Abū Ḥaywa, and Abū Khallād from al-Yazīdī read ﴿تَظّاهَرا﴾ with a tā' and a shaddah on the ẓā'. Ibn Khālawayh said: "Its shaddah is a grammatical error (laḥn), because it is a past-tense verb, and shaddah is only applied to the present tense." Ṣāḥib al-Lawāmiḥ said: "I do not know its meaning." And the author of al-Kāmil fi'l-Qirā'āt said: "It has no meaning."

Abū Ḥayyān gave this reading a rationale: that it is a present-tense verb from which the nūn has been dropped without a governing or jussive particle, and such deletion occurs in a few instances in speech and in poetry. And ﴿ساحِرانِ﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject; the original sentence is: "You two are sorcerers, you support one another" (أنْتُما ساحِرانِ تَتَظاهَرانِ), so ﴿أنْتُما﴾ was omitted, the tā' was assimilated into the ẓā', the nūn was dropped, and the address was maintained. Had it been read as ﴿يُظاهِرا﴾ with a yā', taking it as referring to the two sorcerers or as an implied reference to them, it would have had a valid basis. It seems that they addressed the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, with this, intending him and Musa, upon both of them be blessings and peace, through "you two" by way of predominance (taghlīb). This interpretation of the verse in the manner mentioned involves no strain, and it is perhaps what the grandeur of this sublime composition calls for and what the apparent force of His saying, exalted is He, requires:

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 28, verse 49:

﴿Say: Then bring a Book from Allah that is better guided than both of them, so I may follow it, if you are truthful.﴾ That is, better guided than what was given to the two of them, namely the Qur'an and the Torah. ﴿so I may follow it﴾, meaning: if you bring it, I will follow it. The verb (*atbaʿhu*) is in the jussive (*majzum*) because it is the response (*jawab*) to the imperative (*amr*) that precedes it. A conditional like this is used by one whose proof is manifestly clear, because bringing something better guided than the two Books is plainly impossible. It thus broadens the scope of the speech for rebuke (*tabkit*) and binding argument (*ilzam*). The use of the particle (*in*, "if") in Allah's words ﴿if you are truthful﴾, meaning in your claim that they are two fabricated sorceries, while their truthfulness is impossible, is a form of mockery directed at them. Zayd ibn ʿAli read (*atabiʿuhu*) with a *raf*ʿ (nominative) vowel, as a resumption (*istiʾnaf*), meaning: "I will follow it."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The truth is the Messenger, who confirms the Book, which is miraculous together with all the other miracles." He means that the context calls for the phrase "So when he came to them," i.e. the Messenger, or "So when the Messenger came to them." But he deviated from that to convey those meanings. And what was given to Moses is more general than the Book revealed all at once: the hand, the staff, and other signs of his, peace be upon him. This was objected to: the miracles such as the hand and the like have no connection with the context, and likewise the miracles of our Prophet (ﷺ) other than the Qur'an have no connection with it. The apparent meaning of Allah's words ﴿Say: Then bring...﴾ etc. points to this.

It is also permitted that the pronouns in (*jaahum*, "came to them") and (*qalu*, "they said") refer to the people of Mecca who were present, while the pronoun in (*yakfuru*, "they disbelieve") and likewise the pronoun in (*qalu*) in both places refer to the class of disbelievers known from the context. By them is meant the disbelievers who lived in the time of Moses, peace be upon him. (*Min qabl*, "before") is connected to (*yakfuru*), not to (*utiya*), because the benefit would not be apparent otherwise. By "two sorceries" (*sihrayn*) or "two sorcerers" (*saahiran*) is meant Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, as narrated from Mujahid. Describing them as "two sorceries" is for emphasis (*mubalagha*), or the phrase is read as if it were "two possessors of sorcery" (*dhawa sihrayn*). The meaning is: "Did not the sons of their kind before them disbelieve in what was given to Moses, peace be upon him, just as they disbelieved in what was given to you?" And those disbelievers said: "They, i.e. Moses and Aaron, are two sorceries or two sorcerers who support each other." It has also been said: the pronouns may refer to those present, while the disbelief and the statement mentioned belong to those earlier people in reality, and attributing them to those present is figurative, because of the connection between the two groups.

It has also been said, based on what is narrated from al-Hasan, that the Arabs had a precedent in the days of Moses, peace be upon him. The meaning is: "Did not their forefathers, before Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, disbelieve in what was given to Moses? They said: they, i.e. Moses and Aaron, are two sorceries or two sorcerers who support each other." This is in the style of Allah's words ﴿when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:49] and similar verses. The statement, understood in this way, indicates that their foothold in disbelief is firmly established, and that they have a deep root in obstinacy. That the Arabs had a precedent in the days of Moses, peace be upon him, is beyond doubt, to the extent that it was said that Pharaoh was an Arab from the descendants of ʿAd. But there is discussion about the soundness of explaining the verse in this way. You know that none of these interpretations is one that comforts the heart, and each contains its own forced reading.

Abu Hayyan claimed that the pronouns in (*yakfuru*) and likewise the pronoun in (*qalu*) clearly refer to the Quraysh who said: "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?" He argued that attributing this to them is because their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) is a denial of Moses, peace be upon him, and their attribution of sorcery to the Messenger is their attribution of it to Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, since the Prophets, peace be upon them, are of one valley. So whoever attributes to any one of them what is unbefitting, he is attributing it to all of them. Therefore there is no need to introduce the narration of the group in the matter of attribution, and on this basis it is permissible that by (*kull*, "each") is meant each one of the Prophets, peace be upon them. It is not hidden that what he claimed, regarding the clear reference of the pronoun to what was mentioned, is a matter acceptable to fair-minded people of sound intellect. But directing the attribution of disbelief and the statement that explains its manner to what was mentioned is something whose acceptance is unlikely. It seems he needed this only because the narration of the group was not established according to him.

It is narrated from Qatadah that he explained "two sorceries" as the Qur'an and the Gospel, and "two sorcerers" as Muhammad and ʿIsa (Jesus), peace be upon them both, and he took that statement to be the statement of the enemies of Allah, the Jews. This explanation of the two sorcerers as such is narrated from al-Hasan. It is also narrated from him that he explained them as Moses and ʿIsa, peace be upon them both. All of these, as you see, [are weak]. Their explanation as Muhammad and Moses, peace be upon them both, is what al-Bukhari related in his *Tarikh* and a group related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿAsim al-Jahdari that he used to read (*sihran*) and said: "They are two Books: the Furqan (the Qur'an) and the Torah. Do you not see that He, glorified is He, says: ﴿So bring a Book from Allah that is better guided than both of them﴾."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 50:

﴿Then if they do not respond to you﴾ That is, if they do not do what you have commanded them, namely to bring a Book better guided than these two. He expressed it as "responding" to indicate that the Prophet (ﷺ) was in complete safety regarding his matter; his command to them to bring what was mentioned was a summons to them toward a matter he wishes to occur.

And it has been said: the meaning is, if they do not respond to your calling them to faith after there has become clear to them the miracles contained in your Book which has come to them. Then "responding" is in its apparent sense, because faith is a matter that the Prophet (ﷺ) truly wishes to occur from them. It is, as in al-Bahr, in the sense of ijabah (answering), and it is transitive to the one who calls with the preposition lam, as in this verse, and the Exalted's saying: ﴿So his Lord responded to him﴾ [Yusuf: 34], and His saying, glorified is He: (So We responded to him) [al-Anbiya: 76, 84, 88, 90], and transitive directly, as in the line of the Book:

"And a caller who called, 'O You who answers the call,' but then no answerer answered him."

Al-Zamakhshari said: this verb is transitive to the supplication directly, and to the one who supplicates with lam; and when the supplication is omitted, it is usually transitive to the one who supplicates, so one says: "Allah the Exalted responded to his supplication" or "responded to him," and one hardly says "responded to him his supplication." His saying in the line "so he did not respond to him" is by omitting a modifier, meaning "so he did not respond to his supplication," end of quote. Had he made the pronoun of "yastajib-hu" refer to the supplication understood from "caller," it would not need an assumed element. He made the object omitted here because the caller is mentioned, and he justified it, as has been said, that with the mention of the caller and the responding, it is necessarily the case that the object is the supplication, so mentioning it would be pointless. He permitted that the omission is because it is known from the verb itself, not because the caller was mentioned. This ruling applies to istijabah but not to ijabah, due to His saying: ﴿Respond to the caller of Allah﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31].

﴿So know that they only follow their desires﴾, the deviant ones, without their having any basis whatsoever; for had they had any such basis, they would have brought it. ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire﴾ — this is a rhetorical interrogative of denial, meaning: no one is more astray than one who follows his desire ﴿without guidance from Allah﴾. That is, he is more astray than every astray person, although the apparent construction is for negating "more astray," not for negating equality, as has passed in its similar instances many times. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿without guidance﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the subject of "followed." Restricting the following to this is for added emphasis and elaboration in condemnation and misguidance; otherwise, its combination with His guidance, exalted is He, is of clearly impossible occurrence. It has been said: it is to exclude what contains guidance from Him, exalted is He, for a person may follow his desire and agree with the truth; but there is discussion in this. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ — those who wronged themselves, so they immersed themselves in following desire and turning away

Page 94

from the signs that guide to the clear truth.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 51:

﴿And We have certainly conveyed the Word to them﴾. The pronoun refers to the people of Makkah. The basic meaning of tawsil (conveying, connecting) is joining pieces of a rope to one another. The poet said:

*Say to the sons of Marwan: "What has broken my covenant is a weak rope that is always being joined."*

The meaning is: We have certainly sent down the Qur'an to them in succession, its parts following one another as wisdom requires, or in consecutive sequence, as promise and threat, stories and lessons, admonitions and counsel. It has also been said: We made it into awsal (sections), meaning various kinds, as promise and threat, etc. It has also been said: the meaning is that We conveyed to them the news of the Hereafter along with the news of this world, until it is as if they witnessed the Hereafter. It is narrated from al-Akhfash: We completed the Word for them. Al-Hasan read (wasalna) with a light sad and without doubling. In the reading of the majority, the doubling indicates intensification. From this, al-Raghib said, in explaining what is in the verse according to this reading: We have multiplied the Word for them, its parts joined one to another, ﴿so that they may remember﴾, and thereby believe in what it contains.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 52:

﴿The ones to whom We gave the Book before it﴾: before the Qur'an. This is on the view that the pronoun refers to the (revealed) word, meaning the Qur'an, or refers to the Qur'an as understood from it. Whichever is the case, the meaning is: before its being given to them. ﴿They﴾ are not those whose circumstances were mentioned (in the verses before). ﴿In it﴾, that is, in the Qur'an, ﴿believe﴾.

It is also said that the two pronouns refer to the Prophet (ﷺ). According to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, the relative clause refers to the believers among the People of the Book in general. It is also said that they were Abu Rifa'a and ten Jews who believed and were then harmed. Ibn Mardawayh, with a good chain, and a group (of narrators) reported from Rifa'a al-Qurazi something that supports this.

It is also said: forty people from the People of the Gospel who were believers in the Messenger (ﷺ) before his mission. Thirty-two from Abyssinia came with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and eight came from Syria: Bahira, Abraha, Ashraf, 'Amir, Ayman, Idris, Nafi' and Tamim. It is also said: Ibn Salam, Tamim al-Dari, al-Jarud al-'Abdi and Salman al-Farisi. This is attributed to Qatada.

Abu Hayyan preferred the general application, and held that what was mentioned is by way of example for those among the People of the Book who believed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 28, verse 53:

﴿When it is recited to them﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, ﴿they say: "We believe in it"﴾, i.e., that it is the speech of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿"Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord"﴾, i.e., the truth whose veracity we used to recognize. This sentence is an *istinaf* (a resumptive, new sentence, a sentence that begins a fresh statement) explaining what made them believe in it. It is also permissible that the sentence be *mufassirah* (explanatory) of what precedes it. And His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿"Indeed we were Muslims before it"﴾, i.e., before its revelation, ﴿Muslims﴾, is an explanation that their belief in it was a matter of long standing, since they had witnessed mention of it in the earlier Scriptures, and that they were upon the religion of Islam before the Qur'an was revealed. Their being upon the religion of Islam before its revelation is sufficiently established by their belief in it in general terms.

In *al-Kashshaf* and *al-Bahr* it is stated that Islam is the attribute of every monotheist who affirms revelation. The apparent meaning of this is that Islam is not among the distinctive features of this community (*ummah*) among the nations. Al-Suyuti, may Allah have mercy on him, held that it is among the distinctive features, and he composed a short treatise on that, and at the end of it he said: "When I finished composing this treatise and lay down on the bed to sleep, there came to (me) His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it﴾ (28:52) — the verse — so it was as if a mountain had been cast upon me, because its apparent indication supports the view that it is not distinctive. I reflected on it for an hour and nothing came clear to me, so I took refuge in Allah, Exalted is He, and hoped that He would open the answer to it. When I awoke at the time of dawn, behold, the answer had been opened, and three answers appeared regarding it:

The first: *Muslimin* is an active participle intended to refer to the future, as it is literally meant for that, not for the present or the past, and adherence to the literal meaning is the basic principle. The sense of the verse is: 'Indeed we were, before its coming, resolved to submit to it when it came, because of what we found in our books concerning his sending and his description.' What supports this is that the context guides us to the understanding that their intent is to report the veracity of the Qur'an and that they had been intent on submitting to it when the Prophet ﷺ came with it, and their intent was not to praise themselves in themselves by saying that they had the attribute of Islam first, since the situation does not allow that, as is not hidden.

The second: it is to be understood in the verse as ﴿Indeed we were before it Muslims, through it﴾, so the attribute of Islam is caused by the Qur'an, not by the Torah and the Gospel. What supports this is the mention of the relative clause earlier, where He, glorified is He, said: ﴿they believe in it﴾, for this indicates that the relative clause is intended here as well, but it was omitted out of disliking repetition.

The third: this attribute from them is based on what is the doctrine of al-Ash'ari, that it is among the ways of Allah, Exalted is He, that one dies a believer, so He, Exalted is He, names him a believer in His sight even if he was in a state of disbelief. We do not apply this attribute to him ourselves only because we do not know what is with Allah, Exalted is He. So when Allah, Exalted is He, concluded their affairs with entry into Islam, they reported about themselves that they had been characterized by it before, because the consideration in this attribute is the final outcome, and their description with that is more fitting than describing a disbeliever whom Allah, Exalted is He, knows will die upon Islam, because they were upon a true religion. This is a subtle meaning that we derived in this verse from the principles of the science of *kalam* (theology). End."

It is not hidden that the weakness of this answer is evident, as is also the case with the first answer. As for the second answer, it has the same meaning as what we mentioned concerning the verse, and al-Baydawi and others have mentioned it. He also permitted that *Islam* be taken to mean *inqiyad* (submission), i.e., "Indeed we were, before its revelation, submitting to the rulings of Allah, Exalted is He, as expressed in His Book revealed to us, and among them is the obligation of belief in it, so we were believers in it before its revelation."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 54:

﴿Those﴾ who are described by the qualities mentioned, ﴿they will be given their reward twice﴾: once for their belief in their own Scripture, and once for their belief in the Qur'an. ﴿Because they were patient﴾, i.e., for their patience and steadfastness in both beliefs, or in belief in the Qur'an before its revelation and after it, or in the face of the harm inflicted on them by those of their own religion who emigrated from them and opposed them, and by the polytheists. ﴿And they repel﴾, i.e., they push away, ﴿with good﴾, i.e., with obedience, ﴿evil﴾, i.e., disobedience, for good deeds erase evil deeds.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Mu'adh: "Follow the evil deed with a good deed, and it will erase it." It is also said: i.e., they repel harm with forbearance. Ibn Jubayr said: with what is right, the wrong. Ibn Zayd said: with good, evil. Ibn Salam said: with knowledge, ignorance, and with restraint, anger. Ibn Mas'ud said: with the testimony that there is no god but Allah, shirk. ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾, i.e., in the way of good, as the context of praise requires.

﴿When they hear idle talk﴾ (saqṭ al-qawl, "frivolous speech"). Mujahid said: "It means harm and abuse." al-Dahhak said: "It means polytheism." Ibn Zayd said: "It means what the Jews altered of the description of the Messenger (ﷺ)."

﴿they turn away from it﴾, i.e., from the idle talk, out of nobility of character, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72].

﴿And they say﴾ to them, i.e., to those who engage in idle talk, the meaning of which is understood from the mention of idle talk: ﴿To us our deeds, and to you your deeds﴾, disengaging from them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To you your religion, and to me my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6].

﴿Peace be upon you﴾. They say this as a farewell to them, not as a greeting; or it is also for disengagement, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Furqan: 63]. Whichever it is, there is no evidence in the verse for the permissibility of initiating the greeting of peace to a disbeliever, as al-Jassas (al-Jassas, the Hanafi jurist) claimed, since the purpose of it is none other than disengagement or farewell.

It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the disbelievers: "Do not initiate the greeting of peace to them, and if the People of the Book greet you with peace, say: 'And upon you.'" However, it has been related from Ibn Abbas that it is permissible to say to a disbeliever, when initiating the greeting, "Peace be upon you," meaning "May Allah be upon you," so that it becomes a supplication against him; but this is weak.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾ explains the reason for disengagement and farewell, i.e., we do not seek the companionship of the ignorant, nor do we desire to mix with them.

[p. 96] ﴿Indeed, you cannot guide﴾ with a guidance that inevitably reaches the desired goal ﴿whom you love﴾, meaning every person you love by nature, from among the people, whether your own folk or others. You cannot bring him into Islam, even if you exert the utmost effort in this and go beyond every known limit in your striving. It has also been said: "whom you love" means whose guidance you love.

﴿But God guides whom He wills﴾, that is, guides him by bringing him into Islam. ﴿And He knows best those who are guided﴾, meaning those who are prepared for it. These are the ones whom He, glorified be He, wills to guide, and among them are those whose attributes were mentioned from among the People of the Book. The form *a'lam* (knows best) is for emphasis regarding His knowledge, exalted be He.

It has also been said that it may be taken in its apparent sense. The statement of some of them implies that what is meant is that He, exalted be He, alone knows best who is guided, to the exclusion of others, mighty and majestic is He. Since God's guidance is linked with His knowledge, glorified be He, of the one who is guided, and since He, majestic and exalted, is the One who knows him alone, this indicates that by "those who are guided" is meant those who are prepared (*al-musta'iddun*), not those who are already characterised by the actual act. It then follows that His guidance of them means the capacity to achieve it. Since God's guidance in this sense is the case, and since *lakinna* (but) is placed between it and the guidance negated from the Messenger, peace and blessings of God be upon him, it follows that this guidance too must mean the capacity to achieve it, so that *lakinna* falls in its proper place. For this reason it has been said: the meaning is, "You cannot bring into Islam everyone you love, because you are a servant who does not know who is sealed upon his heart from others, but God, exalted be He, is capable of bringing into it whomever He wills, and He is the One who knows that he is not sealed upon his heart." There is room for discussion on this.

The apparent wording of *al-Kashshaf* (of al-Zamakhshari) is to take the negation of guidance in His saying, ﴿Indeed, you cannot guide whom you love﴾, as negation of the capacity to bring into Islam, and its affirmation in His saying, ﴿But God guides whom He wills﴾, as the actual occurrence of bringing into Islam. This is what we have adopted in explaining the verse. Its justification is that the context of the verse is to console him, peace and blessings of God be upon him, since his warning to those whom he loved and was most eager for, and the truth he brought to them, did not benefit them. Rather, they persisted in what they were upon and said, ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ [Al-Qasas: 48]. Then they disbelieved in him and in Moses, peace be upon them both. Thus they were the opposite of a people who were strangers to him, peace and blessings of God be upon him, since they believed in what he brought of the truth and said, "Indeed it is the truth from our Lord." Then they declared that they had believed in it long before, and by this they pointed to their belief in their own prophet and in what had been brought to them as well. So if "Indeed, you cannot guide whom you love" were not taken to mean the negation of the capacity to bring into Islam whomever he, peace be upon him, loved, but were instead taken to mean the negation of the actual occurrence of his bringing him into it, this would be far from consolation and close to reproach. It would be like your saying to someone who has loved ones who do not benefit them, "Indeed, you cannot benefit your loved ones." If this is not interpreted as "you are not able to benefit your loved ones," then it is said by way of reproach, rebuke or the like, not by way of consolation. Since God's guidance of those who were given the Book has a bearing on what calls for consolation, the fitting reading is to keep ﴿But God guides whom He wills﴾ in its apparent sense, that guidance actually occurs, rather than the mere capacity for guidance. Affirming this for God, exalted be He, is a consequence of affirming capacity, so affirming it entails affirming capacity necessarily. Thus the *istidrak* (the corrective "but") falls upon its target. Taking "those who are guided" to mean those prepared for guidance does not require taking "guides" to mean "is able to guide." So the alleged necessity mentioned is disputed. It is also possible that by "those who are guided" is meant those actually characterised by guidance, and by His knowledge of them is meant His recompense, glorified be He, for their being guided. So it is as if it were said: "He, exalted be He, knows best those who are guided, such as those from among the People of the Book who were mentioned, so He will reward them for their guidance with a reward or two rewards. So reflect."

The verse, as many reports indicate, was revealed concerning Abu Talib.

Abd ibn Humayd, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When the death of Abu Talib approached, the Prophet, peace and blessings of God be upon him, came to him and said, 'O uncle, say: There is no god but God, a word I will testify for you with before God on the Day of Resurrection.' He said: 'Were it not that the Quraysh would reproach me, saying, "It was only his fear of death that made him say it," I would have made you happy by confessing it.' Then God, exalted be He, revealed, ﴿Indeed, you cannot guide whom you love﴾ — the verse."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and others related, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from his father, something similar to this. Abu Sahl al-Sarri ibn Sahl related through the chain of Abd al-Quddus, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, that he said: "﴿Indeed, you cannot guide whom you love﴾, and so on, was revealed concerning Abu Talib. The Prophet, peace and blessings of God be upon him, pressed him to accept Islam, but he refused, so God, exalted be He, revealed this verse." Ibn Mardawayh also related its revelation concerning him from him (Ibn Abbas).

The question of his Islam is a matter of disagreement. The claim of a consensus (*ijma'*) of the Muslims or the exegetes that the verse was revealed concerning him is not sound. The Shi'a and many of their exegetes have held that he embraced Islam, and they claimed a consensus of the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt on this, and that most of his poems testify to it. It seems that whoever claims a consensus of the Muslims does not regard the dissent of the Shi'a as significant, nor rely on their reports. Furthermore, even on the view that he did not embrace Islam, it is not appropriate to revile him or to speak of him with idle talk, for this is something that grieves the 'Alawis. Indeed, it is not far-fetched that it is something that would grieve the Prophet, peace be upon him, whom the verse, on the basis of these reports, describes as loving him. Caution is not hidden from one who has understanding.

*For the sake of one eye, a thousand eyes are honoured.*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 57:

﴿And they say: If we were to follow the guidance with you, we would be snatched away from our land.﴾ That is, we would be driven out of our lands and our dwelling-place. The root of khatf (snatching) is stealing swiftly, and it is metaphorically applied to what has been mentioned. "The verse was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Uthman ibn Nawfal ibn Abd Manaf, when he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and they said: We know that you are upon the truth, but we fear that if we follow you and oppose the Arabs, and we are but a morsel (akalat ra's), they will snatch us from our land. So God, exalted is He, refuted their fear of being snatched by His saying: ﴿Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary?﴾" That is: Did We not preserve them and make their place a sanctuary of security, by the sanctity of the House, around which the Arabs trade while they themselves are secure therein? So the conjunction is upon an elided clause (wa-numakkin), which implies the meaning of "making" (al-ja'l), and for this reason ḥaraman and āminan are in the accusative as a noun of relation, like Laban and Tamir. Abu Hayyan made the predication in it metaphorical, because the one who is truly secure are its inhabitants, so there is no need to make it a relative noun; and this is a good opinion. ﴿To which are brought﴾ That is, it is carried to it and gathered in it from every side and direction. ﴿the fruits of all things﴾ That is, the fruits of many things, with kull being for multiplicity, and its basic meaning is encompassment, though it is by no means intended in its absolute sense. The clause is another attribute of ḥaraman, removing what might be imagined of their harm if they followed the guidance, through the cutting off of supplies. His exalted saying: ﴿a provision from Us﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) from the sense of yujbā, since its outcome is that they are provided for; or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from thamarāt, in the sense of "provided for"; and the use of a circumstantial state from an indefinite noun is valid according to those who do not hold otherwise, because it is specified here by the genitive construction; or it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), with the implied sense "We drive to it that provision." The summary of the refutation is that there is no basis for fear of being snatched if they are secure, for they do not fear it while they are idol-worshippers; so how would they fear when they are secure and combine the sanctity of faith with the sanctity of the station? ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ They are ignorant, not perceiving nor reflecting so that they might know this. Thus it is connected to His saying: ﴿Have We not established﴾, and so on.

It has been said: it is connected to His saying, glorified is He: "from Us," meaning: few of them reflect and thus know that this is a provision from God, mighty and majestic, for had they known, they would not have feared other than Him. The first is more evident, and the discourse upon it is more forceful in censure. Al-Munqari read "tukhtaṭaf" (nutakhattaf) with the nominative (nutakhattafu), as was read in His saying: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾ [al-Nisa: 78] with the nominative of yudrik. It was explained as being by the implied "fa-nahnu nutakhattaf" (so we are snatched), and this is an anomalous explanation.

Page 98
Nafi' and a group from Ya'qub, and Abu Hatim from Asim, read "tujbā" with the feminine ta'. It is also read "tajnī" with the nun, from al-jany, which is cutting the fruit, and its transitivity with ilā, as in your saying yajnī ilayya fīhi and yajnī ilā al-khāffa. Aban ibn Taghlib from Asim read "thumurāt" with a damma on the tha' and the mim, and some read "thamrāt" with a fatha on the tha' and sukun on the mim.

Then, after He, exalted is He, had refuted their fear of the people, He made clear that they deserve to fear the might of God, exalted is He, by His saying: ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed which exulted in its livelihood﴾. That is: and many a people of a town whose condition was like the condition of these people in security, ease of living and comfort, until they became insolent and deluded and did not uphold the due right of the blessing. So We destroyed them and laid waste their dwellings. ﴿Those are their dwellings﴾, which you pass by on your journeys, like the Rock of Thamud, ruined, because of what they did wrong, while they were in that state.

﴿Not inhabited after them﴾, after their destruction, ﴿except a little﴾. That is, except for a little time, since none dwells there except passers-by for a day or part of a day; or, except for a little habitation. Its littleness is in terms of the littleness of those who dwell there, so it is as if it was said: "None of the people dwelt there after them except a few."

It has been permitted that the exception be from the dwellings, meaning: except a little of them that was inhabited, though this is remote. ﴿And We are the inheritors﴾ of them, since no one succeeded them to dispose of their dwellings and all their possessions as they did. In al-Kashshaf: that is, We left them in a state where no one dwells in them, or We ruined them and levelled them with the ground. He indicates that inheritance is either merely the transfer of them from their owners, or their joining to what God, exalted is He, created at the beginning, so that it is as if it returned to its origin and entered the category of God's pure dominion as it was at first; and this is the meaning of inheritance. The accusative of ﻣَﻌِﻴﺸَﺘَﻬَﺎ (ma'ishatahā) is as a specification (tamyīz) according to the school of the Kufans, or it is like the object according to the view of some of them, or it is an object according to the implicit transitivity of ﺑَﻄِﺮَﺖْ (baṭirat) in the sense of a transitive verb, i.e. "ungrateful for its livelihood and did not observe its due right," according to the view of most of the Basrans; or by dropping ﻓِﻲ (fī), i.e. "in its livelihood," according to the view of al-Akhfash; or as an adverbial of place, like "I came at the twinkling of the star," according to the view of al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 59:

﴿And your Lord would never destroy the cities﴾ is an explanation of divine providence following the explanation of the destruction of the cities mentioned; i.e., it was not proper, nor fitting, nor was it, by His past judgment and prior decree, that He should destroy the cities before warning, rather His custom, Mighty and Majestic is He, was not to destroy them ﴿until He sends into their mother (umm, origin) a messenger reciting to them Our verses﴾, i.e., into its origin and chief city to which those cities return, ﴿reciting to them Our verses﴾ that speak the truth, and calling them to it with encouragement and warning. And the reason Glorified is He did not destroy them until He sent to them a messenger is to establish the proof against them and cut off their excuse, so that they would not say: "Why did You not send to us a messenger that we might follow Your verses?" And the sending was into Umm al-Qura because in the people of the great town, the seat of the kingdom and the place of rulings, there is intelligence and discernment, so they are more receptive to the call and more noble.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Qatadah that Umm al-Qura is Makkah and the Messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ).

So what is meant by "the cities" is the cities that existed in his time, peace be upon him, though the first view is more preferable. The turn to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah) in "Our verses" is to cultivate awe and to bring in dread. It was also read as "fi immiha" with a kasrah on the hamzah, following the miim. ﴿And We would never destroy the cities﴾ is coordinated with ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the cities﴾, ﴿except while its people were wrongdoers﴾: this is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of states, i.e., and We were not destroying the people of the cities, after We had sent into their mother a messenger calling them to the truth and guiding them to it, in any state except the state of their being wrongdoers by denying Our messenger and disbelieving in Our verses. Thus the sending is a limit for the impossibility of destruction according to the divine custom, not for its non-occurrence, such that it would necessitate the realization of destruction immediately after the sending.

[Page 99]

﴿And whatever you have been given﴾ means: whatever thing you have obtained of the affairs of this world and its means, ﴿then it is the enjoyment of the life of this world and its adornment﴾. So it is a thing whose nature is to be enjoyed and adorned with for a few days. The word *matā'* (enjoyment) suggests paucity, and likewise He mentions ﴿more lasting﴾ in contrast. The word *al-dunyā* (the nearer, this world) also indicates paucity and baseness. ﴿And what is with Allah﴾ in the Garden, which is the reward, ﴿is better﴾ in itself than that, because it is pure delight and complete joy. ﴿And more lasting﴾ because it is everlasting. How can the finite compare with the infinite? ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ That is: will you not reflect, so that you do not do this clear matter, and thus exchange what is lower for what is better, and fear the loss of what you have obtained of the enjoyment of the life of this world, and refrain from following the guidance that leads to what is with Allah, the Exalted? Accordingly, this is a rebuttal to them concerning their prevention, out of fear of being snatched away, from following him (ﷺ), on the assumption that what they fear would actually occur.

Abu 'Amr read *ya'qilūn* with the third-person *yā'* (ياء الغيبة), by way of *al-iltifāt* (the shift from direct address to third person). This is more forceful in admonition, since it implies that because of their lack of reason they are not fit to be addressed directly. So the shift here is for the sake of rebuking them for their failure to shift (i.e., to heed the address).

It was also read *famatā'an al-ḥayāta al-dunyā*, meaning: then you enjoy it in the life of this world. Here *matā'an* is in the accusative as a *maṣdar* (verbal noun), and *al-ḥayāta* is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarfiyya*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 61:

﴿Is one to whom We have made a good promise, and who will certainly encounter it,﴾ that is, a promise of Paradise and what is in it of pure, lasting bliss, for the goodness of a promise follows from the goodness of what is promised. ﴿He will certainly encounter it﴾, that is, will surely attain it, because it is impossible that God, exalted is He, should break His promise. For this reason the nominal sentence, which conveys that its realization is absolutely certain, was used, and it was joined by the particle fa' (fa, "then/so"), which indicates causation. ﴿Like one whom We have provided with the enjoyment of the life of this world,﴾ which is mixed with pains, clouded by troubles, and followed by regret at its ending. The meaning of the first fa' (fa) is the arrangement of the denial of any resemblance between the people of this world and the people of the Hereafter, based on what precedes it, namely the evident disparity between the enjoyment of the life of this world and what is with God, exalted is He. That is: after this clear disparity, are the two groups still equated?

God's words ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forward﴾ are a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "We have provided" (matta'nāhu), included with it within the scope of the relative clause, emphasizing the denial of resemblance in its statement. It is as if it were said: "Like one whom We have provided with the enjoyment of the life of this world, then We will bring him forth, or We have brought him forth, on the Day of Resurrection to the Fire or to the punishment." The word "muḥḍar" (those brought forth) became specific to this sense for that reason. As for the shift to the nominal sentence, it has been said that it serves to indicate certainty and absolute decisiveness. The fact that its predicate is an adverbial phrase (ẓarf) does not detract from this, and the indication of certainty would still arise had it been said "We have brought him forth"; this does not conflict with that. It may be said that in the sublime composition there is something other than the indication of certainty: it is not present in your saying "then We have brought him forth on the Day of Resurrection," namely the indication of the sense of subsequence (taqwā) or restriction (ḥaṣr), the indication of awe, and the placing of the listener in bewilderment. For the sum of all this the nominal sentence was used. "Yawm" (the Day) is connected to the word "muḥḍarīn" mentioned, and was placed before it for the sake of the rhyme (fāṣila); or it is connected to an implied element, and the discussion of such cases has already passed. "Thumma" (then) here denotes delay in rank rather than in time, although it is valid to take it as temporal, which would keep the word in its literal meaning, since that is more fitting to the context; but the figurative sense is more eloquent and more productive of meaning, and masters of eloquence turn to figurative usage wherever possible, because it contains subtle refinements of meaning.

Ṭalḥa read «a-man wa'adnāhu» without the fa'. Qālūn and al-Kisā'ī read «thumma hwa» with the h sukūn (sukūn on the hā'), as is said of ʿaḍud and ʿaḍd, likening the separated element, namely the final mīm of thumma, to the connected one. The verse was revealed, as Ibn Jarīr narrated from Mujāhid, concerning the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and Abū Jahl. He also narrated by another route from him that it was revealed concerning Ḥamzah and Abū Jahl. It has been said that it was revealed concerning ʿAlī, may God ennoble his face, and Abū Jahl, and this is attributed to Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb and al-Suddī. It has also been said: concerning ʿAmmār, may God be pleased with him, and al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra,
page 100
It has been said: it was revealed concerning the believer and the disbeliever.

﴿And the Day He calls to them﴾ is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with "the Day of Resurrection," since the two differ in designation even though they are identical in essence. Alternatively, it is in the accusative (*manṣūb*) by an implied verb, "remember" (*udhkur*). His calling to them, exalted is He, may be through an intermediary or without one, and it is a call of humiliation and rebuke. ﴿Then He will say﴾ explains the calling. ﴿"Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ That is, those whom you used to claim were My partners, for *zaʿama* (to claim or assume) is among the verbs that take two objects, as in the verse:

*And that he who has lived, O Umm Malik, will die, and I did not consider you exempt from that.*

Both objects are omitted here together, relying on the context that indicates them, as in the proverb *man yasmaʿ yukhill* ("whoever listens, errs"). In *al-Kashshaf*, it is permissible to omit both objects in the category of *ẓanantu* (I thought), but it is not valid to limit oneself to only one of them. Some claimed that the invalidity of limiting to one is the more correct view, and that it is the position of most scholars. Al-Akhfash said: when *ẓanna* (to think) and its sisters enter on a clause such as *ẓanantu annaka qāʾimun* (I thought that you are standing), the second object of the two is omitted, and the estimate is *ẓanantu qiyāmaka kāʾinan* (I thought your standing was existing), because *anna* (with the open hamza) is interpreted as a noun phrase. Sibawayh holds that *anna* with what follows it takes the place of both objects. The Kufans permitted limiting oneself to the first object when something occupies the place of the second, as in the nominal sentence *aqāʾimun akhawāka* (are your two brothers standing?), so they say: *hal ẓanantu qāʾiman akhawāka?* (did you think your two brothers standing?). Abu Hayyan said: if a sign indicates one of them, it may be omitted, as in the verse:

*As if there had never been a separation, when after it there was a meeting, but I do not expect a meeting.*

That is, I do not expect, after the separation, a meeting. The author of *al-Tuḥfa* said: in the category of *kasawtu* (I clothed), it is permissible to limit oneself to one of the two objects, with or without an indicator, because the first of the two is other than the second. Some permitted omitting the first object when it is the grammatical subject in meaning, as in the verse ﴿Do not think that those who disbelieved could escape [Us]﴾ [al-Nur: 57], meaning: "Let not those who disbelieved think themselves able to escape." Al-Tibi said: the omission is not permitted in cases other than those mentioned, and the likely reason for permitting it here is that these verbs are restrictions on the propositions. They enter upon nominal sentences to specify what they are, because the attribution may be from knowledge or from assumption. So if one of the two parts of the sentence were limited to, because a context exists, it would be imagined that what the speech was directed toward, and what is concerned with it, is the mentioned part, and that the unmentioned part is not something cared about. However, when the subject and the object refer to one thing, the matter is easier. Something from the author of *al-Iqlid* supports this. May Allah exalt his resting place, he extended the discussion at this point. Ibn Hisham claimed that it is better to supply here "those whom you used to claim that they were My partners," because the claim in the revelation did not fall on two explicit objects, but on their connection, as in the verse ﴿those whom you claimed that they were partners among you﴾ [al-An'am: 94]. This is open to scrutiny.

The apparent meaning is that "the partners" refers to whatever was worshipped besides Allah, be it an angel, a jinn, a human, a star, an idol, or other than these.

[Page 101]

﴿Said﴾: a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that answers an implied question), built on the report of a question, as if it were said: "What happened after this question?" So it was said: He said: ﴿Those against whom the word has come into effect﴾, meaning: the requirement of the word has been established against them and its consequence has been realized, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ [Hud: 119], and other verses of warning. By the relative clause is meant the associates whom they used to claim were partners, namely the devils and the leaders of disbelief. Specifying them with what is in the relative clause's scope, although its meaning also includes the followers, is because they are the originators of disbelief and deserve punishment. Describing them in this way, rather than as "those whom they claimed to be partners," is to exclude such as Jesus, Ezra and the angels, peace be upon them, since "partners" includes them according to what you have heard. Their hastening to answer, although the question was addressed to the worshippers, is because they perceived that the question from them was a question of rebuke and humiliation, and it calls for their being brought forward and rebuked for misguidance, and for their certainty that the worshippers would say: "These are the ones who misled us."

It has been said: It is possible that the worshippers had already answered by way of excuse, saying: "These are the ones who misled us," and then the associates said what Allah, exalted is He, related, as a reply to their saying that, but He did not mention the worshippers' words, for brevity, since they were evident. ﴿Our Lord, these are the ones whom we led astray﴾ is a preparation for the answer. The pointing to the worshippers is to show that they are saying what they say in their presence, and that they are unable to deny it or refute it. (﴿These﴾) is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is the relative clause after it, and the clause ﴿we led astray﴾ is the relative clause, and the returning pronoun (a'id) is omitted because it is stated explicitly afterwards, meaning: those whom we led astray. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We led them astray just as we ourselves went astray﴾ is the actual answer, meaning: we did not compel them into error; rather we led them astray by way of whispering and enticement, not by force or constraint, so they went astray by their own choice, a going astray like our going astray by our own choice.

It is also permissible that the relative clause be an adjective of the demonstrative (ism al-ishara), and the predicate be the clause ﴿we led them astray just as we went astray﴾. Abu 'Ali [al-Fārisī] in al-Tadhkira prohibited this, saying that it leads to the predicate having no additional benefit, since their leading them astray was already known from the description. It was answered that the comparison indicates that they went astray by choice, not that leading astray is compulsion. As for the statement that "as we went astray" is a supplementary element (fadla), so it does not become essential in the sentence at all, this is no argument, because supplementary elements may become obligatory in some contexts, such as: Zayd, 'Amr is standing in his house.

Aban [ibn Taghlib], from 'Asim, and some of the Syrian readers read "كَما غَوِينا" (kamā ghawīnā) with a kasra on the waw. Ibn Khalawayh said: this is not the preferred reading, because the Arabic usage is "ghawaytu" (I went astray) from error, while "ghawītu" with kasra means "I was satiated" (from excessive eating).

﴿We disown﴾ them and what they chose of disbelief and sins, out of their own desires, directing the disowning and preparing for it, ﴿to You﴾. The sentence is an affirmation of what precedes it, because the admission of having gone astray is in reality a disowning, and for this reason it is not conjoined to it by a conjunction. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It was not us they worshipped﴾, meaning: they did not worship us; rather they were in reality and in ultimate outcome worshipping their own desires. It has been said: "mā" is a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyya) connected to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We disown﴾, and there is an understood preposition, meaning: we disown their worship of us. Taking it as a negation, on the basis that the meaning is "they did not worship us with any right or proof," is nothing. In any case, ﴿iyyana﴾ is the object of ﴿they worshipped﴾, placed first for the sake of the verse's closing rhyme (fāṣila).

[Page 102 begins partway through this passage.]

﴿And it will be said﴾ as a rebuke to them and in mockery of them: ﴿Call upon your partners﴾ whom you claimed [to be partners with God]. ﴿So they call upon them﴾ out of extreme bewilderment. Otherwise there is no real request for an answer in the call. It has also been said that they call upon them out of necessity of compliance, on the basis that there is a genuine request. The purpose of asking them to do this is to expose them before all the witnesses, by having them call upon one who has no benefit for himself. It has been said: the apparent meaning of the command being followed by "fa" (so/then) in the words of God Most High, ﴿so they call upon them﴾, is that the "fa" indicates the request for the call and its being made obligatory. The first interpretation is more eloquent in conveying the terror of the affair of those disbelievers and in pointing to the evil of their condition. The sequence indicated by "fa" (immediacy) facilitates the next words: ﴿but they do not respond to them﴾, since they are necessarily unable to respond and to give help. It is also permitted that the meaning is: ﴿they did not answer them﴾ because they were occupied with an overwhelming preoccupation that distracted them from them, and perhaps their mouths were sealed at that time. ﴿And they see the punishment﴾. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to the ones who call. al-Dahhak said: it refers to both the callers and those called upon together. It has been said: it refers only to those called upon, but this is not valid.

The apparent meaning is that the seeing is visual. The seeing of the punishment is either in the sense of seeing its beginnings, or in the sense of seeing it itself, by treating it as if it were present before them. It is also permitted that the seeing is cognitive, and the second object is omitted, i.e. they saw the punishment connected to them, or overwhelming them, or something similar.

You know that the omission of one of the two objects of verbs of the heart is disputed as to its permissibility. It was mentioned earlier, from some, that most scholars prohibit it. So whoever prohibits it and says, in explaining the meaning, "they saw the punishment connected to them," makes "connected" a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the punishment. ﴿If only they had been guided﴾. "Law" (if only) is conditional, and its answer is omitted, i.e. if they had been guided to one of the ways of contrivance by which they could ward off the punishment, they would have warded it off by it; or, if they had been guided and believing in the world, they would not have seen the punishment.

[Page 102]

It has been objected that what indicates the omitted element is "they see the punishment," which is affirmative, so the omitted element should not be supposed to be negated. This objection is not valid, because attention is to the meaning, and if omission is permitted merely on the basis of the indication of the situation, then when the indication of the speech is added to it, it is more appropriate, and even more so. It is also permitted that "law" is for wishing, i.e. they wished that they had been guided. Then it does not need an answer. The author of al-Taqrib said: this is open to scrutiny, since the proper form would be "law kunna" (if only we had been), unless it is in reported speech, like "he swore: he will surely strike," or by interpreting "they saw" as "they wished for their guidance."

It is also permitted, on the assumption that it is for wishing, that the phrase "if only they had been guided" was placed in the position of "they were bewildered at seeing it," since everyone at that time would wish guidance for them because of that terror and bewilderment, out of compassion for them. Or it is from God, exalted is His glory, figuratively, as was said regarding His words: ﴿And if only they had believed and been mindful of God, a reward from God would have been better﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:103]. al-Tibi considered this placement in that position to be an instance of "mention of the cause for the effect" (ilṭlāq al-musabbab 'alā al-sabab), because their bewilderment is a cause that prompts this statement. He, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the arrangement of the verse on this view fits well.

Imam al-Razi chose that it is conditional, but he did not accept what they said about the estimation of the answer. After relating what they said, he said: "In my view the answer is not omitted, and in its explanation there are several aspects. The first is that when God addresses them with His words, exalted is He, ﴿Call upon your partners﴾, then at that point their fear intensifies, and something overtakes them like fainting and dizziness, so they become such that they see nothing. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they see the punishment﴾; if only they could see something, meaning that they do not see the punishment because they have become such that they see nothing. The second is that when He, exalted is He, mentioned about the partners, which are the idols, that they do not respond to those who called upon them, He said concerning them: ﴿and they see the punishment, if only they had been guided﴾; i.e., these idols would have been witnessing the punishment if they had been living and guided beings, but they are not like that. The use of the pronoun for rational beings is in accordance with the belief of the people concerning them. The third is that the intended meaning of 'seeing' be seeing of the heart, i.e., and the disbelievers knew the truth of this punishment, if only they had been guided. These aspects, in my view, are better than the aspects based on the claim that the answer of 'law' is omitted, for that requires disjointing the structure of the verse." End of his words.

By my life, he has not brought anything, and what refutes him is more evident than that it should be hidden from one who has even minimal discernment between the living and the dead.

And [mention] the Day He calls to them and says, "What answer did you give the messengers?" It is conjoined (*'atf*, coordination) to the first. They were questioned first about their associating partners with God, because that is the purpose of "Where are My partners, those whom you used to claim?" and second about their response to the messengers who had forbidden them from that.

﴿Then the news became blind to them that day﴾. Its original form is فَعَمُوا عَنِ الأنْباءِ (fa-'amū 'ani al-anbā'), meaning they were blind to the news, that is, they did not find their way to it. Here there is an explicit, derivative metaphor (al-isti'āra al-taṣrīḥiyya al-tab'iyya, a metaphor in which the verb or adjective itself is borrowed), in which blindness is borrowed for failure to find the right way. It was then inverted for emphasis, so that the news is made not to find its way to them. The verb 'amiya was also given the sense of being hidden (taḍmīn, implying one verb's meaning within another), which is why it takes ʿalā rather than ʿan. Had it not been for this, it would have taken ʿan and would not have been connected to al-anbā', because news is heard, not seen. In this inversion there is an indication that what comes to mind flows out to it and reaches it from the external world and from reality itself, either directly or through recalling the image that came from it by its external signs. So when the mind errs in receiving the external world, by not reaching it because the path between them is blocked by blindness or the like, it is not able to bring forth or to recall. This is because, when the news that came to them from the external world was made blind, not finding its way, it indicates that they are blind and do not find their way, all the more so, because their finding their way by it would come after it. If the news itself does not find its way, then what of those who find their way by it? So it is said, and let it be pondered. It is also permitted that there be in the phrase an implicit imaginative metaphor (al-isti'āra al-makniyya al-takhyīliyya), meaning that the news became like blindness upon them, not finding its way to them. By al-anbā' is meant either what was asked of them and what they answered the messengers, peace be upon them, or what encompasses that and everything with which an answer is possible. If the messengers, peace be upon them, stammer in answering such questions in that dreadful situation, and entrust knowledge to the Knower of the unseen, despite their freedom from the peril of being questioned, then what do you suppose of those misguided peoples?

Al-A'mash, Jana' ibn Ḥubaysh and Abū Zur'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarīr read فَعُمِّيَتْ (fa-ʿummiyat), with a damma on the ʿayn and a shadda on the mīm.

﴿So they do not question one another﴾, that is, they do not ask one another, because of the extreme of their bewilderment, or because they know that all are alike in ignorance. The fa' here is either explanatory (tafṣīliyya) or consequential (tafrī'iyya), because the cause of the blindness is the extreme of bewilderment.

Ṭalḥa read لا يَسّاءَلُونَ (lā yassā'alūn), with the tā' assimilated into the sīn.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 67:

﴿But as for he who repents﴾, meaning from polytheism, ﴿and believes and does righteous deeds﴾, meaning he combines faith with righteous deeds, ﴿then perhaps he will be among the successful﴾. That is, those who attain what is sought with Him, Mighty and Majestic, and are saved from what is feared. The word (عَسى, ʿasā, "perhaps") is used for certainty, according to the custom of the noble ones, or for hope on the part of the aforementioned penitent, meaning: let him anticipate that he will prosper. As for His saying, Exalted is He, (فَأمّا, fa-ammā, "but as for"), it has been said that it is for elaborating on what is general in the listener's mind, from the explanation of what the state of the polytheists will become, namely how the state of those among them who repent will be, and to indicate that the report about it follows from what came before it. So the verse is connected to what precedes it. Al-Tayyibi said: it is connected to His saying, Exalted is He, ﹙﹚﹙"Is he to whom We have promised a good promise [al-Qasas: 61]﹚. The discussion of the partners is a digression for the mention of the summoning. Al-Kashshaf (al-Kashf) criticized this, saying that the apparent meaning is that it is not connected to that at all. Rather, when He, Glorified is He, mentioned the state of those upon whom the Word was justified, from among the followers and the followed, He, Exalted is His majesty, said, urging them to abandon it: ﴿But as for he who repents and believes﴾. It is as if it were said: what was mentioned is their destination; but as for he who repents, then no (فَكَلّا, fa-kallā, "no" / it is not so).

﴿And your Lord creates whatever He wills﴾: [He creates] His creatures, from the substances (a'yan) and the accidents (a'rad). ﴿and chooses﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "creates." The meaning, according to what has been said, is that He creates what He wills by His choice, so He does not create anything without choice. This is not understood from "whatever He wills," so there is no trace of repetition in the verse. Other things have been said to repel what might be suspected of this, which al-Khafajī transmitted and refuted, and he did not address criticism of this view. I consider it not free from remoteness. I have an interpretation of the verse which I will mention afterwards, God willing.

﴿They had no choice﴾: that is, *khiyara* (choice) like *ṭiyara* (omen) in the sense of *taṭayyur* (augury), and both have the same meaning as *ikhtiyār* (choosing). The apparent meaning of the verse is the outright negation of choice from the servant, as the Jabriyya (Determinists) say. Whoever affirms choice for the servant says: because he is, through the motives which, if God Most High had not created them in him, he would not have been in existence, this is the doctrine of al-Ash'arī, as the scholar al-Dawānī verified. He said: What al-Ash'arī affirmed is the connection of the servant's power and will, which is an ordinary cause for God Most High's creation of the act in him. When we investigate the origins of the act, we find that the will arises from a desire for it and the conception that it is agreeable, and other matters none of which is within the servant's power and choice. The scholar al-Kūrānī, in some of his treatises composed on this question, verified that the doctrine of the Salaf is that the servant has an effective power by God Most High's permission, and that he has choice, but that he is compelled in his choice. He claimed that this is the doctrine of al-Ash'arī, not what has spread, that he has a power that is not effective at all, but rather it is like a paralysed hand. Negating choice from him according to this is similar to what has passed, for since he is compelled by it, his existence is like non-existence.

It has been said: the verse conveys the negation of their ownership of choice, and this applies to one compelled in his choice, that he is not an owner of choice, since he does not dispose of it as he wills the disposition of an owner over his property. It has been said: the meaning is that it is not fitting or proper for them to choose over Him, that is, it is not proper for them to dictate to Him, Glorified is He, by saying: Why did God Most High not do such and such?

This is supported by the fact that the verse was revealed when al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?" or when the Jews said: "If the messenger to Muhammad (ﷺ) were other than Gabriel (peace be upon him), we would have believed in him," as has been said. On this interpretation the sentence is emphatic of what precedes it or explanatory of it, since the meaning of that is: He creates what He wills and chooses what He wills to choose, not what the servants choose over Him. Therefore it is free of a conjunction. According to what has preceded, it is a resumptive sentence answering a question whose implied form is: "What is the state of the servants?" or "Do they have choice?" or the like. It has been said: they have no choice. This view is weakened because there is no indication of this meaning in the sublime composition, and it involves omitting the complement, which is "over God Most High," without any indicating context. And the claim that the cause of revelation is what was mentioned is disputed. The second view, by its apparent meaning, requires that the pronoun in "for them" refer to the Jews, and there is much remoteness in that.

It has been said: *mā* is a relative pronoun, the object of "chooses," and the returning pronoun is omitted; the stop is on "wills" with *lā* as a negation particle; the stop on "chooses" is as stated explicitly by al-Zajjāj, ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān and al-Naḥḥās, as in the two previous views. That is: and He chooses that in which there is good and righteousness for them. His choosing that is by way of grace and generosity according to us, and by way of obligation according to the Muʿtazila (Rationalists). Al-Ṭabarī went to the relative meaning of *mā* and its being the object of "chooses," except that in explaining the meaning on this basis he said: that is, He chooses from among the messengers and the laws what was good for people. He rejected that it be negative, lest the meaning be that they did not have choice in the past and it is theirs in the future. Abū Ḥayyān claimed that it was reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, the meaning that he adopted. He objected that the language does not support it, because the known usage is that *khiyara* means choice, not good, and that it does not fit what follows it, His saying: "Glory be to God" etc., and likewise does not fit what precedes it, His saying: "He creates what He wills." Some have weakened it by saying that it involves omitting the returning pronoun, and it is not hidden that its omission is common. What al-Ṭabarī was objected to has been answered: it is possible that the intended meaning, aided by the context, is the continuation of the negation, or that the intended meaning is what they had in God's knowledge, and this is after granting the necessity that the meaning be what he mentioned if the speech is left on its apparent sense.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: In my view it is correct that *mā* is the object of "chooses" if we take *kāna* as complete, that is: God Most High chooses every existent, and nothing exists except by His permission. His saying: ﴿they had no choice﴾ is a resumptive sentence whose meaning is enumerating the blessing upon them in God's choosing for them, if they accept and understand. End.

That is, and God Most High knows best, that the intended meaning is God's choice for them, that is, His choosing for their benefit. The learned Saʿdī Jalabī has something similar to this, except that he said regarding His saying ﴿they had no choice﴾ that it is in the sense of "Shall they have the choice?" with the interrogative hamza of denial.
