He mentioned that this meaning is suited by what follows it, His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Glory be to God﴾ etc., for it is either an expression of wonder at affirming choice for other than Him, or a declaration of His exaltation above it. The weakness of what these two said is not hidden, because it opposes the apparent sense in several respects. There appears to me in the verse an interpretation other than those mentioned: that "and chooses" be coordinated with "creates," and the stop on it is complete, as several have explicitly stated. It is from choosing in the sense of selecting and preferring, and likewise *khiyara* in the sense of choice in this meaning. The verb is transitive with its object omitted, relying on what precedes it as an indication, that is: and He chooses whatever He wills. The fronting of the predicated subject in each of the two sides of the coordinated and coordinating clause serves to affirm exclusivity. The sentence ﴿they had no choice﴾ is emphatic of what precedes it, since the exclusivity takes on conveying the negation which it contains. The discourse is directed at the ignorance of the polytheists in their choosing what they associated and their selecting of it for worship and intercession for them on the Day of Resurrection, as ﴿call upon your partners﴾ hints at. The use of *mā* has an evident aspect. The meaning is: And your Lord, not other than Him, creates whatever He wills to create, and He alone, not other than Him, selects and prefers whatever He wills to select and prefer. So from what He creates He prefers intercessors and chooses them for intercession, and distinguishes some of His creatures, may His majesty be exalted, over others, and favours it over it by what He wills. It is not for these polytheists to select and prefer what they wish and to distinguish some of God's creatures over others and to make them preeminent with Him, Mighty and Majestic, over others, because that requires complete power and that its doer not be restricted at all. How could they have that? So there is nothing for them but to follow God Most High's choosing, and He, may He be Exalted, did not choose their partners whom they chose for worship and intercession in the manner in which they chose them. So they are nothing but ignorant, misguided people who turned away from what is incumbent upon them and presumed to what is not theirs in any state.

If you wish, consider the verb as intransitive and say: the meaning is: And your Lord, not other than Him, creates whatever He wills to create, and He, Glorified is He, alone, not other than Him, performs choosing and preferring, so He prefers some of His creatures for such-and-such and others for such-and-such, and distinguishes some of them over others and makes it preeminent with God Most High over it. For He, Glorified is He, is Powerful, Wise, not questioned about what He does, and He, may His majesty be exalted, is greater than to be opposed and more majestic. Among the "other" negated from this are those polytheists; so it is not for them to do that, to prefer some of His creatures for intercession, choose them for worship, and make them partners to Him, Mighty and Majestic. Among the choice negated from them is what is included in their saying: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?", for in it is the selection of someone other than him (ﷺ) from al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra or ʿUrwa ibn Masʿūd al-Thaqafī, and distinguishing him by fitness to receive the Qur'an's revelation. If what has been said about the cause of revelation of this verse is sound, that the statement mentioned was its occasion, then the verse also contained a refutation of that against them; but because it includes their ignorance in their choosing partners and their selecting of them as gods and intercessors, just as it includes the aforementioned refutation, it has been placed here, connected to the mention of the partners and the rebuke of the polytheists for their polytheism.

It may be said: since it includes their ignorance concerning what has some connection with God Most High, such as taking partners for Him, Glorified is He, and what has some connection with the seal of His messengers (peace be upon him), such as their distinguishing someone other than him (peace be upon him) by fitness for being sent to him and the revelation of the Qur'an upon him, it is placed after the mention of the polytheists' question about their association and their question about their answer to the messengers who forbade them from it, the messengers whose very essence is the essence of their persons and the heart of their registers, the last of His messengers to them (ﷺ). So it is connected to both matters, but its connection to the first matter is more evident and complete, and its conclusion requires it in the most perfect and firm manner.

It may also be said: it has a connection to everything before it. As for its connection to the two matters mentioned, it is as you have heard. As for its connection to the mention of the state of the repentant, it is because his inclusion in the row of the successful requires God Most High's choosing him, His selecting him for it, and distinguishing him over all others. Therefore it has been placed after the three matters and the mention of the restriction of creation to Him, Exalted is He, and its precedence over the restriction of choosing and selecting, although the basis of the ignorance and the refutation is only the second, to indicate that the restriction of choice follows from the restriction of creation. In mentioning Him by the title of Lordship there is an indication that His creating what He wills is in accordance with benefit and wisdom. The attribution of the Lord to Him (ﷺ) is for honouring him (peace be upon him), and it is most beautiful if what was mentioned earlier about al-Walīd as a cause of revelation is sound. Other possibilities regarding the verse come to mind, so reflect; for I do not say that what I have presented is the preferred one, how could it be, when your Lord, may His majesty be exalted, creates whatever He wills and chooses.

﴿Glory be to God﴾: that is, He is exalted in His essence, a particular exaltation proper to Him, from anyone disputing with Him or competing with His choice, may His majesty be exalted. ﴿And exalted is He above what they associate﴾: that is, above their association, on the basis that *mā* is verbal-nominal (masdariyya). It is possible that it is a relative pronoun with an implied antecedent, that is, above the sharing of what they associate with Him, so it is said. Some made ﴿Glory be to God﴾ an expression of wonder at their associating with Him those who harm them with One who wishes for them every good, blessed and exalted is He. This is on the basis that *mā* in what preceded is a relative pronoun, the object of "chooses," and the meaning is: and He chooses what was good and righteous for them. It may also be an expression of wonder at their choosing their partners whom they prepared for intercession, and their undertaking what was not theirs. This is based on what has appeared to us and on the apparent sense of much speech, that the verse is not of the type of *iʿmāl* (the grammatical phenomenon of two verbs sharing a complement). It has been allowed that it is of that type, in that each of "Glory be to God" and "exalted" is seeking what they associate. The more appropriate view, it has been said, is that it is not of that type.

Your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they divulge. That is, what they harbor and hide within their breasts of false beliefs, and of their enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the like; "and what they disclose" means what they manifest of shameful deeds and reproach against him, peace be upon him, and other things. Perhaps this is for emphasis on the vileness of their inner state, since what is within is the source of the vices that appear outwardly; so He did not say "what they conceal" in the way it was said "what they disclose."

And Ibn Muhaysin read "tukannu" (تَكُنُّ) with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the kaf.

﴿He is Allah﴾, that is, He, exalted is He, is the One who alone possesses divinity and is exclusively characterized by it. His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿there is no deity except Him﴾ is an affirmation of this, like your saying: "The Kaaba is the qiblah; there is no qiblah except it."

﴿To Him belongs praise in the first and the last [life]﴾: that is, this belongs to Him, exalted is He, and not to anyone else, because He, majestic is His majesty, is the One who bestows all blessings directly, while everything else is only an intermediary. The praise intended here is that which occurs in return for blessings, as indicated by the context that He mentions after it in His saying, ﴿Say: Have you considered...﴾, etc.

Some scholars claimed that praise here is more general than gratitude (shukr), and they took the restriction (ḥaṣr) to apply to the totality of the praise of both abodes, asserting that praise in this world, even though others share it with Him, the Exalted, but praise in the Hereafter is only for Him, the Exalted. In response: praise in absolute terms is exclusively His, the Exalted, because all virtues and beautiful attributes are by His creation, so praise for them returns in the Hereafter to Him, the Exalted, since He, majestic and exalted, is their manifester and originator. Had one looked only at the outward meaning, the praise of the Hereafter would not be exclusively His, glory be to Him, either, for our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, will be praised by the first and the last at the Great Intercession (al-Shafa'a al-Kubra). Many have also explained His praise in the Hereafter by the words of the believers: ﴿All praise is for Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾ [Az-Zumar: 74], and their saying: ﴿All praise is for Allah, who has removed grief from us﴾ [Fatir: 34], and their saying: ﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Al-Fatiha: 2]. They said: the praising there is out of pleasure, not hardship. And in a ḥadīth narrated by Muslim and Abu Dawud from Jabir, describing the people of Paradise: "They are inspired to glorify (tasbīḥ) and declare the oneness of God (tahlīl) just as they are inspired to breathe."

﴿And to Him belongs the judgment (ḥukm)﴾: that is, the binding decree over everything, without anyone else sharing in it, exalted is He. And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, it is reported: that is, to Him belongs judgment among His servants, so He judges in favor of the people of His obedience with forgiveness and grace, and in favor of the people of His disobedience with misery and perdition. ﴿And to Him﴾, glory be to Him, and not to any other, ﴿you will be returned﴾ by resurrection.

﴿Say﴾, affirming what was mentioned: ﴿Have you considered?﴾, that is, inform me. Al-Kisa'i read "a-ra'aytum" with the hamza removed. ﴿If Allah makes the night perpetual over you﴾, that is, continuous. According to some, it is from sard, which means continuity and succession, and the letter mīm is added, the derivation indicating it; its pattern is fa'mal, and its parallel is dulāmiṣ from al-dilāṣ; one says: "a coat of mail (dir') dilāṣ," that is, smooth and soft.

Some grammarians chose that the mīm is original, so its pattern is fa'lal, because the addition of mīm in the middle is not a regular pattern. Its accusative case is either as a second object of ja'ala, or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of al-layl. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾, is either attached to sarmadan or to ja'ala. Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that it be attached to an omitted element that functions as an adjective of sarmadan, and that He made it so by holding the sun beneath the earth, for example.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿who is a deity﴾ (man ilāhun) is a subject and predicate. His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿other than Allah﴾ is an adjective of ilāhun. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿who brings you light (ḍiyā')﴾ is another adjective of it, and upon this the rebuke and the demand for an admission turn, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?﴾ [Saba': 24], and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Then who would bring you clear water?﴾ [Al-Mulk: 30], and their like. The purpose is to show the non-existence of the qualified by the non-existence of the quality. He did not use hal, which is for seeking affirmation (taṣdīq) that corresponds to the apparent situation, but used man, which is for seeking specification (ta'yīn), which implies the existence of the essence, in order to present the rebuke and the demand, according to their assumption, since it is more forceful, as is clear. The clause ﴿who is a deity﴾, etc., Abu Hayyan said: it is in the position of the second object of a-ra'aytum, and layl (night) is among what a-ra'aytum and ja'ala both compete for; he said: the second one has been given the governing role, so the first object of the first verb is omitted. Since that clause is placed in the position of its second object, it is necessary to supply a returning pronoun in it, that is: who is a deity other than Him that brings you light in its place, for example. The answer to in (if) is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, and the same applies to the verse that follows. From Ibn Kathir, it is reported that he read "biḍā'in" with two hamzas. ﴿Will you not then listen?﴾ listen with understanding and acceptance to the manifest proofs and the consistent texts, so that you may know that other than Allah, exalted is He, has no power over that.

[Page 108]

**Qur'an 28:72:** ﴿Say: "Have you considered: if Allah made the day perpetual for you until the Day of Resurrection,﴾ by placing the sun at the middle of the sky, for example, ﴿who is a god other than Allah who could bring you a night in which you may rest,﴾ resting from the fatigue of labour, ﴿will you not then see?﴾ The manifest signs that point to complete power, so that you may realise that other than Allah the Exalted has no power over that." It is known from what we have mentioned that each of the two clauses, ﴿will you not then hear?﴾ and ﴿will you not then see?﴾, is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) for the rebuke conveyed by His saying, ﴿Have you considered: if Allah made...﴾, etc., which precedes it.

Al-Zamakhshari (the author of al-Kashshaf) stated that the apparent antithesis requires mention of the day and its disposal, but the shift from that to light (diya'), which is the sunlight, serves to indicate that it contains many benefits, among them disposal. Had he mentioned the day, it would have called for restricting it to that benefit, by necessity of the antithesis. Also, the benefits belong to the light, not to the day, though the day is also one of its benefits. He then sensed that someone might ask: why was the darkness (zalam) not mentioned instead of night (layl) in the second verse, so that the antithesis would be complete in this respect? He answered that it does not have that status: it is neither intended in itself as light is, nor are benefits its consequence, along with what is in both of them of intimacy and aversion. Rather, if one considers it carefully, one would judge that night is also one of the benefits of light, and darkness is a necessity of the sun's being luminous under the earth and casting the shadow of night. He then stated that the concluding phrase mentioned in the verse serves as a guide to this subtle point: His saying, ﴿will you not then hear?﴾, indicates that the rebuke for not reflecting on light is greater, insofar as the faculty of hearing has a wider scope. What is meant is what the intellect perceives through hearing, so it is not objected that what hearing perceives is sounds alone, while the faculty of sight has a wider scope than that. This is because what is not perceived by any sense at all is perceived through hearing when a speaker expresses it with an intelligible expression. As for what is perceived by sight, it comes from seeing visible things, and these are few. As for reading books, its scope is narrower than hearing, and so it is in al-Kashf. Al-Allama al-Tibi affirmed the wording of al-Kashshaf with what has been affirmed, then said: "Further from artificiality is to take ﴿will you not then hear?﴾ as a concluding phrase for the rebuke derived from ﴿Have you considered...﴾ preceding it. Likewise ﴿will you not then see?﴾, according to what is in al-Ma'alim: ﴿will you not then hear?﴾ means hearing with understanding and acceptance; ﴿will you not then see?﴾ means what you are upon of error, so that deafness and blindness gather for them, from turning away from hearing the proofs and closing the eyes to seeing the signs."

Since the perpetuity of night is harder than the perpetuity of day, because sleep, which is the greatest purpose in it, resembles death, and seeking bounty from Allah the Exalted, which is part of the benefits of day, resembles life, it was said that the first is ﴿will you not then hear?﴾, meaning hearing with understanding, and the second is ﴿will you not then see?﴾, meaning what you are upon of error, so that each of the two concluding phrases matches the preceding discourse of emphasis and rebuke. He mentioned the general meaning as we mentioned earlier, then said: "In it, the indication of the text is prior and more primary than reason." Sahib al-Kashf stated the wording in the way you have heard, and mentioned that this does not contradict what is in al-Ma'alim but affirms it and clarifies the benefit of the two rebukes. Al-Tibi quoted from al-Raghib in Ghurrat al-Tanzil that he said: "The replacing of night by the greatest luminary is more eloquent in benefits and more guaranteed for interests than the replacing of day by night. Do you not see that the Paradise has a perpetual day with no night in it, because its people have no need of rest? So mentioning night first, because it is revealed from the day, which is more beneficial than the scattering of the staff, and the benefits of its sunlight are more than can be counted, is more deserving and more fitting." The meaning of His saying, ﴿will you not then hear?﴾, is: will you not hear as one who reflects on what is heard, so as to grasp from it the speaker's intent and encompass the greater part of what Allah the Exalted placed in the day of benefits? For after hearing comes the grasping of the intended meaning of what is heard, if there is contemplation and reflection on it. And the meaning of ﴿will you not then see?﴾ is: will you grasp from that what must be grasped? End of quotation.

In al-Kashf it is said that this supports what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned. It may be said: He, glorified be He, first mentioned the hypothetical making of night perpetual, and second the hypothetical making of day in the same way, because night, as they say, precedes day in law and custom. Also, that is more in harmony with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose﴾ [al-Qasas: 69]. So in the example, night is more concealing for the wrongdoer. Likewise with His saying, glorified be He: ﴿To Him belongs praise in the first and the last﴾. In a report, creation was in darkness, and Allah the Exalted spread over them some of His light. Perhaps, out of regard for the first and the last, the first verse was concluded with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿will you not then hear?﴾, on the basis that the meaning is: will you not hear from those who preceded you among your fathers, or from what has preceded us, that your gods are not able to do the like of that? And the second with His saying, glorified be He: ﴿will you not then see?﴾, on the basis that the meaning is: will you not see for yourselves their incapacity to do the like of that? Light was brought unqualified in the first verse, and night qualified in the second, for what al-Zamakhshari stated.

It has also been said regarding the reason the first verse is concluded with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿will you not then hear?﴾ rather than His saying, glorified be He: ﴿will you not then see?﴾, that if what is supposed were realised, hearing would remain with it without sight, since the darkness of night does not veil hearing but veils sight. And regarding the reason the second is concluded with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿will you not then see?﴾ rather than ﴿will you not then hear?﴾, that the realisation or non-realisation of what is supposed is equal in the matter of hearing but not of sight, since the light of day has a role in sight and has no role in hearing at all. This is, as you see, [weak]. (Know that there is a difficulty here: if the making of night perpetual until the Day of Resurrection were realised, it would be inconceivable that light would come at all; and likewise if the making of day perpetual until the Day of Resurrection were realised, it would be inconceivable that night would come in that way. As for [the possibility] from other than Him, the Exalted, it is obvious, because that is the source of incapacity for everything. As for from Him, glorified and majestic be He, it is because it entails the gathering of night and day, for if they did not gather, night would not be realised as continuing until the Day of Resurrection; and likewise making day so, which contradicts the supposition, while the gathering of the two is impossible, and the impossible has no fitness to be the object of power, so it is not intended.)

It is answered that the meaning, if He, glorified be He, intends that, is: who is a god other than Him, the Exalted, who would bring you the opposite of His intention, by cutting off continuity, so that He brings a day after a night and a night after a day. It is objected that it is understood from the verse, in that case, that He, the Majestic, the Exalted, is the One who, if He intends that, brings them the opposite of His intention, the Exalted, so He cuts off continuity. This is also problematic, because His bringing the opposite of the intention of the Majestic, the Exalted, entails the non-fulfilment of the intended by the will, and that is impossible. So when Allah the Exalted wills something in a manner of will that has no conditionality in it, it is not possible for Him to will it in a manner contrary to that. It is answered that it is permissible that the meaning, if Allah the Exalted intends that without making it conditional on His will, the Majestic in His majesty, its opposite should not be brought by other than the Majestic, the Mighty. He did not state the condition, because clear reason indicates that unconditioned will cannot be followed by bringing about the opposite of its requirement at all. Some people held that He, glorified be He, does not finalise His will, so all that He, glorified be His majesty, wills is conditional. It was said: the better view is to say that the meaning is nothing other than that their gods are not able to bring a day after a night and a night after a day when Allah the Exalted in His majesty wills the continuity of one of them, and that the one capable of bringing that is Allah, glorified be He, alone, without regard to whether that bringing is restricted by that will. So reflect.

**[Ruh al-Ma'ani, al-Alusi, on Surah 28, verse 73]**

﴿And of His mercy﴾, i.e., because of His mercy, may His majesty be exalted, ﴿He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein﴾, i.e., during the night, ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾, i.e., during the day, by striving to earn through various kinds of gain. So in the verse there is what is called *al-laff wa-l-nashr* (the figure of "wrapping and spreading," in which several items are mentioned together and then each is matched with its counterpart), which is also called *al-tafsir* (the figure of "explanation"), as in the saying of Ibn Hayyush:

*A cupbearer in a qurtaq (a kind of robe) who makes the boon companion forget, by his face, his full cup and his ewer:*

*The effect of the wine, its color and its taste, are in his two eyes, his two cheeks and his saliva.*

The pronoun in *fadlihi* (His bounty) refers to Allah, may He be exalted. Abu Hayyan permitted that it refers to the day, by way of metaphorical attribution (*al-isnad al-majazi*), but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. In the verse there is also an indication of the praiseworthiness of striving in seeking sustenance.

It has been related: "The earner is the beloved of Allah."

This does not contradict reliance upon God (*tawakkul*), and that what comes to the servant through his means is a bounty from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and is not something that He is obligated to give, glorified is He. ﴿And that perhaps you may be grateful﴾, i.e., and so that you may be thankful for His blessing, exalted is He, He did what He did; or so that you may recognize His blessing, exalted is He, and thank Him for it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 74:

﴿And on the Day He calls to them﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "remember" (u_dhkur).

﴿Then He will say: "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ is a rebuke following upon a rebuke, to signal that nothing provokes the anger of God Most High more than associating partners with Him, just as nothing brings His good pleasure more than affirming His Oneness, Mighty and Majestic is He. Or the first [rebuke] is to demonstrate the corruption of their opinion, as indicated by His saying there: ﴿The Word has been justified against them﴾ [al-Qasas: 63]. And this [second rebuke] is to demonstrate that their association of partners was not based on any authority, but was pure caprice, as indicated by His saying afterwards: ﴿Bring your proof﴾. Or the first [rebuke] is the summoning of the partners, by their unfitness for what He, glorified is He, says after it: ﴿Call your partners," so they call them, but they do not respond﴾. This is a declaration of loss, that they were not in anything in their taking [of partners]. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what they used to fabricate will have vanished from them﴾?

﴿Wa-nazaʿnā﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿yunādīhim﴾. The past-tense form is used to indicate certainty, or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to its subject, with or without the particle qad. The shift to the first-person plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama) serves to show the full concern with the matter of extraction and to magnify it. The meaning is: We brought out swiftly ﴿from every community﴾ of the nations ﴿a witness﴾, one who testifies against them concerning what they used to be upon. He is the prophet of that community, as narrated from Mujāhid and Qatāda. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every community a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 41]. This refers to one of the standing-places of the Day of Resurrection, so it does no harm that the witness in another standing-place is other than the prophets, peace be upon them. They are the community of Muḥammad (ﷺ), or they are the angels, peace be upon them, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the prophets and the martyrs will be brought﴾ [al-Zumar: 69], for this apparently indicates that the martyrs are distinct from the prophets, peace be upon them.

It has been said: it is possible for the standing-place to be one and the same, and the indication of distinctness is not conceded. Even if it were conceded, the testimony of the prophets, peace be upon them, does not contradict the testimony of others along with them. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from every community﴾, and the singular form of "witness" (shahīd), are apparent in what preceded. From here, al-Baḥr (Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ) said: it was said, meaning: just ones (ʿudūlan) and chosen ones (khiyāran). The word "witness" (shahīd) here is a noun of genus (ism jins).

﴿Then We said﴾ to each of those communities: ﴿Bring your proof﴾ for the soundness of what you used to adhere to. ﴿Then they will know﴾ on that day ﴿that the truth belongs to Allah﴾ in divinity, and no one shares with Him, glorified is He, in it.

﴿And what they used to fabricate will be lost to them﴾, meaning it will be absent from them with the absence of a lost thing. The verb ḍalla is here used metaphorically for the meaning of "ghāba" (was absent), by way of a subsidiary metaphor (istiʿāra tabaʿiyya). ﴿What they used to fabricate﴾ in the world of falsehood.

**[Page 110]**

﴿Indeed, Qarun﴾: it is a non-Arabic name, not declined (*munima'a al-sarf*) because of its status as a proper noun (*'alamiyya*) and its foreignness (*'ujma*).

﴿was of the people of Musa﴾: that is, of the Children of Israel, as is the apparent meaning. Ibn 'Atiyya reported scholarly consensus (*ijma'*) on this. Scholars differed about the nature of his kinship to Musa, peace be upon him.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and from Ibn Jurayj, Qatada, and Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i) that he was a paternal cousin of Musa, peace be upon him. So Musa is the son of 'Imran, son of Qahath (with a qaf, an open ha, and a triangular tha), son of Lawi (with a short vowel), son of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. And he is the son of Yasahar (with an open yaa underdotted, an unpointed sad, a closed ha, and a dammed ha), son of Qahath, and so on.

In *Majma' al-Bayan*, it is reported from 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas that he was the maternal cousin of Musa, peace be upon him. This was also narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him.

It is related from Muhammad ibn Ishaq that he was the paternal uncle of Musa, peace be upon him. This is evident according to the view of those who say that Musa, peace be upon him, is the son of 'Imran ibn Yasahar ibn Qahath, and that Qarun is the son of Yasahar ibn Qahath. He was called *al-Munawwar* (the Illuminated) for the beauty of his appearance. He was the most learned of the Children of Israel in the Torah and the best of them in recitation. But he became a hypocrite, just as al-Samiri did, and he said: "If prophethood belongs to Musa and the altar and the sacrifice belong to Harun, then what is left for me?" It is reported that when Musa, peace be upon him, led them across the sea, prophethood and the high priesthood went to Harun, who offered the sacrifice and became the head over them. The sacrifice had been Musa's duty, but he assigned it to his brother Harun. Qarun felt envy in his soul and envied both of them. So he said to Musa: "The matter is yours and your brother's, and I am of no account. How long shall I endure?" Musa, peace be upon him, said: "This is the doing of Allah, Exalted." He said: "By Allah, I will not believe you until you bring a sign." So Musa commanded the leaders of the Children of Israel that each one should bring his staff. He bundled them together and placed them in the tent in which revelation used to descend upon him. They used to guard their staffs at night. In the morning, behold, the staff of Harun was moving, and it had green leaves, and it was of almond wood. Qarun said: "This is no more marvelous than what you do of magic." ﴿So he rebelled against them﴾: that is, he sought superiority over them and that they should be under his command, or he behaved arrogantly towards them. Among his arrogance it is counted that he lengthened his garment by a span, or that he oppressed them and sought what was not his right. It was said that this occurred when Pharaoh made him ruler over the Children of Israel.

It was also said: he envied them and sought the removal of their blessings. This is what is mentioned of him concerning Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both. The *fa* (in ﴿fa-baghā﴾) is an eloquent *fa* (*fa-sīḥa*), meaning: he went astray, so he rebelled. It is also permitted that it be on its literal sense, since kinship often leads to rebellion. ﴿And We gave him of the treasures﴾: that is, of stored wealth. It is then a metaphor, by treating what is stored as what is buried, if "treasure" is specific to him. It is related in *al-Bahr* that his wealth was called treasures because its zakat had not been paid from it, though Musa, peace be upon him, had commanded him to pay it, and he refused. This was among the causes of his enmity towards him. It was also said: the treasures here are buried wealth, and it was, as narrated from 'Ata', that Allah had granted him a great treasure from the treasures of Yusuf, peace be upon him. ﴿What, its keys﴾: that is, the keys of its chests. This is either by a suppressed noun, or by a connection of the slightest relation. It is the plural of *miftah* (with a kasra), which is that by which something is opened.

al-Suddi said: that is, its treasuries. Similar to this is the statement of al-Dahhak: that is, its containers and vessels. Something similar is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. The singular of it by analogy would be *maftah* (with a fatha), since it is a noun of place. What supports what preceded is the reading of al-A'mash, *mafatihahu* with a yaa, as the plural of *miftah*. *Ma* is a relative pronoun and is the second object of *ataynā*. *Mafatihahu* is the subject of *inna*, and the statement of Allah, Exalted: ﴿lata'una bil-'usbati ulī al-quwwah﴾ (its predicate) is its predicate, and the clause is the relative clause of *ma*, and the returning pronoun is the genitive pronoun. The Kufans prohibited the permissibility of a clause introduced by *inna* being a relative clause for a relative pronoun. al-Nahhas said: I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman, meaning al-Akhfash al-Saghir, say: "How ugly is what the Kufans say about relative clauses, that it is not permissible for the clause of *alladhī* to be *inna* and what it governs." And in the Qur'an, ﴿what its keys﴾, he concluded. There is no hiding that if the prevention of this is the absence of hearing (attestation), then the refutation of them is not complete except with evidence that admits of no other meaning. The *ma* in the verse may be an indefinite qualifying noun. If the prevention is that *inna* occurs at the beginning of speech, then the clause introduced by it is not connected to what precedes it. Then the refutation of them with the mentioned verse is complete, because the prevention mentioned, just as it prevents the clause being a relative clause, prevents it being a qualifier. So reflect.

﴿tanū﴾ is from *nā'a bihi al-ḥiml*, when the load weighed him down until it inclined him. So the *bā'* is for transitivity, as in *dhahabat bihi* (she took him away). ﴿al-'uṣba﴾ is a large group, without specification of a particular number, according to what al-Raghib mentioned. Some lexicographers specified a quantity for it and differed about it. It was said: from ten to fifteen, and this is reported here from Mujahid. It was said: what is between fifteen and forty, and this is reported from al-Kalbi. It was said: what is between three and ten. It was said: from ten to forty, and this is reported from Qatada. It was said: forty, and this is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: seventy, and this is reported from Abu Salih, client of Umm Hani. al-Khafaji said: It may be said that the original meaning of it is an unrestricted group, as the derivation indicates. Then custom restricted it to a number, and this number was disputed, or it differed according to its uses.

Abu Zayd said: *tanū* means one who is lifted with a load when you stand up with it. The poet said:

*tanū bi-ukhrāhā falā'iyan qiyāmuhā
wa tamshī al-hūaynā 'an qarībin fa-tubhiru*

In this verse, according to this, there is an inversion (*qalb*) in the view of Abu 'Ubayda and those who followed him. The original is: *tanū al-'uṣbatu bihā*, meaning the group rises with them. It was said that there may be no inversion here, because the keys rise together with the group when the group rises with them. The preferred view is what we mentioned first, and it is transmitted from al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and al-Farra'. al-Nahhas preferred it. Its meaning is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Salih, and al-Suddi.

Badil ibn Maysara read *li-yanū'a* with a yaa. Abu Hayyan explained this by supposing a masculine suppressed noun to which the pronoun returns, meaning: "what, if it carried its keys, or their quantity, or something like that." Ibn Jinni said: he gave the masculine form to that amount and extent, so he took into account the sense of the singular and treated it accordingly, like the saying of the rajiz:

*mithla al-firākh natafat ḥawāṣiluhu*

meaning: its entrails, that is, the entrails of that, or the entrails of what we mentioned. al-Zamakhshari said: its explanation is that the keys are interpreted as treasuries, and they are given the ruling of what they are attributed to, because of connection and association, like your saying: "the people of Yamama went." And he interpreted the keys as treasuries rather than what is opened with them, so that the connection is complete, for the connection of treasuries with what is stored is stronger than the connection of keys with it; indeed the second has no connection at all. In that case the masculine gender is taken from the genitive noun, just as the feminine was taken from the opposite, as in the example he mentioned. What was previously reported from others is preferable.

In *al-Kashshaf* it is said: because interpreting the keys as treasuries is extremely weak, since the hyperbole is lost. It was said: the keys in that sense are not well known, and I have heard that it is a transmitted interpretation. If that is established, then nothing said in this and in *al-Kashshaf* is to be considered.

Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned that Badil ibn Maysara read *mā inna miftāḥahu* in the singular, so his reading *li-yanū'a* with a yaa needs no interpretation. It has been exaggerated regarding the multitude of his keys. It is reported from Khaythama that they were a load of sixty mules, white-blazed and white-footed, and no single key exceeded a finger, and for each key there was a treasure. In another narration from him: the keys of Qarun's treasures were of leather, each key for a separate storeroom. When he rode, the keys were carried on seventy white-blazed and white-footed mules.

In *al-Bahr* it is said: they mentioned about the multitude of his keys things that are a lie or close to a lie, so I have not written them down. Among what has no exaggeration is what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that the keys are the treasuries, and his treasuries were carried by forty strong men, and they were four hundred thousand, each man carrying ten thousand. And upon this, the likes of Qarun among people are more than his treasuries. Perhaps the verse points to what he was given beyond that. I do not think the matter is as reported from Khaythama.

Abu Muslim went too far in interpreting the verse. He said: the keys mean knowledge and comprehensiveness, as in the statement of Allah, Exalted: ﴿and with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ (Al-An'am: 59). The meaning is: "And We gave him of the treasures that their safekeeping and knowledge of them would be heavy for the group," that is, these treasures, because of their abundance and variety of kinds, would exhaust their guardians who are charged with their protection.

﴿when his people said to him﴾.

al-Zamakhshari said: it is connected to ﴿tanū﴾, and it is weak, because the weight of the keys upon the group is not restricted to the time of his people's saying. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is connected to *baghā*, and it was weakened in a similar way. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is connected to *ataynā*. It is also permissible that it be an adverbial of time for a suppressed verb indicated by the context, meaning: "he rebelled against them when he said." Each of these has what has already been mentioned. al-Hawfi said: it is in the accusative governed by *udhkur* (remember), suppressed. He permitted that it be connected to what follows it of His statement, Exalted: ﴿He said: "I was only given it"﴾, and the clause is an explanation of his rebellion. He preferred that it be connected to a suppressed verb, and the estimate is: "He displayed boasting and exultation in what he was given," ﴿when his people said to him: "Do not exult"﴾, that is, do not be insolent. Exultation in this world for its own sake is blameworthy, because it is the result of love for it, contentment with it, and heedlessness of its passing away. For the knowledge that the pleasure in it is bound to depart inevitably brings sorrow, as Abu al-Tayyib said:

*ashaddu al-ghammi 'indī fī surūrin
tayaqqana 'anhu ṣāḥibuhu intiqālā*

The worst grief to me is in a joy
whose possessor is certain he will be parted from it.

And Ibn Shams al-Khilafa said:

*wa idhā nazarta fa-inna bu'san zā'ilan
lil-mar'i khayrun min na'īmin zā'ilin*

When you consider, a passing hardship
is better for a man than a passing bliss.

And for this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And do not exult in what He has given you﴾ (Al-Hadid: 23). The Arabs praise abstaining from exultation at the arrival of good. The poet said:

*wa lastu bi-mifrāḥin idhā al-dahru sarranī
wa lā jāzi'in min ṣarfihi al-mutaqallibi*

I am not one who exults when fortune pleases me,
nor one who wails at its changing turns.

And another said:

*in tulāqi manfasan lā talqanā
faraḥa al-khayri wa lā nakbū li-ḍurr*

If you meet a respite, we will not meet
the exultation of good, nor will we stumble from harm.

And Allah, Glorified, gave the reason for the prohibition here as the fact that exultation is a barrier to His love, Mighty and Majestic, so He said, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the exultant﴾. This is evidence that exultation in this world is legally blameworthy. We said that exultation in it for its own sake is blameworthy, because exultation in it as a means to some matter of the Hereafter is not blameworthy. The love of Allah, Exalted, according to many, is an attribute of action, meaning that He, Exalted, does not honor the exultant with the adornments of this world, nor does He bestow blessings upon them, Mighty and Majestic, nor does He draw them near, Mighty and Majestic. The meaning is that He, Exalted, hates them, humiliates them, and removes them from His presence, Glorified be He.

Some of them said: in the negation of His love, Exalted, towards them, there is an alert that the absence of His love, Exalted, is sufficient as a deterrent from what He has forbidden. So what of hatred and punishment? This is good.

Isa ibn Sulayman al-Hijazi related that it was read *al-fārihīn* (the boastful ones).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 77:

﴿But seek, through what Allah has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter﴾ from the treasures and wealth, ﴿the Abode of the Hereafter﴾, that is, its reward, meaning Allah's reward therein, by directing that [wealth] toward what will be a means to it. The "fi" (in) is either of place, meaning "seek while moving about in it and disposing of it," or of cause, meaning "seek by means of disposing of what Allah has given you in that [manner]." It has also been read as "ittabi'" (follow).

﴿And do not forget﴾, that is, do not abandon [it] in the manner of one who has forgotten, ﴿your share of this world﴾, that is, your portion of it. According to what al-Firyabi and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, it means that you should work in it for your Hereafter, and this was also related from Mujahid.

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Qatadah that it means you should take from this world what Allah has made lawful for you. Abdullah ibn Ahmad transmitted in Zawa'id al-Zuhd from Mansur, who said: "It is not a commodity from the commodities of this world; rather, your share is your lifespan, in which you should advance for your Hereafter." Ibn al-Mundhir and a group transmitted from al-Hasan that he said regarding the verse: "Send forward the surplus and keep back what suffices you." Malik said: it is eating and drinking without extravagance. It has also been said:

They meant by his share of this world the shroud, as the poet said:

"Your share of all that you gather throughout time
is two garments in which you are wrapped, and some camphor."

[Page 113]

In their prohibiting him from forgetting this there is a great exhortation to him to provide for the Hereafter from his wealth, for whoever's share of his worldly life and of all that he possesses is the shroud, it is not fitting for him to abandon providing (for the Hereafter) from his wealth and to send forward what will benefit him in his Hereafter.

﴿And do good﴾ to the servants of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿as Allah has done good to you﴾, that is, the like of Allah's goodness to you in what He has bestowed upon you. The comparison is either in general goodness, or on account of Allah's goodness to you, so that the kaf (as) is causal. It has also been said: the meaning is "and do good by thankfulness in obedience, as Allah, Exalted is He, has done good to you by bestowing favours," and the kaf there also admits of both comparison and causation.

﴿And do not seek corruption in the land﴾, a prohibition against persisting in what he was upon of injustice and transgression.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the corrupters﴾. The discussion of this is like the discussion of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love those who exult﴾. This exhortation in its entirety came from the believers of his people, as is apparent from the verse. It has also been said that it came from Musa, peace be upon him.

[Page 113]

﴿He said﴾, replying to the one who advised him, ﴿"I have been given it only on knowledge that is with me"﴾. It seems he intends to answer their saying, "As God has been good to you," because he informs them that God bestowed upon him those wealths and treasures without any cause or entitlement on his part. The sum of it is a claim to deserve what he was given, because of the knowledge he possesses.

His saying ﴿on knowledge﴾: according to most grammarians (ʿAmmah al-muʿrabīn, those who give i'rab, grammatical analysis), it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject (marfūʿ) of "I have been given it" (ūtītuhu). The governing verb is qualified by it, to indicate the cause of the giving and the reason he deserves it. That is, "I have been given it while possessing knowledge." It is also permitted that ʿalā be causal (taʿlīliyyah), and that the prepositional phrase be connected to "I have been given" as a loose adverbial phrase (ẓarf laghw), as if it were said, "I have been given it on account of knowledge." And ʿindī ("that is with me") is in the position of a qualifier of ʿilm ("knowledge"), and what is meant is "knowledge specific to me, apart from you." It is also permitted that it be connected to "I have been given," and its meaning would be "in my estimation and opinion," as in your saying, "The ruling on such-and-such is permissible according to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him." In al-Kashshaf (Al-Kashshāf, the commentary of al-Zamakhsharī) there is something that clearly indicates that when ʿindī carries the meaning "in my estimation and opinion," it is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "it is, in my estimation and opinion, thus," and the sentence in this case is a new, independent clause (mustaʾnafah) confirming that what he mentioned is a settled opinion that he holds. Al-Kashf (the commentary of al-Ṭībī) says: "This is the correct way."

As for what is meant by this knowledge: it has been said it is the knowledge of the Torah, for he was the most knowledgeable of the Children of Israel in it. Abu Sulayman al-Darani said it is the knowledge of trade and the ways of earning. Ibn al-Musayyib said it is the knowledge of alchemy (al-kīmiyāʾ, the art of transmuting base metals into gold). Moses, peace be upon him, knew that, and he gave Yusha ibn Nun one third of it, Kaleb ibn Yufuna one third of it, and Qarun one third of it. Qarun deceived the two of them until he added their knowledge to his own, and he used to take lead and copper and turn them into gold. It has also been said that God Most High taught Moses, peace be upon him, the knowledge of alchemy, and Moses taught it to his sister, and his sister taught it to Qarun. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is restricted to the knowledge of the craft of gold-making. It has also been said it is the knowledge of extracting treasures and hidden hoards. And it is narrated from Ibn Zayd that what is meant by the knowledge is the knowledge of God Most High, and the meaning is, "I have been given it on knowledge from God Most High and a specialization from Him, may He be glorified, that He intended for me." And ʿindī in it has the meaning "in my estimation and opinion."

It has also been said that "knowledge" here means "the known," like the phrase of God Most High: ﴿and they do not encompass anything of His knowledge﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. To this refers what is narrated from Muqatil, that he said: "That is, on a good thing (khayr) which God Most High taught me," with ʿindī [meaning "with me"]. Interpreting it as the knowledge of alchemy is widespread among its practitioners. In Majmaʿ al-Bayan (the commentary of al-Ṭabrisī) it is also reported from al-Kalbī. Al-Zajjaj denied it and said: "It is not sound, because the knowledge of alchemy is false and has no reality." Al-Ṭībī criticized this, saying: "Perhaps it was among the things that are beyond human capacity (al-muʿjiz), like a miracle." This was objected to, on the grounds that it is not correct, for otherwise Qarun could not have acquired it.

The denial of alchemy: the word is Greek, meaning "trickery," or it is Hebrew, its origin being kīm yah, meaning "that it is from God Most High." Or it is Persian, its origin being kī mīyā, meaning "when will it come?", said in the manner of astonishment. It came to dominate the acquisition of the two precious metals (gold and silver) by a particular method. This denial is not confined to al-Zajjaj alone; rather, a group of eminent scholars denied it and said that it is impossible to achieve. Others took the opposite view.

[Page 114]

If you want a summary of the discussion on this matter, then listen to what is recited to you. Some researchers (al-muḥaqqiqīn) have mentioned that the basis of discussion in this craft, according to the philosophers (al-ḥukamāʾ), rests on the state of the seven metals that take a hammer (al-maʿādin al-sabʿah al-munṭariqah), namely gold, silver, lead, tin (qazdīr), copper, iron, and zinc (kharṣīnī). The question is: are they different in their differentiae (fuṣūl, the specific differences that determine a species), so that each of them is a species different from the other? Or are they different only in their properties and qualities, so that all of them are varieties of one single species?

The view adopted by the Teacher (al-Muʿallim), Abu Nasr al-Fārābī, and followed in it by the philosophers of al-Andalus, is that they are one species, and that their difference lies in qualities, such as moisture, dryness, softness, hardness, and colors like yellowness, whiteness, and blackness. All of these are varieties of that one species. On this basis, the possibility of one of them being transformed into another, by changing its accidents through natural processes or through craft, was built.

Abu Bakr ibn al-Ṣāʾigh, known as Ibn Bājja, reported in one of his works from the aforementioned Teacher that he said: "Aristotle has made clear in his books on minerals that the craft of alchemy falls within the realm of possibility, but it is of a kind of possibility that is difficult to actualize, unless there come together circumstances by which its actualization becomes easy. This is because he first examined it by way of dialectic, and he proved it by one syllogism and refuted it by another, following his usual method regarding matters over which disputes abound. Then he finally proved it by a syllogism he composed from two premises placed at the beginning of the book. The first premise: the metals are one in species, and the difference among them is not in their quiddities (māhiyyāt, essences) but in their accidents; some of it is in their essential accidents and some of it is in their accidental accidents. The second premise: any two things under one species that differ by an accident, it is possible for each of them to pass into the other. If the accident is essential, the transition is difficult; if it is separable, the transition is easy. The difficulty in this craft is only because most of these substances differ in their essential accidents. It seems that the difference between gold and silver is very small indeed." End of quotation.

As for what the Shaykh Abu ʿAli ibn Sina (Avicenna) held, and what the philosophers of the East followed him in, is that they differ in their differentiae, and that they are distinct species. On this basis he built the denial of this craft and the impossibility of its existence, because a differentia cannot be reached by craft; rather, it is created by the Creator of things and its Determiner, who is God, Mighty and Majestic. This is what Ibn Khaldun reported from him.

The Imam (Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī) said in al-Mabāḥith al-Mashriqiyyah (his work on Eastern philosophy), in the eighth section of the fourth part of it: "The Shaykh (Ibn Sina) conceded the possibility that copper be dyed with the dye of silver, and silver with the dye of gold, and that most of the deficiency in lead be removed. Then either the differentiating differentia is stripped away or it is clothed. He said: 'It has not yet become clear to me that it is possible, since these sensible matters are likely not to be the differentiae by which these bodies become species; rather they are accidents and concomitants, and their differentiae are unknown. And when a thing is unknown, how can one intend to bring it into existence or to annihilate it?'" End of quotation.

Al-Ṭughrāʾī (Al-Ṭughrāʾī, the famous alchemist), who was one of the great figures of this craft and had several books on it, criticized him and refuted him, saying: "Management and treatment do not consist in creating and originating the differentia; rather they consist in preparing the matter to receive a particular property, and the differentia comes after the preparation from the One who created and originated it, may His majesty be exalted and His power be great, just as He, glory be to Him, pours light upon bodies through polishing. We have no need, in that, to conceive it or to know it. And since we have indeed come upon the creation of some animals, such as the scorpion from earth and straw, and the snake from hair, and other things, what prevents us from coming upon the like of that in minerals? All of this is by craft, and the subject of craft is only matter. So management and treatment prepare the matter to receive those differentiae, and nothing more. We therefore attempt the like of that with gold and silver: we take a matter, and we subject it to management after it has a first readiness to receive the form of gold and silver, then we treat it by treatment until readiness for receiving their differentiae is complete in it." End of quotation, in meaning. This refutation, as far as appears, is sound.

[Page 115]

The Imam, after mentioning what you have heard of the Shaykh's statement, said: "It is not strong, because we observe from theriac (al-tiryāq, a compound antidote) effects and specific actions. Either we do not affirm for it a theriac form, but say that the theriac actions arise from that temperament and not from another form. Or it is also permissible to say: the yellowness and heaviness of gold arise from the temperament it contains, and not from an established form. Then gold has no specific differentia except mere yellowness and heaviness; but these two are known, so it is possible to intend to remove them and to acquire them, and so what the Shaykh said is refuted. And if we affirm for it an established form, then we say: there is no doubt that we do not conceive of that form except as a reality that necessitates the specific actions issuing from theriac. Either this degree of knowledge suffices for the intention of bringing into existence and annihilating, or it does not suffice. If it does not suffice, then it must be that we cannot make theriac. If it suffices, then it is also present in our question, because we know from the golden form that it is a quiddity that necessitates melting, yellowness, and heaviness."

It is also answered: although we do not know the established form in detail, we know the accidents that suit it and those that do not suit it. We know that an unsuitable accident, when it becomes intense in the matter, nullifies the form, like the watery form. We know that heat does not suit it, even though we do not know its quiddity in detail. Therefore it is possible for us to nullify the watery form and to acquire it. As for nullifying it, that is by heating water; as for acquiring it, that is by cooling air. So likewise in our question."

Some of the philosophers argued for its impossibility with several considerations. The first: nature only forms these bodies from elements unknown to us, and those elements have determined quantities unknown to us as well, and their qualities have known degrees which are unknown to us, and the completion of the action and reaction has a determined time unknown to us. With ignorance of all of that, how can we make these bodies?

The second: the dyeing substance either is more resistant to fire than the dyed thing, or the dyed thing is more resistant, or they are equal. If the dyer is more resistant, then the dyed thing must perish while the dyer remains after its perishing. If the dyed thing is more resistant, then it must remain after the perishing of the dyer. If they are equal in resistance to fire, then they are of one species, since they are equal in resistance to fire, and so neither of them has more claim to being the dyer and the other the dyed than the reverse.

The third: if it were by craft, for example, it would not be by nature; but the consequent is false. As for the first: we have found no like of it. As for the second: because if it were possible for what arises by nature to be found by craft, it would also be possible for what arises by craft to arise by nature, until a sword or a bed would be found by nature. And since the impossibility of the consequent is established, the impossibility of the antecedent is established.

The fourth: these bodies have natural places, which are their mines, and these are for them like wombs are for animals. So whoever permits their generation outside those mines is like one who permits the generation of animals outside the wombs.

The Imam answered the first by saying that it is refuted by the craft of medicine. He answered the second by saying that the equality of the dyer and the dyed in resistance to fire does not entail their equality in quiddity, because two different things may share some attributes. He answered the third by saying that something may be found by craft just as it is found by nature, like the fire produced by striking, and sal ammoniac (al-nūshādir) may be made from barley, and likewise many vitriols. Then, even on the assumption that we do not find an example of it, it does not follow that we must categorically deny it, nor does the possibility of a natural thing being produced by craft entail the possibility of the converse; rather, the matter in that depends on proof. He answered the fourth by saying that whoever wishes to turn copper into silver is not like one who originates a thing, but like one who treats a sick person, for

[Page 116]

[Page 117]

...the copper from the essence of silver, except that it has defects and diseases. And just as treatment is possible, though not at the place of formation, so too in this case. The gist of the argument is that what forms in the mountains cannot be produced by craft, and this is where the dispute lies. Ibn Khaldun, after citing the words of Ibn Sina and the refutation by al-Tughra'i against him, said: "We have another line of refutation against the people of this art, from which the impossibility of its existence and the falsity of all their claims become clear. That is because the sum of their treatment is that, after identifying the matter that is receptive by its first readiness, they make it a substrate. They imitate, in its management and treatment, the management of Nature for the body in the mine, until they transform it into gold or silver. They double the active and passive powers so that the process is completed in a shorter time, because it has been shown in its proper place that doubling the strength of the agent reduces the time of its action. It has also been shown that gold is completed in its mine only after eighty thousand years, the Great Solar Cycle. So when the powers and qualities are doubled in the treatment, the time of its formation becomes shorter than that, necessarily, according to what we have said. Or they aim, by their treatment, to bring about a temperamental form in that matter, which makes it like leaven for bread: it turns the dough into its own nature and acts upon it with the swelling and lightness it has acquired, so that its digestion in the stomach is good and it quickly turns into nourishment. Then that form performs the desired effects, and that is the elixir. Know that every thing generated from elemental generated substances must contain a mixture of the four elements in unequal proportions, for if they were equal in proportion, their mixing would not occur. Therefore there must be a predominant part over the whole. Every mixed generated thing must also have an innate heat, which is the active agent, because it preserves its form. Then every thing that forms over a period of time must necessarily undergo varying stages and transitions from stage to stage during the time of its formation until it reaches its end. Consider the case of man in his development: a drop of semen, then a clinging clot, then... and so on to his end. The proportions of the parts in each stage differ in their quantities and qualities; otherwise the first stage would itself be the last. Likewise, the innate heat determined for each stage differs from that of the other stage. So consider gold: the stages it passes through in its mine for eighty thousand years, and the conditions it undergoes. The alchemist would need to keep pace with the action of Nature in the mine, and to match it through his management and treatment until it is completed. And it is a condition of craft in general to conceive of what is aimed at by it. Among the proverbs current among the sages on this is: 'The first of the work is the last of the thought, and the last of the thought is the first of the work.' So it is necessary to conceive of these states of gold in its various conditions, and its differing proportions in each stage, and the quantity of the multiplied powers that stands in for it and takes its place, until by that one matches the action of Nature in the mine, or prepares for some matters a temperamental form that is like the form of leaven for bread, and acts upon this matter in accordance with its powers and quantities."

All of this is comprehended only by the all-encompassing Knowledge, which is the Knowledge of Him, Mighty and Majestic. Human sciences fall short of that. The situation of one who claims to attain gold by this art is like that of one who claims the craft of creating a human being from semen. Even if we grant him comprehensive knowledge of its parts, its proportions, its stages, and the manner of its creation in the womb, and grant that this is known as detailed knowledge such that nothing escapes his knowledge, we would still grant him the creation of this human being, but how could he do so? The conclusion is that the artificial act, as their discourse implies, is preceded by conceptions of the states of the mineral nature which are aimed to be made equal and matched, and by the action of the matter with its powers in detail. Those states have no end, and human knowledge is incapable of what falls short of them. Therefore, aiming to turn copper into gold is like aiming to create a human, an animal, or a plant. This is the most solid of the proofs I know that indicate impossibility. The impossibility does not lie in the differentiae, nor in the nature of things, but in the impossibility of comprehension and the inadequacy of humans to attain it. What Ibn Sina mentioned is entirely beside this point.

There is also another aspect of impossibility from the standpoint of its purpose, namely that God's wisdom in the two stones and their rarity is that they are the mainstays of people's gains and their wealth. If they were obtained by craft, God's wisdom in this would be nullified, since they would become so abundant that no one would benefit from possessing them. And there is another: Nature does not abandon the nearest ways in its actions and adopt the farthest. So if this artificial method, which they claim is sound and which is nearer than the method of Nature in its mine and shorter in time, were sound, Nature would not have abandoned it for its own way which it took in the formation and refinement of gold and silver. As for al-Tughra'i's comparison of this management with what has been found of similar single items in nature, such as the scorpion and the snake and their creation, that is a correct matter in this regard, as the finding indicates, as he claims. But as for alchemy, it has not been reported from any of the people of knowledge that they arrived at it or at its way. Its practitioners have continued to grope in it like a blind camel, and they achieve nothing but false stories. And if it had been correctly attained by any of them, his son or his student or his companions would have preserved it from him, it would have been transmitted among friends, and its correctness would have been guaranteed after him, until it spread and reached us or others.

As for their saying that the elixir is like leaven, and that it is a compound that transforms what is in it and turns it into its own nature, that is nothing, because leaven only turns the dough and prepares it for digestion, and that is corruption, and corruption in materials is easy, occurring by the simplest of actions and natures. What is required of the elixir is to turn the mineral into something nobler and higher than it, and that is generation, and generation is harder than corruption. Therefore the elixir cannot be compared to leaven. Then he said: "The truth of the matter is that if alchemy's existence is sound, as the sages who speak of it claim, it is not one of the natural crafts, is not completed by an artificial act, and their discourse about it is not in the mode of natural sciences but in the mode of their discourse on magical matters and other wonders. Maslama al-Majriti mentioned something similar in his book al-Ghaya (The Aim), and his discourse on it in the book Rutbat al-Hakim (The Rank of the Sage) is of this same kind, and so is Jabir's discourse in his treatises."

In sum, if attaining it is sound, it occurs beyond crafts and natures. It comes about only through the influences of the soul and the breaking of customary patterns, like walking on water and creating birds. So it is nothing but a miracle, a marvel, or sorcery. That is why the sages' discourse on it is in riddles, and no one attains its realization except one who has plunged into the depths of the sciences of magic and has come to know the soul's influence over the world of nature. Matters of breaking custom are not restricted, and no one aims at attaining them." End of quotation. Al-Razi went to affirm its possibility, saying: "The truth is its possibility, because the seven metals share in being bodies that melt, endure fire, and are malleable, and gold is distinguished from the others only by its yellowness and heaviness, or by the golden form which gives these two accidents, if that is established. What is the source of difference is not necessarily what is the source of commonality. Therefore it is possible for the body of copper to take on the yellowness and heaviness of gold, and that is what is sought. The truth is that alchemy is possible and that it belongs to the natural crafts, but knowledge of it is among the most remote and difficult sciences, which none attains except one whom God has enabled for it and specially chosen from among His servants and friends. It is a science in whose pursuit minds have wandered and dreams have been bewildered. Its origin is from divine revelation, and some have attained it through purification and much reflection together with experiment, and it has reached one who is not fit for revelation, and one who has not practiced what others have practiced by learning from one whom God has graced." Ars said: "He is among the great people of this science. Its beginning was revelation from God, Exalted, then it was effaced and vanished, so whoever extracted it extracted it from books." The custom of God, Exalted, has been with whoever found it to conceal it, except for whom God wills, and the sages agreed to conceal it from those who are not its people. Indeed it is said that God, Exalted, took from the intellects in their innate nature covenants to conceal it, guard it, and be careful to avoid spreading or squandering it.

[Page 118]

For this reason you see the sages have made it into the most intricate riddles and obscured it to the utmost degree, so that whoever does not know their intent considers their discourse to be a tale of nonsense and judges its speaker to be foolish and frivolous. By this concealment the wisdom of God, Exalted, which Ibn Khaldun claimed concerning the two precious metals, has been preserved, and his argument which you heard earlier collapses.

[p. 119]

Jabir ibn Hayyan, who is a leading authority in this craft (al-sina'a, the Art), explicitly stated it in his book *Sirr al-Asrar* (The Secret of Secrets), as we have quoted. He said: "Every sage has set down his symbols and his book on an ambiguous meaning concerning the procedures of dissolution (al-hall), sublimation (al-i'sad) and washing (al-ghasl) upon the four natures. He called them 'the heavy bodies,' and he described the procedures in a wording and meaning that are obscure. For the sage it is open, and for the ignorant it is closed. Sometimes they go so far as to take those very bodies and test them, and they gain nothing from them. They then revile the sages for concealing this work. The building of the world is only by dirhams and dinars, and people, craftsmen and soldiers alike, work only out of desire or fear. So the sages knew that if they disclosed this secret until everyone knew it, the affairs of the world would not be completed, it would fall into ruin, and no one would work for anyone else. Therefore they withdrew from this and concealed it." End of quotation.

Then it is not hidden that what Ibn Khaldun mentioned first, namely that the impossibility is due to the lack of comprehensive knowledge, is nothing if it is established that the art came from revelation, and, even if that is not established, it still has its own problems. The same applies to what he mentioned, that nature does not leave the nearest path in its actions and adopts the farthest. For we say that what comes from the natures also happens in other ways. So there are two paths for it: a distant one, which wisdom has ordained be followed in most cases, and a near one, which wisdom has also ordained be followed rarely, through whomever Allah the Exalted wills among His servants. As for the claim that the pretenders have continually stumbled about like a blind camel (khabt 'ashwa') — if by them he means the leading masters of this craft, such as Hermes, Socrates, Plato, Agarimun, Pythagoras, Heraclius, Porphyry, Maria, Zosimos, Ars, Dhu Miqrat, Safidus, Balinas, Mahrariy, Jabir ibn Hayyan, al-Majriti, Abu Bakr ibn Wahshiyya, Muhammad ibn Zakariyya al-Razi and others too numerous to count, then they did not stumble. To establish their stumbling is an impossible task (khart al-qatad, "like plucking the thorny qatad shrub"), and their riddling, for a purpose they stated, does not indicate that they stumbled. And if by them he means those who practise it among the pretenders (al-mashsha'in) in his own age and in these times, then what he mentioned holds true of most of them, but he does not deny its possibility.

Al-Tughra'i has censured this type of people. He said in his book *Tarakib al-Anwar* (The Compositions of Lights): "A sincere teacher exists in every craft except this art. How can sincere counsel be hoped for from a people who call one another 'envious' among themselves, and who have agreed among themselves never to clarify these mysteries ever? This is especially so in this age, in which this knowledge has entirely perished, and the one who approaches it or searches after it has become a laughingstock among people. For a period of time I have made it my concern to search for everyone who thinks he has a share of this knowledge, but I have found no one who has smelled its scent or from whom half a word of it has been known. I have found the pretenders to this noble craft to be of two kinds: a deceiver who sells his religion and his integrity for a meagre worldly gain, and who wastes people's wealth on experiments born of ignorance; and a deceived person, diverted from his right guidance by a vain hope, a false expectation, and occupation with falsehood instead of seeking a good livelihood, relying on wishes and lies. The most that any one of them achieves is to look into the books of Jabir and his like, take their outward words, and be deceived by their glittering claims, without grasping the realities of their meanings. Yet they, and all the sages of this craft who have gone before, warn people against being deceived by the outward words of their books, and they proclaim about themselves that they speak in symbols and riddles, and their words are not to be heeded nor believed." Up to the end of what he said.

The matter has in our time reached a point that expression cannot contain its description. As for alchemy being among the effects of souls and extraordinary customs (khawariq al-'adat), so that it can only be a miracle, a charisma (karama), or magic, this is nothing. Rather, it is through ordinary causes, but these are hidden from most people; the influence of souls has no role in it at all. Yes, what comes from a prophet or a saint (wali) may also come from the alchemist without the practice of those causes, and then it is a charisma or a miracle. And that the manner of some sages' words about it is the manner of their words about magical matters does not indicate that it is one of the kinds of magic or its adjuncts, for that is part of their riddling about its affair. They have varied greatly in riddling about it and have pursued every path in it. Balinas wrote his book on it in terms of the spheres and the stars; others spoke about it through parables; others spoke about it through stories that most resemble fables; and so on. In sum, it is a craft that very few truly know, and whoever writes about it, without being a sage who knows its symbols, prepares for himself the occupation with it and the pursuit of knowing it, as the ignorant pretenders of today do, which is pure madness. That its origin is divine revelation or something similar is what prevails in assumption. Al-Tughra'i has cited in his books, such as *Jami' al-Asrar* and others, what indicates this. He mentioned that it was related from Hermes that he said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed to Shith ibn Adam, peace be upon them both, to sow gold in white, pure earth and to water it with the water of life." Maria said: "I am not saying this to you from my own self, but I am telling you what Allah the Exalted commanded His prophet Moses, peace be upon him, and informed him that the stone *nastarisis* is what holds the dye." Zosimos and Ars attributed it to Moses, peace be upon him. Ars mentioned that the working of it was the province of the Jews in Egypt, and that Joseph, peace be upon him, who was the first of the Children of Israel to enter Egypt, knew this, so Pharaoh honoured him for the wisdom that Allah the Exalted had given him. He also mentioned a section on it, expressed in symbols, which he attributed to Solomon, peace be upon him.

Al-Tarsusi said in his book: "When Allah the Exalted sent Adam, peace be upon him, down from the Garden, He compensated him with the knowledge of everything, and the knowledge of the Art was among what He taught him. It passed from people to people, just as the other sciences passed down, until the days of the first Hermes." He also said: "They related to us from Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, by a continuous chain of his own, that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'The earth was folded up for me, so I was shown its easts and its wests, and I was given the white and the red sulphur.'"

Jabir related from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, many narrations on this matter, to the extent that he ascribed to him several of his books. I neither verify his statement nor deny it, and I hold him in honour for his position in knowledge and practice, so as to keep him clear of fabricating against the Imams. It is related from the Commander of the Faithful, 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, that he was asked, and it was said to him: "What do you say about what people have delved into concerning the knowledge of alchemy?" He lowered his head for a long while, then raised his head and said: "You have asked me about the sister of prophethood and the twin of chivalry. Indeed there was, and indeed there is, and there is no tree, no clod, and no thing except that it has a root and a branch, or a root or a branch." It was said: "O Commander of the Faithful, do you not know it?" He said: "By Allah the Exalted, I know it better than those who know it, for they speak of knowledge by its outward form and not its inner reality, while I know the knowledge both outwardly and inwardly." It was said: "Then mention to us something of it, that we may take it from you." He said: "By Allah the Exalted, were it not that the soul commands to evil, I would have said." It was said: "So what would you say?" He said: "I know that in the quicksilver that trembles, the gold that glitters, the iron tinged with saffron, and the green verdigris of copper, there are treasures whose last cannot be reached; some of them are fertilised by others, and then they yield hidden gold." It was said: "O Commander of the Faithful, we do not know this." He said: "It is solid water, still air, intervening fire, and flowing earth." They said: "We do not comprehend this." He said: "If it were lawful for the sages among the believers to speak to people in any other way than this, the children in the schools would know it." End of Tughra'i's words, abridged.

In his book *Miftah al-Rahma wa Masabih al-Hikma* (The Key of Mercy and the Lamps of Wisdom), he mentioned, from sixty prophets and sages, that they affirmed the truth of this knowledge. There is some doubt in the heart concerning the soundness of these reports. The strong assumption is that if there were a reliable report about alchemy accepted by the scholars of hadith, it would have spread widely.
