And if someone among their great ones had not denied it, such as Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ahmad ibn Taymiyya, who did deny its establishment and wrote a treatise against it. Perhaps the rebuttal by Shaykh Najm al-Din Ibn Abi al-Dharr al-Baghdadi, and his refutation of what was said about it, as al-Safadi claims, concerned only what belongs to the realm of rational proofs. For in the domain of transmitted matters, that man is not matched by Najm al-Din mentioned, nor by those like him. In the domain of rational matters, while Najm al-Din is also distinguished, he falls short of him in transmitted matters. The question is subtle, to the point that some of those whom people point to with their fingers (ta'uqad 'alayhi al-khanasir, i.e., the most eminent) wavered regarding it, denying it at one time and affirming it at another. Here is Shaykh of the sages and their chief, Abu 'Ali ibn Sina. You have heard what was reported from him first, and it is related that he retracted it. Despite the keenness of his intellect and the loftiness of his standing in philosophy in all its divisions, he did not grasp the reality of its practice, to the point that al-Tughra'i said in *Tarakib al-Anwar*: "My wonder at Abu 'Ali ibn Sina knows no end. How did he permit himself to compose a treatise on this art, by which he exposed himself, contradicted the principles he himself held, and fell short of many of the base literalists, the dark-minded and dull of understanding."

He also said in *Jami' al-Asrar*: "Shaykh Abu 'Ali ibn Sina, due to his excessive passion for this knowledge and his strong intuition that it is true, wrote a treatise on it. He did well in what concerns the principles of natural sciences. But because the path of these people was hidden from him and they had kept it from him, he did not mention in the procedures specific to our science a single correct term, nor did he point to the true temperament, the weights, the concealed compositions, the fires and their layers, and the vessel without which the work cannot be completed, which is one of the ten conditions. He did not go beyond what the literalists have of procedures with mercury, the sulphurs, burial in horse dung, and occupation with these filths. Were it not for the bane of self-admiration, a person's good opinion of his own knowledge, and his eagerness that nothing of the sciences escape him, it would have been obligatory for someone like him, despite the abundance of his knowledge and the height of his rank in true investigations, to be content with what he has and not to meddle with what he does not know. It has reached us from his procedures, through his companions who witnessed them, that he did not know the reality of our knowledge. We have seen in his own handwriting, among the collected notes taken from the words of Jabir ibn Hayyan and Khalid ibn Yazid, what also indicates this." End of abridged quotation.

The discussion of this matter is long, and what we have mentioned is sufficient for whoever wishes to learn something of what has been said about it. And Allah the Exalted is the Granter of success.

Furthermore, the view that the meaning of "knowledge" in the verse is the knowledge of extracting treasures and hoards requires the establishment of this knowledge. The people of the science of letters (ilm al-huruf) and the science of talismans (ilm al-tilasamat) hold this view and have lengthy statements on it, and reason permits its establishment. Allah the Exalted knows best whether it is established in reality.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 28, verse 78 (part 4 of 4):

﴿Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations that were greater than him in strength and more abundant in numbers?﴾ This is an affirmation of his knowledge of that, and a warning about his error in being deceived, while he knew this from the Torah (*al-Tawrat*), or from Musa (peace be upon him), or from the books of histories, or from the (*al-Qussas*, the storytellers). Strength (*al-quwwah*) may mean physical strength (*al-quwwah al-hissiyyah*) or moral strength (*al-quwwah al-ma'nawiyyah*), and abundance (*al-jam'*) may mean abundance of wealth or abundance of men. The meaning is: did he not come upon what gives knowledge, and did he not know what Allah, exalted is He, did to those who were greater than him in strength, whether physical or moral, and greater in wealth or in a group who protected him and served him, so that he would not be deceived by what deceived him? It is also possible that the interrogative particle *hamzah* (the interrogative *alif*) is for denial (*lil-inkar*) and enters upon an implied clause (*muqaddar*), and the clause *awa lam ya'lam* (did he not know) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) that affirms the denial and indicates the negation of what the particle entered upon, as in your saying: "Do you claim to be a jurist while you do not know the conditions of prayer?" The intent is to reject his claim to knowledge and to his self-magnification through it, by negating this knowledge from him; that is, does he know what he claims, and did he not know this, so that he would protect himself from the fate of those who perished? It has been said that (*lam ya'lam*, did not know) is coordinated (*'atf*) upon that implied clause, and the negation of knowledge from him is because he did not act according to its requirement.

﴿And the guilty will not be asked about their sins.﴾ The apparent meaning is that this refers to the Hereafter, and that the pronoun in *dhunubihim* (their sins) refers to the guilty (*al-mujrimin*). The doer of the asking is either Allah, exalted is He, or the angels (peace be upon them). The asking that is negated here, and likewise in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So on that Day no one will be asked about his sin, neither man nor jinn﴾ [al-Rahman: 39], is, as it has been said, the asking of inquiry (*su'al al-istila'*). The negation of this with respect to Him, glorified and exalted is He, is clear, and with respect to the angels (peace be upon them), it is because they are aware of their records, or they recognize them by their marks, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿The guilty will be known by their marks, so they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ [al-Rahman: 41].

The asking that is affirmed in His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92] is the asking of rebuke and reproach (*su'al al-tawbikh wal-taqri'*), so there is no contradiction between the two verses. It is also permitted that the asking in both places has one meaning, and that the negation and affirmation are with respect to two places or two times, and the stations on the Day of Resurrection are many and the Day is long, so there is no contradiction here either.

The apparent meaning is that the sentence is not included within the scope of knowledge (*fi hayyiz al-'ilm*). Perhaps the connection of this sentence with what precedes it is that when He, exalted is He, threatened Qarun by mentioning the destruction of those before him of his kind in this world, He followed that with what contains a threat to all the guilty with something more grievous and more grievous than the punishment of the Hereafter, for the non-questioning of the sinner, together with the intensity of anger against him, indicates that he will certainly be struck. Al-Zamakhshari made the sentence a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) for what precedes it. It has also been said that this refers to this world.

The intent is that He, exalted is He, destroyed those He destroyed from the generations with knowledge from Him, glorified is He, of their sins, so He, exalted and glorified is He, had no need to ask them about them. It has also been said that the pronoun in *dhunubihim* (their sins) refers to those who were greater in strength, namely the destroyed generations, and the singular and plural forms are according to the wording and the meaning. The meaning is: the sins of those destroyed are not asked about by others among those who committed crimes, and it is known that those who did not commit crimes are not asked about their sins, all the more so, because of the enmity between the two groups. So the outcome of the meaning is: the sins of the destroyed are not asked about by others among those who committed crimes and those who did not commit crimes; rather, every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned. Both views, as you see, are weak. Perhaps there may occur to your mind the coordination (*'atf*) of this sentence upon the interrogative sentence, or making it a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the subject of *ahlaka* (destroyed) or of its object. But if you reflect even slightly, you will remove that from your mind and refuse to attribute such a reading to the noble speech of Allah, exalted is He.

Abu Ja'far, in one narration, read *wa la tas'al* (and do not ask) with the second-person address (*ta' al-khitab*) and the jussive (*al-jazm*), and *al-mujrimin* (the guilty) with the accusative (*al-nasb*). Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Sirin read *wa la tas'al* in the same way, but we do not know whether they read *al-mujrimin* in the accusative as Abu Ja'far did, or in the nominative as in the reading of the majority (*al-Jumhur*). The apparent meaning is the first. The author of *al-Lawami'h* permitted the second and mentioned for it two aspects. The first is that the pronoun in *dhunubihim* refers to those destroyed from the generations, and *al-mujrimin* is nominative by implying the subject (*mubtada'*), that is, they are the guilty. The second is that *al-mujrimin* is a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in *dhunubihim*, on the basis that its original case is nominative, because the construction of *dhunub* to it is like the construction of the verbal noun (*masdar*) to the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*). It was objected to this that *dhunub* is a plural, and if a plural is a verbal noun, then its government (*'amal*) is disputed.

[Page 121]

﴿So he went out to his people﴾ is coordinated with (*'aṭf*, a conjunction) ﴿he said﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (*i'tirāḍ*). His words ﴿in his adornment﴾ (*fī zīnatihi*) may be connected to ﴿went out﴾, or to something omitted that is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) of its subject, meaning: so he went out to them, being in his adornment.

Qatadah said: "It has been related to us that he went out, he and his retinue, upon four thousand mounts, wearing red garments, among them a thousand white mules, and upon their mounts were saddle-cloths of purple (*urjuwān*)." Al-Suddi said: "He went out with white maidens, on saddles of gold, over purple saddle-cloths, and they were on white mules, wearing red garments and gold ornaments." It was also said: "He went out on a grey-white mule, upon which was purple, and on it was a saddle of gold, and with him were four thousand servants, upon them and upon their horses was red brocade (*dībāj*), and on his right were three hundred boys, and on his left three hundred white maidens, upon whom were ornaments and brocade."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam that he went out with seventy thousand, upon whom were garments dyed with safflower (*mu'aṣfarāt*), and that was the first day on earth in which dyed garments were seen. It was also said other things regarding the manner (of the procession). That departure, it is said, was on a Saturday.

﴿Those who desired the life of this world said: "Oh, would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given!"﴾ It was said: they were a group of believers, and they said this following the natural human disposition (*jibillah*) of desiring abundance and wealth. And it is related from Qatadah that they wished for this so that they might draw near to God Most High by it and spend it in the way of good. Their desire for "the life of this world" may have been for the sake of reaching the Hereafter through it, not for its own sake, since desiring it for its own sake is not the way of believers. It was also said that they were disbelievers and hypocrites, and their wish for "the like of what he was given," without wishing his own state, is of the category of *ghibṭah* (admiring envy, wishing for a similar blessing without wishing it removed from the other), which is not harmful according to the well-known view. It was also said: its harm is less than the harm of envy (*ḥasad*).

It has been related: "It was said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): Does *ghibṭah* harm? He said: No, except as the beating (*khabt*) harms the thorny trees (*'iḍah*)."

In al-Kashf al-Zahir it is said: this is a negation of harm in the most emphatic form, for a tree may even benefit from being beaten, let alone be harmed. In it is also (the point) that it may lead to harm, indicating the object of *ghibṭah*, whether religious or worldly. If those who said this were disbelievers, then there is in it the censure of envy what there is.

﴿Indeed, he is truly one of great fortune﴾. Al-Dahhak said: "What a great rank!" It was also said: "a great portion of this world." The word *ḥaẓẓ* means fortune and good luck, and it is said: "So-and-so is fortunate (*dhū ḥaẓẓ*), (he is) *ḥaẓīẓ*, and *maḥẓūẓ*." The clause is an explanation of their wish (*ta'līl*) and an emphasis of it (*ta'kīd*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 80:

﴿And those who had been given knowledge said﴾, that is, of the affairs of this world and the Hereafter as they should be known, and among them was Yusha' (Joshua), peace be upon him. They were not described as desiring the reward of the Hereafter in order to alert the reader that knowledge of the conditions of both lives necessarily entails turning away from the first and turning toward the second, and that the wishing of those who wish (for the wealth and status of Qarun) arises only from their lack of proper knowledge of both.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "knowledge" is knowledge of reward and punishment. It has also been said: knowledge of reliance upon God (tawakkul). And it has been said: knowledge of reports. What came before is preferable.

﴿Woe to you!﴾ (ويلكم, waylakum) is, originally, a supplication for destruction, and then its use became common as a rebuke against what is not approved. The intended meaning here is a rebuke against wishing, and it is in the accusative as a masdar (masdariyyah, a verbal noun governed by a verb implied from its meaning), that is, an infinitive standing in place of an implied verb of rebuking.

﴿The reward of God﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is better﴾ than what you wish for ﴿for those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. Therefore it is not fitting for you to wish for it without being content with the reward of Him, mighty and majestic. This is according to the view that those who wished were believers, or that they should believe so that they may succeed in His reward, which is better than that. The object of comparison (what is "better than") is supplied as "what you wish for," because the context requires it. It is also permissible to supply it in a general sense, so that what was mentioned enters into it at the first level, that is: better than the world and all that is in it.

﴿And it is not granted﴾ (wa la yulaqqaha), that is, this statement, or the word that the scholars spoke. What is meant by it is the linguistic meaning, or the reward. The feminine form is due to its being in the sense of "recompense" or "Paradise" understood from "reward." It has also been said that it refers to faith and righteous deeds, and the feminine and singular form is due to their being in the sense of "conduct" or "way." The meaning of "receiving it" is either understanding it or being granted success in acting upon it.

﴿except the patient﴾, those who are steadfast in acts of obedience, and in abstaining from disobedience and desires. Perhaps the intended meaning of "the patient" according to the last view regarding the referent of the pronoun is those who are characterized by patience in the knowledge of God, the Exalted. So reflect.

[Page 123]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 81:

﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home.﴾ Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Qarun was a paternal cousin of Musa, peace be upon him. He used to pursue knowledge until he had gathered a great deal of it, but he continued in that state until he rebelled against Musa, peace be upon him, and envied him. Musa said: "Allah the Exalted has commanded me to take the zakat (obligatory alms)," but he refused.

[Page 123]

He said: "Musa, peace be upon him, wants to devour your wealth. He brought you the prayer and brought you other things, and you bore them, so will you bear to give him your wealth?" They said: "We cannot bear it. What do you think?" He said to them: "I think we should send for a prostitute (baghiyy) from among the prostitutes of the Children of Israel, and we will send her to him, and she will accuse him of having tried to seduce her." They sent for her and said to her: "We will give you your reward on condition that you testify against Musa that he committed fornication with you." She said: "Yes."

Qarun then came to Musa, peace be upon him, and said: "Gather the Children of Israel and inform them of what your Lord has commanded you." He said: "Yes," and he gathered them. They said to him: "What has your Lord commanded you?" He said: "He has commanded me that you worship Allah the Exalted and associate nothing with Him, that you maintain the ties of kinship, and such and such." [Musa said:] "He has also commanded me that an adulterer who commits adultery after being married (ihsan) should be stoned to death."

They said: "Even if it is you?" He said: "Yes." They said: "Then you have committed adultery." He said: "I?" They sent for the woman and she came. They said: "What do you testify against Musa, peace be upon him?" Musa, peace be upon him, said to her: "I adjure you by Allah the Exalted, tell the truth." She said: "As for your adjuring me by Allah the Exalted, they called me to this and offered me a reward on condition that I accuse you with myself, and I testify that you are innocent and that you are the Messenger of Allah." Then Musa, peace be upon him, fell prostrate, weeping. Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "What makes you weep? We have given you authority over the earth. Command it, and it will obey you." He raised his head and said: "Seize them." So it seized them up to their ankles, and they began to say: "O Musa! O Musa!" He said: "Seize them." So it seized them up to their knees, and they began to say: "O Musa! O Musa!" He said: "Seize them." So it engulfed them. Allah the Exalted revealed: "O Musa, My servants asked you and humbled themselves before you, but you did not answer them. By My might, had they called upon Me, I would have answered them."

In some narrations it is said that he offered (lil-baghiyy) a thousand dinars, and it was also said: a basin of gold filled with gold.

In another account, he, peace be upon him, said in his prostration: "My Lord, if I am Your messenger, then be angry on my behalf." Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "Command the earth as you wish, for it is obedient to you." He said: "O Children of Israel, Allah the Exalted sent me to Qarun just as He sent me to Pharaoh. Whoever is with him, let him remain, and whoever is with me, let him withdraw." They all withdrew except two men. Then he said: "O earth, seize them." So it seized them up to the knees, then to the waists, then to the necks, while they humbled themselves before Musa, peace be upon him, and implored him by the ties of kinship, but he, peace be upon him, did not heed their words because of the intensity of his anger, and he said: "Seize them," until it closed over them.

Allah the Exalted then revealed: "O Musa, how harsh you are! They sought your help repeatedly, and you did not show them mercy. By My might, if they had called upon Me even once, they would have found Me near and responsive."

In another narration, Allah the Exalted, glorified is He, revealed to him: "How hard is your heart! By My might and My majesty, if he had sought help from Me, I would have helped him." He, peace be upon him, said: "My Lord, I did it out of zeal for You."

Then the Children of Israel said: "Musa, peace be upon him, only did that to him so that he could inherit from him." So he called upon Allah the Exalted until the earth swallowed him up along with his home and his wealth.

In some reports it is said that the swallowing of him and his home occurred at the same time, and that his house, it was said, was made of plates of gold. It is related in several traditions that he is swallowed a man's height every day, and that he sinks through the earth, not reaching its bottom until the Day of Resurrection. Allah the Exalted knows best the soundness of this. Indeed, it is problematic if what the philosophers have said about the measure of the earth's diameter is correct, and if they did not hold that the earth has any motion at all. As for the swallowing (khasf) of the earth, there is no doubt about its possibility, both in itself (dhatiyy) and in fact (waqu'iyy), and its ordinary cause is explained in its proper place.

﴿So he had no company (fi'ah) to help him﴾: that is, a specific group. The word fi'ah is derived from fa'uta qalbahu, meaning "I inclined his heart when I turned it." The group was so named because some of its members incline toward others. Its root has a deleted lam, and its pattern is fi'ah. Al-Raghib said that its root has a deleted 'ayn, so its pattern is filah, and that it derives from al-fay', which means returning, because some of the group return to others. (Min) here is a connecting particle, meaning: "He had no group ﴿who would help him against Allah﴾ by averting the punishment from him. ﴿Nor was he among those who could defend themselves﴾," that is, those who protected themselves from His punishment, glorified and exalted is He. It is said: "He helped him against his enemy, so he defended himself," meaning he prevented him and he was able to protect himself. It is possible that the meaning is: "Nor was he among those who defended themselves with his helpers," and this is mentioned for emphasis.

[p. 124]

﴿And those who had wished to be in his place awoke﴾, that is, [wished for] a position and station like his, in accordance with their earlier statement ﴿such as was given to him﴾. It was also permitted to take this in its literal sense, with ﴿like﴾ (مثل) here being superfluous (muqhamah), but this is not the preferred view. ﴿Yesterday﴾ (بالأمس) means "a short time ago," which is a common figurative usage. It was also permitted to take it literally, with the prepositional phrase governed either by ﴿wished﴾ or by ﴿in his place﴾. It has been said that the conjunction with fa' (then), which implies immediate sequence, in ﴿so We caused [the earth to swallow him]﴾ indicates this.

In al-Bahr [al-Muhit], it is noted that if ﴿awoke﴾ is taken in its literal sense, it indicates that the swallowing of him and his house occurred at night, which is the most dreadful form of punishment, since night is the time of rest and tranquility. Some scholars said that it means "became," i.e., those who had wished became [the ones who wished].

﴿They said, "Woe! It is indeed God who extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts [it]"﴾, that is, each of extending and restricting is done [by God], meaning constriction and narrowing, not because of honor that requires extension nor because of humiliation that requires restriction. According to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, *way* (وي) is an *ism fi'l* (a noun functioning as a verb, i.e., a verbal-noun particle), and its meaning is "how wonderful!" It is also used to express regret and remorse, as they have stated. It is reported from al-Khalil that the people regretted and, expressing their remorse over what had passed, said "wayy," and everyone who regrets and wishes to show his regret says "wayy." Yet the more evident intention is that of wonder, in that they first marvelled at what had happened and then said secondly, "It is as if [God]..." (كأن إلخ). In *ka'anna* here there is a sense devoid of the meaning of comparison; it is used for emphasis (lil-tahqiq), as has been said regarding the line:

*"And the floor of Makkah has become horrified, as if the land had no Hisham in it."*

Abu 'Ali recited:

*"As if I, when I become evening, [she] does not speak to me, a lovesick man who desires what is not present."*

It has also been said that it is not devoid of that meaning, and that the intention is to liken the absolute state to what is within its domain, indicating that because it is established and well known, anything may be likened to it. But this is, as you see, not [an acceptable view]. Al-Hamdani claimed that al-Khalil held that *wayka* expresses regret and *ka'anna* expresses wonder, and the meaning is "they regretted, marvelling that God, exalted is He, extends..." etc. But in this there is the objection that using *ka'anna* for wonder is not something known. Whatever the case, the pause, as in al-Bahr, is on (ويْ). Analogically it should be written separately, but it has been written joined to the *kaf* due to frequent usage. It was written according to analogy in the verse of Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl:

*"Woe! As if he who has wealth is made to... and he who is in need lives a life of hardship."*

Al-Akhfash said: the *kaf* is joined to it, and it is an *ism fi'l* meaning "how wonderful," and the *kaf* is a *harf al-khitab* (particle of address) having no place in the grammatical structure, as they said regarding that and similar. The pause is on *wayka*, and on this basis came the verse of 'Antarah:

*"And indeed it has healed my soul and cured its sickness: the words of the horsemen, 'Woe, 'Antar, advance!'"*

The *hamza* of ﴿that God﴾ (أن) here is open, with the implied sense of knowledge, i.e., "I know that God..." etc. Al-Kisa'i, Yunus, Abu Hatim and others went to the view that its origin is *waylaka*, which was lightened by dropping the *lam*, leaving *wayka*, which is used for deterrence, rebuke, and urging to abandon what is not pleasing. Abu Hayyan said it is a word of grief, and cited in confirmation the line:

*"Ah, woe to you! Harm does not endure, nor does bliss remain upon misery."*

According to this, the *kaf* is in the genitive position by way of annexation, and the governing element for *anna* is the implied verb of knowledge, as you have heard, or it is [governed] by an implied *li-anna* (because), meaning that it is an explanation of the cause for which *wayka* was said. Ibn Qutaybah reported from some scholars of learning that the meaning of *wayka* is "mercy upon you" in the dialect of Himyar. Al-Farra' said: *wayka* in the speech of the Arabs is like a man saying, "Do you not see the handiwork of God, exalted is His majesty?" Abu Zayd and a group with him said: It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that *wayka'anna* is a single particle in its entirety, and it means "Did you not see?"

﴿Had God not been gracious to us﴾ by not giving us what we wished for, namely giving us the like of what He gave Qarun, ﴿He would have caused the earth to swallow us﴾, that is, the earth [would have swallowed us] just as it swallowed him. Or: had God, exalted is He, not been gracious to us by overlooking our shortcoming in wishing that, He would have caused the earth to swallow us as a recompense for it, just as it swallowed him as a recompense for what he was doing.

Al-A'mash recited *"lawla (manna)"* with the omission of *an* while it is intended. It is reported from him *"Mannu Allah"* with *mannu* in the nominative and an annexation.

Most readers recited *"lakhusifa bina"* in the passive voice, with *bina* as the substitute for the subject. It was also permitted that the pronoun refer to the verbal noun, i.e., *lakhasafa huwa*, meaning the swallowing itself, in the sense of "He would have done the swallowing to us." Ibn Mas'ud, Talha and al-A'mash recited *"lankhusifa bina"*, also in the passive voice, with *bina* or the pronoun of the verbal noun being the substitute for the subject. Also from him: *"latukhussifa"* with a *ta'* and a doubled *sin*, in the passive.

﴿And woe! Indeed, the disbelievers do not prosper﴾ in the favor of God, exalted is He, or those who deny His messengers, peace be upon them, and what they were promised of the reward of the Hereafter. The discussion of *wayka'anna* here is as it was above, except that it was permitted here that *li-anna*, under some of the possibilities, be a causal explanation of an implied element by context, i.e., "because the disbelievers do not prosper, [God did] that act," namely the swallowing of Qarun. The consideration of its counterpart earlier, but not of this here, is noted. The pronoun in *wayka'anna-hu* refers to the matter (the situation).

Furthermore, in Majma' al-Bayan it is stated that the story of Qarun is connected to God's words: ﴿We recite to you [some] of the news of Musa﴾ [al-Qasas: 3], peace be upon him. It was also said that it is connected to His words: ﴿Whatever you have been given is the enjoyment of the worldly life, but what is with God is better and more lasting﴾. It was said: since the disgrace and exposure of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection had been mentioned earlier, God, exalted is He, mentioned after it that Qarun is among them and that he will be exposed on the Day of Resurrection just as he was exposed in this world. And when He, glorified is He, mentioned earlier the saying of the people of knowledge ﴿The reward of God is better﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 83:

He mentioned the place of that reward with His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿That is the Abode of the Hereafter﴾, pointing with a sign of magnification and exaltation to what, because of its fame, has become like something sensed and witnessed, as if it were said:

"That which you have heard of and whose description has reached you." (*al-Dar*) is an attribute (*sifah*) of the demonstrative (*ism al-isharah*) that stands as the subject (*mubtada'*). It is described by a non-derived noun (*jamid*), and there is no need to posit an elided genitive construction, meaning "the bliss of the Abode," as the words of al-Bahr may suggest. (*al-Akhirah*) is an attribute of *al-dar*, and what is meant by it is Paradise. The predicate (*khabar*) of the subject is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We shall make it for those who do not desire exaltation (*'uluww*) in the earth﴾, that is, domination and tyranny, ﴿nor corruption (*fasad*)﴾, that is, wrongdoing and aggression against the servants, like the way of Pharaoh and Qarun. The relative pronoun is not restricted to these two. The repetition of *la* (not) indicates that each of exaltation and corruption is intended by the negation. And making the promise conditional upon abandoning the desire for them, rather than upon abandoning them themselves, is a further warning against them.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ikrimah that he said: "Exaltation in the earth is arrogance and seeking rank and status with its rulers and kings, and corruption is acting in acts of disobedience and taking wealth unlawfully."

And from al-Kalbi: "Exaltation is refusing to believe out of arrogance, and corruption is calling to the worship of other than Allah, Exalted is He." And it is related from Muqatil that he explained exaltation in the same way as related from al-Kalbi.

[Page 126]

Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he used to walk alone in the markets, while he was a governor, guiding the one who had gone astray, helping the weak, and passing by the grocer and the seller, and the Qur'an would open up to him, and he would recite ﴿That is the Abode of the Hereafter﴾ to its end, and he would say:

"This verse, ﴿That is the Abode of the Hereafter﴾ etc., was revealed concerning the people of humility and modesty among the rulers and the people of power among all other people."

Ibn Mardawayh related "from Adi ibn Hatim that when he entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ), he threw him a cushion, but he sat on the ground. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, peace and blessings be upon him: 'I bear witness that you do not seek exaltation in the earth nor corruption.'

So he became Muslim, may Allah be pleased with him."

And from al-Fudayl that he recited the verse and then said: "Wishful thinking has vanished here." And from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that he used to repeat it until he died.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "A man may love that the thong of his sandal be finer than the thong of his companion's sandal, and so he enters into this verse."

Perhaps this applies when he loves that in order to boast over his companion and belittle him; otherwise,

Abu Dawud related from Abu Hurayrah: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was handsome, and he said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I am a man to whom beauty is beloved, and I have been given of it what you see, to the point that I do not like anyone to surpass me,' or he said, 'with the strap of a sandal, or the thong of a sandal.' 'Is that arrogance?' He said: 'No, but arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down upon people.'"

Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn Mas'ud "that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'No one who has in his heart an atom's weight of arrogance will enter Paradise.' A man said: 'A man loves that his garment be fine and his sandal be fine.' He said: 'Indeed Allah is Beautiful and loves beauty. Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down upon people.'"

Some of the Mu'tazilah used the verse as evidence, on the basis that exaltation and corruption in it are general, for the eternal abiding of the perpetrator of a major sin in the Fire. In al-Kashshaf there is something apparent in that regard. Some of them, in responding, committed to explaining exaltation and corruption as al-Kalbi explained them, and another said that what is meant by them is what is like the exaltation and corruption that were from Pharaoh and Qarun. It was refuted by saying that the closing with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the good end is for the God-fearing﴾, indicates that the essential element is piety, and abandoning the restricted exaltation and corruption is not sufficient.

It was answered that the God-fearing here is the one who fears the exaltation of Pharaoh and the corruption of Qarun, or the one who was not among the believers like Pharaoh in arrogance toward Allah, Exalted is He, by not complying with His commands and not restraining himself from His prohibitions, and was not like Qarun in desiring corruption in the earth and removing everything from being beneficial, especially himself, for the greatest corruption of it is refraining from worshipping its Lord, since it was created for worship. So when it refrains from that, it has left its state of being beneficial, and the meaning of the God-fearing is nothing other than that.

The author of al-Kashf criticized this, saying: "The first is a restriction without evidence, and the second is what the Mu'tazili seeks." And al-Fadil al-Khafaji said: "Either the good end is meant in its perfect form, or the God-fearing is meant as one who fears what Allah, Exalted is He, does not approve, like the state of Qarun, by the indication of the context, and the texts indicating that non-disbelievers do not abide forever in the Fire. So there is no basis for saying that this is a restriction without evidence, especially since the basis of the argument is that the *lam* (for) indicates exclusivity (*lam al-takhsis*), and that is disputed."

Some said, in answer on the assumption that the generality is intended in *'uluwwan* and *fasadan*: "What is meant by making Paradise for those who do not desire any of them is enabling them to enter it in the most complete way, like your saying: 'The sultan made the city of so-and-so for so-and-so.' This does not preclude that others among the perpetrators of major sins enter it, and they will be in it at a lower rank than theirs. Perhaps they entered it through the intercession of some of them." Close to this is what was said: "Making it theirs is in regard to their being its first inhabitants and its foremost kings, and others are only assigned to them, and it descends upon them." And regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the good end is for the God-fearing﴾, it is said in the manner already mentioned from al-Khafaji.

There remains another discussion regarding the verse: some of them used it as evidence that Paradise does not exist today, on the basis that the meaning of ﴿We shall make it for those who do not desire﴾ etc. is "We shall create it in the future for their sake." It was answered that it is possible that the *ja'l* (making) is transitive to two objects, the second being ﴿for those who do not desire﴾ etc., so the meaning becomes "We shall make it existing and present for them in the future time." Thus the verse indicates that making it existing for them is not yet realized, not the making of it itself.

[Page 127]

And this is the point of dispute. It was refuted by saying that what is understood from making the abode belong to Zayd is enabling him and not preventing him from having access to it, whether or not he actually gains access to it. So the meaning of ﴿We shall make it for those who﴾ etc. is that they will be enabled in the future to have access to it. But its weakness is not hidden, because enabling them to have access to it is necessarily tied to its existence, not separable from it, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It has been prepared for the God-fearing﴾. So it is not possible that Paradise itself exists now while the making of it existing for them is in the future. And the making was interpreted as an actual enabling and enabling to have access. Even though enabling access to it is necessary for the existence of Paradise, actual access to it is not necessary, but rather it is a departure from what is understood in what will come. For what is understood from your saying, "Your making the abode belong to Zayd," is enabling him to have access to it, not that Zayd is made actually having access to it. So reflect on all of that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 84:

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him there is⦅in return for it⦆ something better than it﴾, in its quality, its attribute and its measure, according to what has been said. He also permitted that "khayr" (good) here is of the type that does not take the superlative form, meaning it is not the comparative (af'al al-tafdil), and that "min" (from) is causal (sababiyyah), so that the meaning is: for him there is good because of doing it. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the discussion of this has already passed. ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except with what they used to do﴾. Here the relative pronoun and the apparent noun were placed in the position of the pronoun, to condemn the state of the evildoers by repeating the attribution of evil deeds to them. As for using the plural "evil deeds" but the singular "good deed", it has been said that this indicates the scarcity of the doers of good and the abundance of the evildoers. It may also be said that it indicates that adding an evil deed to another evil deed does not increase its recompense; rather, its recompense when it stands alone is like its recompense when other things are joined to it. Likewise, not joining a good deed to another good deed does not affect its being repaid with something better than it. Perhaps the scarcity of doers of good is understood from the absence of considering plurality in "min" in His saying: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him there is something better than it﴾, while the abundance of evildoers is understood from considering plurality in it, since the relative pronoun stands in place of its pronoun in His saying: ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except with what they used to do﴾. That is, except with the like of what they used to do. The word "the like" has been omitted and "what they used to do" has been put in its place, for emphasis in the equivalence. This is a kindness from Him, glorified and exalted, since He multiplied the good deed and did not accept an increase in the recompense of an evil deed by even an atom's weight.

It has also been said that there is no need to consider an omitted word (al-mudaf), for their deeds themselves will appear on the Day of Resurrection in the form of that by which they are punished. But what is in this is not hidden. In mentioning "they did" (amilu) a second time rather than "they came" (ja'u), there is an indication that what they are recompensed for is what was done intentionally, because the deed is specific to the one who does it, as al-Raghib said. In the Tafsir al-Kabir of Imam al-Razi, in the course of discussing His saying: ﴿Did you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription...﴾ [al-Kahf: 9], the verse, he says that in using the expression "came" rather than "did", such as saying "whoever does a good deed, for him there is something better than it, and whoever does an evil deed, etc.", there is an indication that the entitlement to reward, and punishment, is derived from the final outcome and not from the beginning of the action. What confirms this is that if he spent his life in disbelief and then embraced Islam at the end, he would be among the people of reward, and vice versa. This is not devoid of beauty. Perhaps the subtle point of using "they did" a second time is also achieved by this.

In His saying: ﴿so he will not be recompensed﴾ and so on, rather than "then for those who did evil deeds is what they used to do," or "so what is for those who did evil deeds except what they used to do," there is an indication that pardon from punishment may occur. How wondrous are the secrets of the Revelation! The verse's implication that the recompense of an evil deed is its like raised a difficulty: that whoever disbelieves and dies in disbelief will be punished with eternal torment, and where is that compared with the disbelief of an hour? It was answered that the matter of equivalence is unknown to us, especially according to the view that denies rational good and evil in actions. The most we know is that God, Exalted, has assigned to every sin a recompense which He has informed is equivalent to it, and He, glorified be He, has informed that the recompense of disbelief is eternal torment. So we believe in it, and that it is among what wisdom requires. And there is nothing upon us if we do not know the aspect of equivalence and the wisdom in it. The same applies to sins for which God, Exalted, has prescribed prescribed penalties in this world, such as fornication, drinking wine, and slandering a chaste person, and the penalties He has prescribed for them, may He be exalted in glory.

[Page 128]

For we do not know the reason for assigning each of these sins to a particular penalty among those differing penalties, but we firmly affirm that this is not devoid of wisdom. Imam al-Razi answered the question of disbelief and eternal punishment by saying that this is because the disbeliever was resolved that, if he lived forever, he would remain in that disbelief. It has also been said regarding the reason for punishing the disbeliever for everlasting ages that the recompense for disobedience varies according to the greatness of the one disobeyed: the greater the one disobeyed, the greater the recompense. Since disbelief is disobedience toward the One whose greatness is unlimited, glorified be His state, its recompense is unending. By analogy, the recompense of every act of disobedience should be likewise, but it is not so with other than disbelief, as a favour from Him, may His state be exalted, owing to the presence of faith. It has also been said: every disbelief, whether in word or in deed, returns to attributing deficiency to Him, glorified and exalted, which contradicts necessary existence (wujub al-wujud), which requires His existence, glorified be He, from eternity to eternity. If one supposes an extended time there, it would be unending. So since disbelief entails the negation of His existence, exalted be His state, for what is unending, its recompense is unending. This is not so for the other sins. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 85:

﴿Indeed, He who ordained the Qur'an for you﴾ means: He who made it obligatory upon you to act by it, as is related from ʿAṭāʾ and from Mujāhid, that is, He gave it to you. And from Muqātil, and to this view went al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayda, that is, He sent it down upon you. The reliance, however, is upon what has preceded.

﴿will surely bring you back to a place of return (maʿād)﴾ means: to a place of great worth, to which you are accustomed and attached, taking maʿād from ʿāda (custom) and not from ʿawd (return). This is as in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, and Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil narrated it through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbās that it is Mecca. This is also related from Mujāhid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. It is also permitted that it be from ʿawd (return), and the intended meaning is likewise Mecca, based on what is in Majmaʿ al-Bayān from al-Qutaybī, that the maʿād of a man is his homeland, because he travels through lands and then returns to it. It may be said: maʿād was applied to Mecca because the Arabs used to return to it every year on account of the House there. This is a promise from Him, mighty and majestic, to His Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, while he was in Mecca, that he, upon him be prayer and peace, would emigrate from it and return to it. It is related from more than one source that the verse was revealed at al-Juḥfa after he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, had left Mecca as an emigrant and longed for it. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that it contains the promise of the good outcome in this world, just as what came before it contained the promise of the good outcome in the Hereafter.

It is said: when He, exalted is He, mentioned the story of Mūsā, peace be upon him, and his people with Qārūn, his insolence, his arrogance over them, his destruction, and the victory of the people of truth over him, He, glorified is His majesty, mentioned here what includes the story of our master, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and his Companions, with his people, their arrogance over him, their expulsion of him from his birthplace, then his being honoured, peace be upon him, by returning to Mecca and conquering it victorious and honoured. Glorified is He, placing between the two what serves as a transition from the first to the second.

Al-Ḥākim in al-Tārīkh and al-Daylamī related from ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, from the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, that he interpreted maʿād as Paradise. Ibn Abī Shayba, al-Bukhārī in his Tārīkh, Abū Yaʿlā and Ibn al-Mundhir related its interpretation as Paradise from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī. Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh related it from Ibn ʿAbbās. The indefiniteness (in maʿād) is also for magnification. The connection of the verse with what precedes it is that it is like an explicit statement of some of what that contains.

It was raised as a difficulty that His returning him, peace be upon him, to Paradise implies that he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was previously in it, whereas he, peace be upon him, was not in it.

It is answered by accepting the said precedence, and it suffices for it that he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was in it potentially, since he was in the loins of Ādam, peace be upon them both, when Ādam was in it. It is also said: since he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was prepared for it from before, it was as if he were in it, so the precedence is by way of that preparation, in the manner of what was said about His saying concerning the disbelievers: ﴿Then indeed their return is to the Hellfire﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 68]. The distance of both views is not hidden. Close to them is what is said: that this is by way of his, peace be upon him, having entered it on the night of the Mi'rāj. It may also be said: interpreting it as Paradise is an explanation of some of what maʿād implies, in that it is an expression for the Place of Gathering (al-maḥshar), so it has become almost literal in that sense, for it is the beginning of the return to the life in which the maʿād is. Making it great, as the tanwīn indicates, is due to the greatness of what he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, has in it, and of it is Paradise. So maʿād, through its tanwīn which indicates magnification, implies Paradise, for it contains what has been prepared for him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, of great matters that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that has not occurred to the heart of any human. Close to its interpretation as the Place of Gathering is its interpretation as the Hereafter, as ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī; and its interpretation as the Day of Resurrection, as Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd from ʿIkrima, except that according to what was mentioned it is the name of a time, while according to what preceded it is the name of a place. Among what indicates that the intended meaning is not merely the return to the Place of Gathering, or the Hereafter, or the Day of Resurrection, is what al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Mujāhid, that he said concerning the verse: "Indeed, for him is a maʿād which Allah will raise him to on the Day of Resurrection, then He will admit him to Paradise." It follows in the manner of what we have said that its interpretation as the Praiseworthy Station (al-maqām al-maḥmūd), which is the station of the Greatest Intercession on the Day of Resurrection.

In another report, transmitted by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī also, it came that its interpretation is death. Along with them, al-Firyābī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ṭabarānī narrated it from the scholar (al-Ḥabr) al-Firyābī. Its being a maʿād is in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you were dead and He gave you life﴾ [al-Baqara: 28]. Perhaps its magnification is in consideration of its being the gateway to his, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, arrival at what Allah, mighty and majestic, has prepared for him of the Praiseworthy Station and the high rank in Paradise, up to what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that has not occurred to the heart of any human. The main purpose is what the magnification indicates. Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Nuʿaym al-Qārrī that he interpreted it as Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It seems that the application of maʿād to it is in consideration of his, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, having been taken by night to it on the night of the Mi'rāj, and the promise of his, peace be upon him, return to it is a promise of his being taken there once more; or in consideration that his land is the land of the Place of Gathering, so the return to it means the return to the Place of Gathering. This is the utmost that can be said in directing this. If it is accepted, well and good; otherwise the matter is up to you. I think you would choose what is in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, and what the group mentioned earlier related from Ibn ʿAbbās, that it is Mecca. It may occur to the mind that maʿād is intended as a beloved matter by way of some figurative extension, and is made to include Mecca, Paradise and other things beloved to him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him; and his return, peace be upon him, to the beloved matter means bringing it to him repeatedly. The return here is then like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they put their hands into their mouths﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 9]. On this basis, the difficulty of the differing reports you have heard concerning it becomes easy, so reflect.

﴿Say: My Lord knows best who has come with guidance﴾ — by this He means himself, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him; and by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and who is in manifest error﴾ — the polytheists to whom he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was sent. "Who" (man) is in the accusative, governed by a verb indicated by "a'lamu", not by "a'lamu" itself, because the superlative (af'al) does not govern a direct object in the well-known view; that is, "He knows who has come…" etc. Some permitted that it be in the accusative governed by "a'lamu" on the basis that it has the meaning of "ʿālim" (knowing). The meaning is that He, mighty and majestic, recompenses each of those who came with guidance and those who are in error according to their deeds. The sentence is a confirmation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, He who ordained the Qur'an for you﴾, etc. In Maʿālim al-Tanzīl it is said: this is a reply to the disbelievers of Mecca, when they said to the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, "You are in error." Perhaps for this reason, and because the cause of it was his, peace be upon him, coming to them with guidance, it was said on his side "who has come with guidance," and on their side "who is in manifest error," and these two were not presented in the same pattern.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 86:

﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you﴾ is also a confirmation of that, i.e., He will certainly return you to the place of return (ma'ad), just as He sent down to you the Qur'an, which is of great station, and which you did not expect. Abu Hayyan and al-Tabarsi said: it is a reminder of His favor, Mighty and Majestic is He, upon him, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿but as a mercy from your Lord﴾ — according to what al-Farra' and a group went to — is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), i.e., but rather He, Exalted is He, cast it to you as a mercy from Him, Mighty and Majestic is He. It is also permissible that it be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) from the most general of causes (a'amm al-'ilal) or from the most general of states (a'amm al-ahwal), on the basis that the intended meaning is the negation of the casting in the most emphatic manner. The meaning then is: the Book was not cast to you for the sake of any thing except for the sake of mercy, or in any state except the state of mercy. ﴿So never be a supporter (zahir) for the disbelievers﴾, i.e., a helper to them in their religion. Muqatil said: when the disbelievers of Makkah invited him, may God bless him and grant him peace, to the religion of his forefathers, God, Exalted is He, reminded him of His favors and forbade him from supporting them in what they were upon.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 87:

﴿And let them not turn you away﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, ﴿from the signs of Allah﴾, i.e., from reciting them and acting upon them.

﴿After they have been sent down to you﴾, i.e., after the time of their being sent down and revealed to you, which necessitates your prophethood and the increase of your nobility. Ya'qub (Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Hadrami) read "yasuddannka" with a light nun (al-nun al-khafifa), and it was read "yusiddannaka," the present tense of asadda, with the meaning of (sadda) (to turn away). Abu Zayd related this from a man of the Kalb tribe, who said: "It is the dialect of his people." And the poet said:

"People who turned the people away from them with the sword, turning away like the water-channels turned away from the noses of the thirsty camels."

(And call) the people ﴿to your Lord﴾, to His worship, may He be exalted and high, and to His Oneness, glorified is He, ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾ by backing them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 28, verse 88:

﴿And do not invoke with Allah another god﴾, that is, do not worship, along with Him, the Exalted, anyone other than Him, Mighty and Majestic. This verse and what precedes it are meant to stir and rouse (al-tahyij wal-ilhab), to cut off the hopes of the polytheists of obtaining his (ﷺ) assistance in this matter, and to show that what is forbidden is so repugnant and evil that it is prohibited to one whom it is not conceivable could ever commit it at all. Muhyi al-Sunnah (al-Baghawi) related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: the address is outwardly to the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is meant is his community (ahl dinihi). This is in the sense of what al-Tabarsi reported on this point: that this and similar expressions are of the type of "It is you I mean, but listen, O neighbour" (iyyaki a'ni wasma'i ya jarah).

﴿There is no god but Him﴾ alone. ﴿Everything﴾ that exists, absolutely, ﴿is perishing﴾, that is, utterly non-existent, and what is meant is that it is like the non-existent and in its ruling. ﴿Except His Face﴾, that is, except His Essence, Mighty and Majestic. This is because the existence of all else besides Him, glorified is He, is not essential to it; rather, it depends upon the Necessary Existent, exalted is He, at every moment, is susceptible to non-existence and liable to it, and so it is as though it had no existence. This is what many of the eminent scholars have chosen. The discussion on this is of the type of eloquent simile (al-tashbih al-baligh). The "face" in the sense of the essence is a metonymic figure (majaz mursal), and it is a common metonymy, though it may be restricted to what is noble among essences, and this may be taken into account here, and it may be made a subtle point for the shift from "except Him" to the phrasing of the sublime text.

In the verse, based on what is the basic principle of the exception being connected (to the preceding), there is evidence for the validity of applying the term "thing" (shay') to Him, exalted is He.

[Page 131]

Close to this is what has been said: the meaning is that everything that can be called existent is, in itself, non-existent, except His Essence, exalted is He. It has also been said: "face" means essence, except that what is meant is the essence of the thing, and its being attributed to His pronoun, exalted is He, is by way of consideration that it is created by Him, glorified is He. This is similar to what has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You know what is in my soul and I do not know what is in Your soul﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], that the second "soul" means the soul of 'Isa, peace be upon him, and its attribution to Him, exalted is He, is by way of consideration that it is created by Him, Exalted and Majestic. The meaning is: everything is susceptible to ruin and non-existence except the essence insofar as it turns toward its Lord and stands in the niche of its nearness, for from that aspect it does not accept non-existence. It has also been said: "face" means the direction that is intended and turned toward, and the meaning is: everything is non-existent in itself except the direction attributed to Him, exalted is He, which is the existence by which it became existent. Its upshot is that all the aspects of the existent, of its essence, its attributes and its states, are perishing and non-existent in themselves, except the existence which is the Divine Light. Among people there are those who made the pronoun of "His face" refer to "thing" and explained "thing" as "existent" in the sense of what has a relation to the presence of true existence, subsisting by itself, which is the very reality of the Necessary Existent, glorified is He. They explained "face" as this existence, because the existent turns toward it and is attributed to it. The meaning is: everything attributed to existence is non-existent except His face which he intended and turned toward, which is the true existence subsisting by itself, which is the very reality of the Necessary Existent, Exalted and Majestic. The good and the bad of these opinions are not hidden. And upon all of them enter the Throne, the Footstool, the heavens, the earth, Paradise, the Fire, and the like, in generality.

Others have said: what is meant by perishing is the thing's leaving being benefited by the purpose for which it was made, either by its parts scattering or otherwise. The meaning is: everything will perish and leave being benefited by the purpose for which it was made, except His Essence, Mighty and Majestic. Apparently he intended by "thing" the existent in an absolute sense, not only the existent at the time of the revelation. So the meaning reverts to our saying: everything that exists at any time will perish after its existence, except the Essence of Allah, exalted is He. Thus the apparent meaning of the verse indicates the perishing of the Throne, Paradise and the Fire, whereas the evidence has indicated that the latter two do not perish.

It has come in a report: "Paradise's ceiling is the Throne of the Most Merciful." For this reason, this verse has been raised as an objection against those who hold that Paradise and the Fire exist now, and against those who deny this and say they will be brought into existence on the Day of Recompense and will endure forever. They differed in answering this. Some said: "kull" (all) here is not for comprehensiveness but for plurality, as in your saying "all the people came except Zayd," when most of them came but not Zayd. This is supported by what is reported from al-Dahhak, who said regarding the verse: everything is perishing except Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the Throne, Paradise and the Fire. Others said: what is meant by perishing is death, and the generality is with regard to the living who exist in this world. This is supported by what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said in explaining the verse: every living thing is dead except His face.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "When the verse (every soul will taste death) [Al 'Imran: 185; al-Anbiya': 35; al-'Ankabut: 57] was revealed, it was said: O Messenger of Allah, what about the angels? Then this was revealed: ﴿Everything is perishing except His face.﴾"

So in this verse He clarified the perishing of the angels and the two weighty ones (jinn and humankind), and the rest of Allah's world and His creation, from the birds, the wild beasts, the predators, the cattle, and every creature with a soul, that it is perishing and dead. You know that specifying "thing" to the living existing in this world requires some indicator. If it is considered that its being ruled as perishing, given that its use has become widespread for death, and death occurs only in this world, is an indicator, then that is fine; otherwise it is as you see. Some people committed to what the apparent generality requires: that everything that exists at any time in this world or the next becomes perishing after its existence, on the basis of the renewal of substances (tajaddud al-jawahir) and the non-persistence of any of them for two moments, like accidents (al-a'rad) according to al-Ash'ari. Its falsity is not hidden, though some eminent Sufis, may their secrets be sanctified, went to this view.

[Page 132]

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "His face" is the righteous deed which is directed toward Him, Mighty and Majestic. It was said, regarding the construction of the exception: the deed mentioned had been in the realm of non-existence, but when the servant performed it, complying with His command, He, whose majesty is great, preserved it for him until He recompenses him for it; or, by its being accepted, it became non-perishable, because the reward for it took its place and it remains.

It is reported from Abu 'Abd Allah al-Rida, may Allah be pleased with him, that he endorsed something similar, and said: the meaning is that everything from the deeds of the servants is perishing and void, except what is intended by it the face of Allah, exalted is He. Al-Khafaji claimed that this is an outward (literal) statement.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: what is meant by "face" is His standing (jah) which He placed among the people. And this, as you see, has no basis. The Salaf say: "the face" is an attribute we affirm for Allah, exalted is He, and we do not occupy ourselves with its modality (kayfiyyah) or with its interpretation (ta'wil), after declaring Him, Mighty and Majestic, free of any bodily part (al-jarihah). ﴿To Him belongs the judgment﴾, that is, the binding decree over creation, ﴿and to Him﴾, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿you will be returned﴾ at the resurrection for recompense, with truth and justice, not to any other than Him, exalted is He. The return of servants to Him, exalted is He, according to the Sufis of unity (ahl al-wahdah), means in the sense of what lies beyond the realm of the intellect (ma waraa' tawr al-'aql).

It has been said: the pronoun in "to Him" refers to the judgment. 'Isa read "turji'un" (you are returned) in the active voice. This, and the discourse on the allusive interpretation (al-ishara) in the verses of this surah, is mostly, in what we have come to know of it, of the type of applying what is in the horizons (al-afaq) to what is in the souls (al-anfus). It is probably known with a little reflection on what has passed us in its like. So reflect. And Allah, exalted is He, is the Guide to the straight path, and He, exalted is He, is sufficient for us and the best Disposer of affairs.
